en: The Six-Limbed Yoga (*Ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), titled *Guṇabharaṇī*, together with its commentary on the Eight-Limbed Yoga (*Aṣṭāṅgayogatippaṇī*). Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
To him whose cloud-mass of all obscurations has been dispelled, and who is the wind that brings an end to the entire multitude of conceptual constructions—homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
Having paid homage to the Lord Śrī Kālacakra and to my gurus and the lineage of gurus for their qualities, I, [Abhayākaragupta],
compose here this *Ṭippaṇī* entitled *Guṇabharaṇī* on the glorious Six-Limbed Yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

Indeed, the teacher Anupamarakṣita— whose mental continuum was purified by the practice of both external and internal sciences— spent twelve years at the glorious Kha-sarpaṇa through the cultivation of the instruction on the reality of the "Cloudless" (*nirālambakalpa*) state.
And there, as he failed to attain any special realization and fell into a state of dejection, sleep overcame him; while he was thus asleep, Vajrayoginī gave him this instruction:

"Go, my son, to Vikramapura; there you will attain a special realization. Taking that command upon his head, and followed by the great paṇḍita Śrīdhara—the son of a virtuous man who had been his disciple at that time—he went to Vikramapura.

And on a certain festival day, at the hour of midnight, having assumed the *avadhūta* posture, he was directly instructed by the Blessed One: "O son, this is the reality. Upon merely receiving that instruction, he entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*). And at that very moment, the Blessed One vanished.
In the meantime, the night passed and he emerged from his absorption.

That great-souled and illustrious Guru [spoke]: "The venerable Sahakārin has arisen in the realm of space; like the full moon of the Lord of the World (*Lokeśvara*), he shines brilliantly in the world."

The illustrious Śrīdhara himself attained it and taught it; that illustrious Guru, being supremely compassionate, having found a worthy vessel in every respect, graciously bestowed his own realization upon the great scholar Bhāskaradeva. From him, the great scholar and illustrious Guru, the omniscient one in this age of degeneration (kaṣāyakāla), taught Dharmākaraśānti. And from that illustrious Guru—who is an ocean of jewels such as ineffable, irreproachable compassion and other virtues—I, Raviśrī, who am skillful in the service of the feet of the illustrious Guru, have likewise attained the reality. Such is the lineage of the Gurus.

Thus, at the request of a true disciple, the master named Anupamarakṣita, desiring to compose the *Ṣaḍaṅgayoga*—the cause for attaining the state of a Vajradhara—illuminated the *Ṣaḍaṅgayoga* by means of a hymn to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), beginning with the words "dispelled" (*nirasta*) and so forth.

In that [state], all obscurations (*sarvāvaraṇa*)—meaning those which cover everything—are dispelled and rejected. It is where the clouds, meaning masses of clouds, have vanished. Therein, by way of total enumeration—that is, completely—the conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is like a bird because it has the nature of wandering, or like the wind (*nabhasvān*) because it moves through space, has been utterly destroyed and eliminated.

And therefore, in his own space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), within the surface of the autumnal, stainless sky, the Buddha Lokīśvara has arisen and become manifest; or else it is Padmapāṇi, whose own light is a light of auspicious bliss. Because he gladdens all people, he is the full moon;
and everything [previously stated] regarding the moon should be applied here as well, with the specific meaning being that he is to be honored.

When the net of all clouds of obscurations has been cast aside and one is free from the superimposition of the grasped and the grasper, these two limbs of yoga—withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)—are described:

withdrawal is the non-engagement of the ten objects and their perceivers within the body; meditative concentration consists of discernment (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), delight (*rati*), and unwavering bliss (*acalasukha*), as well as one-pointedness of mind.

Thus, by means of the complete enumeration, he is the one who has reached the end, whose cessation is restrained, who is bound by the absence of outward emission, who is devoid of support for the pacification of *saṃsāra*, and who is non-different from those two— the all-pervasive Void (*śūnya*) which is also composed of compassion; he is the Lord of the Grounds who has transcended stability, as well as speech and conceptualization characterized by the eighty-four thousand moments of mind along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the winds of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, by whom and wherein [all this is held].
By this, the two limbs of *prāṇāyāma* and *dhāraṇā* have been stated;

thus, *prāṇāyāma* is the deviation from the two paths, as well as the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the central channel, the entry of the vital breath into the *bindu*, and indeed the cessation of both movements. And *dhāraṇā* is one-pointedness of mind.
Thus, one's own self is the mind; that itself is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the universal image (*viśvabimba*) perceived in all its aspects.
In this regard, the limb of recollection (*anusmṛtyaṅga*) has been explained by this.

And thus it is said: "The vision of Caṇḍālī occurs indeed within the body, and in the sky there shall be *anusmṛti*. Due to the touch of Caṇḍālī, that which has arisen from the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra is the "Self-Light" (*svāloka*) because it is a manifestation free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*).
It is the "Lord of the World" (*lokeśvara*) because it is the support for all worlds, and because it is held by all Buddhas upon their heads and at the tip of the vajra.
Because it consists of the semen of sixteen joys, it is the "full moon";
this is a compound [formed] subsequently, and by this, the limb of meditative concentration (samādhi) is also stated.
"Because of the power of the non-emitting bliss consisting of wisdom and means, there is meditative absorption in the image of gnosis"—
thus they say;
it shines forth and is victorious.
By this, the act of salutation is implied; from that, it is understood that one has bowed down toward him.
Now, demonstrating the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) by way of resolving apparent contradictions, he says:
"Yaḥ" and so forth:
that which is the "nātha" (protector) is *saṃsāra*, the continuous succession of birth and death, which is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

Quiescence is the cessation of those two; ultimate truth is the object of each of them respectively, because [the Protector] is devoid of both of them—conventional and ultimate truth—and is thus such.

Therefore, may that Protector, who bestows all happiness upon those who have come [to him], who is free from conceptual construction, who is without departure, and in whom thought has arisen as non-thought, adorn the mind of the world.

[kha] Having a slight conceptual grasping, he is like a crocodile with a firm grip for the sake of devouring; undivided and non-dual in form, he is "yoked in union" (*yuganaddha*) because the three worlds have a single nature. He is "all-pervading" (*vibhu*).

He is "empty" (*śūnya*) because he is luminous through the emptiness of the empty, the exceedingly empty, the great empty, and the all-empty; the meaning is that he transcends the nature of even the subtlest atom (*paramāṇu*).

Because he is endowed with the excellence of all aspects while being like a reflection in a mirror, he consists of compassion; the meaning is that he is both "possessing all aspects" and "devoid of aspects."

"Having transcended stability" means that his mind is unattached to objects through the yoga of non-abiding; he is "well-established. The stages (*bhūmi*) are specific states of the excellence of non-conceptual knowledge;
the Lord of these is the "Lord of the Twelve Stages."

Expanding and spreading all-encompassing bliss— the bliss of enjoying the five supreme unchanging sensual desires— to those who possess movement and who have penetrated the instruction of non-conceptual knowledge,
he is free from conceptual construction and devoid of dualities.
He is the "Exit" because of his imperishability; he is of an immovable nature;
he is the "Lord" (Nātha) because he is to be served by the world;
and he is "Someone" (Kaścit) because he is beyond the reach of speech.

May he adorn and preside over the mind of the world— the world-mind that is "devoid of mind" (vicitta), which arises as the "mind devoid of mind" (acittacitta); thus it is called the "arising of the mind devoid of mind" (vicittodaya).
The contradiction, however, is easily understood:
"The Guru is the Buddha, the Guru is the Dharma, and likewise the Guru is the Sangha;

the glorious Vajradhara is the Guru, for the Guru alone is the cause here. Thus, preceded by the proclamation of his truly existing qualities, he pays homage to the glorious Guru, the teacher of the unerring reality.
"Something" (*kiṃcit*) refers to the grasping of something as being merely a conceptual construction; it is the acceptance that "something exists," however slight.

"It exists" means the view of eternalism; it is a "firm grasp" because, being necessarily a cause of suffering, it leads to grasping for the sake of devouring— that is, for the experience of the sufferings of saṃsāra within the good realms.
And it has been said: "Even a thorn the size of a sesame seed inevitably causes pain. The sudden abandonment of that [thorn] produces a fall into the abyss for a very long time.

Thus, when the true path is lost, I joyfully and forever bow to that excellent Guru, who reveals the image of the sky—the nature of the sky-like compassion—which transcends the mind. Therefore, for such a great-souled Guru, the proclamation of his own awakening is indeed his true fame;
for a brilliant crest of smoke is not perceived apart from the fire whose form is flashing forth.
The abandonment of even that slightest trace of conceptual construction (*vikalpaleśa*) is the "abandonment of that"; the meaning is that it is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
That [abandonment] is "suddenly discarded" means it is abandoned without investigation; that is to say, it is the view of annihilationism.

Because it is the cause of suffering for infinite eons and because it is the cause of intense, great suffering, it is a "long-lasting precipice. It is both that and a precipice; it brings about the fall into the hells such as Avīci, or it produces it there, or it impels one toward it. And so it has been said:
"But those for whom emptiness is a [mere] view were declared incurable.
Thus, in this manner, when there is a collapse of the true path— that is, when the way to liberation is destroyed— [it is said].

I bow with body, speech, and mind, and always at the three times with joy and gladness, to that excellent Guru, the illustrious Guru, who bestows— upon his true disciples, it is implied— the orb of the sky, the universal image of all forms beginning with smoke, which transcends the mind, whose nature is non-mind-yet-mind, whose essence is the union of space and compassion, and which is inseparable from emptiness and mercy.

One might object: "If the discovery of the true path occurs solely through the grace of the venerable Guru, then one ought to do nothing but praise the qualities of the true Guru; why then have you set out to compose this treatise on the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*)?
To this he replies with the words beginning "tataḥ" (therefore).

Since it is so, therefore—on account of that—the praising of such a Guru, the great-souled one who teaches the path as it truly is and whose nature is supreme compassion, namely the manifestation of his qualities, is indeed the proclamation of one's own awakening; it is precisely the making manifest of the knowledge belonging to oneself which was obtained through the Guru’s grace.
He states this very point by means of an illustrative corroboration (arthāntaranyāsa):
For, since no one who is aware [of the facts] would consider anything other than Dhanañjaya, whose form is ever-shining, to be the cause of my success;
how could a person proceed toward the accomplishment of their desired goal when the speaker of an example remains uncertain?

Those practitioners whose minds are arrogant regarding the realization of the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) have abandoned the path; due to their dull wisdom, these ministers do not perceive even the prohibitions through the gateway of the ritual injunctions.
Without the blazing fire, the crest of smoke—though brilliant and firmly rooted—is not perceived.
By this it is stated: "It is solely through the grace of the venerable Guru that I possess the skill to compose this work."

"Is it not the case that for you, who have attained the path of reality (tattvamārga) free from all conceit, how can there be the attainment of knowledge of reality? [It would be] an inflation of the mind. To this, he states the rebuttal: "No. The ellipsis is: "The pride of my awakening does not become a cause of fault."
Because it accomplishes the welfare of others by acting as an incentive for those seeking liberation.
This is the meaning:

my revelation of knowledge is not out of a desire for gain and so forth; rather, it is for the purpose of inciting those who fear the terrors of existence by demonstrating the nature of the means [to liberation].
He states the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle):

When some matter, which is the cause for action, has been cited—that is, spoken of—and remains undetermined or doubtful, how can a person who is himself uncertain proceed toward the speaker or the proponent for the sake of attaining his desired goal? The meaning is that he certainly cannot; or rather, [it refers to] when a statement connected to the speaker or the proponent has been cited.

Those of poor counsel who, through the commentaries and other works composed by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) on various tantras, possess minds arrogant in their understanding of the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), go to hell.

However, through the commentary composed by the noble Avalokiteśvara, there is the realization of the distinction between the provisional and definitive meanings (*neya-nītārtha*) within the *Śrī-laghukālacakra-tantra-rāja*. Thus, illuminating the majesty of this sovereign tantra, he says: "The provisional... and so forth.
The interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) is the meaning according to the literal expression.
Those who have abandoned the path are unskilled in distinguishing between the conventional and the ultimate.

Precisely because of this dullness of wisdom, they do not understand the negations that are presented by way of affirmation; having considered this, by the command of the glorious Vajradhara—the command of the Blessed Lord Kālacakra—the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī spoke the *Śrīlaghukālacakra-bhagavat-tantra* and recited it in the land of Sambhala.
By this, the greatness of the illustrious Vajrapāṇi—the requester, who is effectively both the teacher and the compiler—is illuminated.
By the command of the glorious Vajradhara, for the sake of the three worlds, the Lord Mañjuśrī spoke the Bhagavat Laghukālacakra Tantra in lucid verses.

Wherein the glorious and most compassionate Lord, the Blessed One Lokeśvara, has manifested himself and composed this commentary (*ṭīkā*) called *Vimalaprabhā* with perfectly pure words and all meaningful purposes;

indeed, having obtained that *Buddharatnahṛdaya* revealed therein, those of meritorious nature, by partaking of the nectar of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), shatter the poison of cyclic existence and rejoice.

In that abode of all objects of knowledge, which possesses the designation "Omniscient One" for the Blessed One and is the source of the true nature of reality, even the Perfection of Wisdom—which utterly destroys the tree of all emerging conceptual constructions—is but a blade of grass compared to that which was proclaimed by Īśvara and others; for it is the mother of the Buddha, the pure-souled one who has arisen from the sky.
Regarding the term "the Glorious One" (*śrīmān*):
in this Great Tantra, there is the one named Śrī Puṇḍarīka, who is an emanation-body (*nirmitakāya*) of Lokeśvara.
He is [called] "by all purposes" (*sarvārthaiḥ*) because he indicates all purposes.
And it has been said:

"A commentary (*tīkā*) indicates all meanings. He composed the commentary named *Vimalaprabhā*. By means of that commentary, they clarify and manifest the Heart of the Buddha-jewel, which is the essence of the instruction on the true path. Having received this from the presence of the venerable Guru, who is a treasury of merit, and through the service of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), by attaining the nectar of the supreme fourth bliss (*paramārthacaturthānanda*), they shatter the poison of existence—the great poison of the cycle of birth and death—and lead it to the state of the supreme syllable (*paramākṣaratā*).
For this very reason, they always rejoice because the bliss of their constant enjoyment is uninterrupted; by this, he also illuminates the greatness of the commentator.
Furthermore, it demonstrates the majesty of the Sovereign Tantra (*tantrādhirāja*).
Regarding the word "all" (*sarva*):
it refers to the locus, that is, the foundation, of the entire collection of fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), both external and internal, which is to be known by the Omniscient One.
And it has been said:
"There is nothing that was not taught in the Ādibuddha,
wherein [is contained] the Bhagavān Buddha in this king of tantras."
The notion of "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) is the designation "the All-Knowing. It was meaningful and followed the true purpose.

And therein, the reality of existence (*sattattva*), which is a mine of jewels, rendered the doctrines propounded by Īśvara and others as worthless as straw, because they were merely floating away and lacked essence.
The Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is also the practice of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*).

It is that [Perfection] in which there is the destruction of all those trees of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which, when they open up and become thick, [otherwise proliferate]—and wherein occurs the state of being of one flavor with the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara-samarasībhāva*).
She is the mother, the progenitor of the Buddha who arises from space, who arises as the universal reflection, the pure self whose form is unstained by any conceptual construction.
When he fashioned that half-eye in the stainless sky, from a heart moistened by the radiance of vast compassion,

there suddenly arose— unbreakable by the conceptualization of existence, non-existence, both, or neither— the entire sequence of smoke and other signs of emptiness, which consumes all that is based on grasping.

[jha] Thus, for the sake of clarifying the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*), in accordance with the cultivation of the path of Mahāmudrā, [the author] speaks the jewel of words from the *Śrīmad-Ādibuddha-tantra* and other sources regarding the Perfectly Awakened One. Now, teaching the tradition of the venerable Guru (*śrīgurusaṃpradāya*), which is the basis for the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) and the cause for the arising of the signs beginning with smoke, he says:
"In the stainless," and so forth. In that stainless sky (*vimalanabhas*), which is free from obstructions such as clouds;
When the emanation is directed by being suspended in the intermediate space,

and when the half-eyes— the eyes half-closed and half-open— are active, then from a heart that is moist with great, throbbing compassion, one consumes— that is, renders devoid of intrinsic nature— the substratum, which is the conceptual mind;
therefore, by this, the oral tradition is stated.
And it has been said:
"In darkness, one should not think of anything at all"—this is the general instruction. And elsewhere:
Having uprooted the very root of the mind and performed the rubbing in emptiness—
what medicine could be greater than this for those blinded by the cataracts of ignorance?
Thus it was said by Saraha-pāda as well:
"One should regard all phenomena as being like space, even unto death."
One should maintain the state of being as vast as space;
that too should be practiced without effort,
and thereby supreme enlightenment is attained.
That which bestows the fruit of the two accumulations is summarized here from the *Ādibuddha*, the king of tantras, which is the jewel-casket of the Buddhas.

For the identity of the first and last letters [A and HA] is like that of the moon and the sun; the seat of the Thunderbolt-Holder is not merely the syllable HŪṂ, nor is another transformed form of color desired.
This is because for this divine sense-faculty—which has arisen from the letter and reached the end of flux—it is said by this [text] that the cause is both with-form and formless in every respect.

The remainder [of the statement] is that self-experience (*svānubhava*) arises spontaneously, without depending on the causes of conceptual construction, as it pierces through the existence and non-existence of both being and non-being, and is free from the four extremes such as being and non-being;
arising— that is, being produced— it follows all ten signs such as smoke and so forth, and thus belongs to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

In the *Jñānapaṭala* of the *Kālacakra*, following the one hundred and twenty-six verses, there is a verse beginning with "oneness" (*ekatvam*) and so forth, which elucidates the unity of the relative and ultimate truths and illuminates the stages of generation (*utpannakrama*).

Since there is a negation of the conceptualization of the form, color, arms, and configuration of the signs produced from the transformation of the *hūṃ* syllable—which rests upon the lotus, moon, and sun of the *āli* and *kāli*—and of the innate body (*sahajakāya*) arising from the syllables, it is therefore called the Blessed One’s accomplishment of the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*).

The "beginning" (*ādi*) is the collection of vowels beginning with *a*, which is the moon; the "ka-group" (*kādi*) is the collection of consonants beginning with *ka*, which is the sun. Their "oneness" (*ekatva*) is their unification. The "seat" (*āsana*) is the support: the lotus consisting of the consonant *pa*, the lunar mandala consisting of the vowel *a*, and the solar mandala consisting of the letter *ra*.

For the Vajrins who possess the knowledge of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), [the notion that] it is "not" is rejected; likewise, the symbol of the vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, and the dharma consisting of the conceptualization of the body, color, arms, faces, and shape of the deity transformed from that [vajra], are not accepted as having the characteristic of a support (*ādheya*),
because they possess a perishable nature due to their being characterized by dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*).

Of the supreme Lord of Jinas, Vajrasattva—the *bindu* which has arisen through the syllable (*akṣara*), the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*); which, for that reason, has reached the cessation of emission (*kṣara-nidhana*); which is devoid of forms and so forth imagined by ordinary people; which is free from arising and cessation; which possesses divine faculties; which is produced through mastery over the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); which possesses all aspects; and whose nature is the bliss of the three worlds.

Of the Holder of Universal Illusion— the Supreme Victor who possesses all forms, whose bindu is the universal illusion, the universal mother, the Great Seal (mahāmudrā)— of that Holder of Universal Illusion. [LKC V]

Since this is so, therefore, a yogin who delights in the means for achieving supreme immutable bliss—one who has received the instructions of a true guru, has abandoned evil company, has cultivated the signs such as smoke and so forth, is a beginner, has purified the central channel, whose mind is bound by supreme affection for all sentient beings as if they were an only son, who relies upon the mundane and supramundane truths, is indifferent toward his own body, children, wife, and so on, is excluded from the enjoyment of the property of the monastery, the vihāra, or the guru, relies on the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, dwells in the four sublime abodes of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, is free from the desire to achieve mundane accomplishments such as rites of pacification and the like, has received the instructions of a true guru, and has obtained the glorious lineage of the gurus—[should practice].
By one who is free from the eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), who has avoided evil friends (*pāpamitra*),

who has cultivated the signs such as smoke because he has cultivated those signs of smoke and so forth, who is uniquely skilled in stabilizing the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) because he is a beginner (*ādikarmika*),
and who has purified the central channel because the middle [channel] has been purified.
And it has been said: "Having meditated upon smoke and the other [signs], having made the mind immovable,
and having purified the central channel, one should meditate upon the supreme syllable."
A *matha* is a residence for [holding] parasols and other such items;
a *vihāra* is the dwelling belonging to the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃghika*).
Just as all-aspect emptiness exists within the universal image in the element of space, so too is there a mirror therein, like a reflection or like the thought of the practitioner.

By means of the vision of non-arisen phenomena—that is, by one who has vision regarding phenomena that are free from conceptual construction—because external objects imagined by foolish people do not exist, and because the mind perceives objects as manifestations of its own mental projections similar to a dream; and because it does not fall within the positions of the Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, or Yogācāra schools; and because it is empty of any investigation into phenomena consisting of an aggregation of atoms.
Because he has distanced himself from the doctrine of nihilism by keeping far away from entering the Cārvāka school, he is one who has distanced himself from the emptiness of annihilation.

One who desires to ascend to the state of omniscience through the very bliss of the inner self (*adhyātmasukha*), which is divine and supreme, must abandon the cultivation of conceptualizations such as the maṇḍala-circle and so forth. By beholding all-aspect emptiness (*sarvākāraśūnyatā*) within the expanse of space like a reflection in a mirror or a prognostic image (*pratisenā*), one perceives unarisen phenomena. With a mind that views objects as being like a dream—a manifestation of the radiation of one’s own mind—one is empty of any investigation into phenomena consisting of an aggregation of atoms. Having distanced oneself from the emptiness of nihilism (*ucchedaśūnyatā*), one is devoted to the phenomena of self-cognizable internal bliss and has abandoned the phenomena of bliss cognizable by the external senses. Being of the nature of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*), and uniquely skilled in stabilizing the bodhicitta, one has obtained the instruction on the path of the wisdom-knowledge of supreme immutable great bliss (*paramākṣaramahāsukhaprajñājñāna*). For such a person, the dharma of conceptualizing deities—consisting of the support and the supported, along with their signs, colors, arms, and postures—is not desired.

Likewise, one who is devoid of the path does not attain that reality which was proclaimed by the Tathāgata— the Dharma which is blissful and personally realized. Therefore, being devoted to that [Dharma], one should, through non-attachment to the bliss arising from the karmic and gnosis wombs, arrest the movement of the drops (*bindu*) of the external senses within the wheels (*cakra*), and restrain those drops within the *vajra*.
Thus,
with a mind constantly absorbed in Mahāmudrā,

or by means of the series of Āryā verses spoken in the *Vimalaprabhā* beginning with "tathā" and so forth, he illuminates the majesty of this king of paths; now, he speaks of the failure to attain reality for one who has strayed from the path.

Regarding the passage beginning with "tathā mārge" (thus, by the path), that which was taught by the Tathāgata—the sixteenfold fourfold division—is the fourth reality (*tattva*). The non-yogi does not attain it through the path of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and so forth. "Various conceptual constructions" refers to the transformation of the lotus, sun, moon, Rāhu, Kālāgni, seed-syllables, and hand-symbols; the faces, arms, colors, and postures; the *vīrakrama*, the *svādhiṣṭhānakrama*, and so on.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes] the doctrine of the emptiness of the annihilation of all phenomena. Thus, the sixteenfold fourfold division [is not attained] by means of the path of various conceptual constructions and so forth.

The yoga of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), which is free from conceptualizations such as the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* and is described as the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), is the reality; there is no other means for realizing that reality.

This reality is made manifest in the chapter on initiation: first, the bliss of desire (*kāmānanda*), which is trembling and characterized by the syllable *A*; through the fourfold yoga, it becomes the arising of power (*śakti*) and is indeed the second, supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), consisting of the flame (*jvālā*), the drop (*bindu*), and the whirling (*ghūrmā*). Thus, the third is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), where the piercing (*oddā*) and resonance (*nāda*) become sleep. Thus, the fourth is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
Therefore, that reality is not [attained] by the path of conceptual construction.
Nor can that which is called "non-reality" serve as a means of proof for reality;
if this is not a means of proof, what else could it be? To this, he says:
"In its arising," and so forth.

The "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) is that by which reality (*tattva*), namely great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is accomplished; it is reality itself and nothing else. It is not the conceptualization of a lotus and so forth.

What is that reality? It is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) as previously described, devoid of the sequence of entering the womb, consisting of the mantra "HŪM PHAṬ," and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the conceptualization of mudrās and so forth.
To the question, "What is that reality devoid of this? he says: "the yoga of the stage of completion" (*utpannakramayoga*).
"Completion" (*utpanna*) means perfected; it is accessible through the meditation on space. Its "stage" (*krama*) is the path beginning with smoke and so forth.
Its yoga is the union with the reflection of wisdom (*prajñābimba*), which is the arising of the knowledge of the immutable (*akṣarajñāna*).
Now, with two noble verses, [the author] speaks of the means for seeing the bodhicitta that is accompanied by a visible object, as well as the rejection of non-means,
beginning with the words "situated in wood" (*kāṣṭhastha*) and so forth.
Just as fire, though always present within wood, is not seen [as such], yet is seen there through means such as cutting, splitting, and the friction of reeds,
stalks, or hands; even so [is the Self].
Just as that [object] is not seen by means of conceptual cultivation, so too the appearance of the mind is not seen; it is seen only there through the singular union of the *lalanā* and *rasanā*.
It is perceived through breath control (prāṇāyāma) characterized by smoke and other signs via the central channel (madhyavāha);
let it be that for now it is not perceived when without support— the meaning of the word "even" (api) is that it is [perceived] even when situated within wood—
by means of methods such as cutting and splitting.
The third case is used for the instrument,
as in "cutting with axes and the like" (*kuthārādibhiḥ*) or "splitting with tree-splitters and the like" (*vṛkṣabhidādibhiḥ*).
The shaft is the means, the arrowhead is the door, the stock is the staff, and the hand is the fist.
By means of those two [the upper and lower parts of the fire-drill], that fire is produced; "situated therein" (*tatrastha*) means it abides within those pieces of wood used for churning.

Like that [fire], the "appearance of the mind" (*cittābhāsa*)—which is the perception of the three realms—is not seen by means of the methods of conceptual cultivation (*kalpabhāvanopāyaiḥ*), which consist in repeatedly bringing conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) before one's mind through the gateways of mental engagement.
"That appearance of mind is seen through the single union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*"—
here the third case (*tr̥tīyā*) denotes the instrument; "single union" means non-dual union, and that occurs in that very place, namely, within one's own mind.
It has been stated in the *Paramārthasevā*:

"Let those who are worthy take firewood from wood, water even from a moonstone, curd and ghee from [the milk of] cows, and iron ore from stones; and let them obtain unimpaired bliss from union with the female organ through the application of the appropriate means."
In the mind, nothing is to be removed, nor is anything to be added; there is neither decrease nor increase in the mind.
The triple world is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, like the reflection of the sun upon water.
Thus,
the meaning is that the single mind, when reflected in the mirror of wisdom, becomes manifold;
demonstrating this very point, he says:

Since this is so, therefore, that which was stated both collectively and individually—that [the practice] is for those who have attained the five limbs beginning with withdrawal (pratyāhāra) in order to clarify the branches of meditation (dhyānāṅga) and is uniquely skilled in stabilizing the bodhicitta—is accomplished by means of the vidyā-vow (*vidyāvrata*) alone, through the "vajra-fall" (*vajrāpāta*), by which the semen flows upward.
By this path, the yogin easily attains the supreme unchanging accomplishment of all Buddhas, or the innate [state] of all female messengers.
Thus he says "smoke," and so forth:
that for which smoke is the beginning is the "cause" (nimitta); by that cause, the intended cognition is indicated.
Prāṇāyāma is *kumbhaka* consisting of the restraint of the three channels— above and below—
which is the entry of the movement of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) into the channel of the mind (*cittanāḍī*) by means of the central flow.
The "vow of knowledge" (*vidyāvrata*) is the vow in which knowledge is primary, namely, celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
A consort who has been consecrated by her own victor, who possesses virtuous qualities, should be accepted by the Guru; furthermore, according to the *Abhidhānottara*,
one may also obtain a Pukkasi adorned with beauty and youth.
She who has practiced through the single yoga, who knows the ritual observances, and whose vows are firm.
The knower of mantras himself should practice the vow of knowledge together with her, who is shameless, free from desire, steadfast, devoid of thirst, and without egoism.
Thus, from that, by the "vajra-fall"— that is, by the paralyzing descent of the vajra.
"By means of the upward-pointing semen," it is said, refers to that which has gone from the *maṇipadma* to the forehead by way of reverse movement; and thus,
the yogi should always have a stiff *liṅga* and always be one whose semen flows upwards (*ūrdhvaretas*).
Through devotion to Mahāmudrā, he is empowered by vajra-possessions.
And with twenty-one thousand six hundred supreme syllables.
Thus [it is said].

By means of this path characterized by the six-limbed yoga beginning with smoke (*dhūma*), the practitioner who possesses the yoga of the arisen sequence attains the innate (*sahaja*). This is the bliss of all Buddhas, which is beyond the senses and the means for accomplishing the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*); for by that [path], the supreme unchanging is accomplished—that is, brought to completion—everywhere.
It is said that the "innate" is the void of the *dākinīs*, who are the seventy-two thousand channels whose nature has been ceased.
The Innate (*sahaja*) is devoid of the three realms and is the Unstruck (*anāhata*); it does not consist of the fourth enclosure (*turyāvaraṇa*) according to worldly convention.
For unity is said to exist in the Void (*śūnya*) because of the departure of all coverings; such is the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*).

Through the conceptualizations of form and so forth, and through the practice of meditating on the mandala circle and other such things, worldly accomplishment is achieved; how much more so, then, the desired great accomplishment?
The path arises for pure disciples through the grace of the true guru.

Now, since it has been stated that the yoga of the arisen stage (*utpannakrama*) is the reality (*tattva*) and that there is no means to reality other than this, one might ask: "Let that alone suffice; what is the use of anything else that is of no practical benefit? To this, he says "form," and so forth.

The world (*loka*) is the triple realm (*traidhātuka*); that which exists therein is "worldly" (*laukikī*), and this is also "attainment" (*siddhi*). Thus, attainment is the sovereignty up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven that is accomplished through the mental constructions of form and so forth. Form (*rūpa*) is so called because it is "shaped" (*rūpyate*) or "afflicted" (*bādhyate*); that which has this as its primary object is its "construction" (*kalpana*), which is a mental action (*mānasa-karma*). In this context, the cultivation of form is the *karmamudrā*.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), knowledge is intended; its cultivation is the *jñānamudrā*. Through the practice of meditating on the mandala circle and so forth—wherein the "mandala" is the characteristic of the support (*ādhāra*) and the "circle" is the collection of deities which is the supported (*ādheya*)—and by the word "and so forth," mantra, mudrā, posture (*āsana*), and so on are included. Their "cultivation" is the act of bringing them into presence; their "practice" is repeated engagement and intense application.
If this is so, then by this very path all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are achieved.
"Enough with the instruction on the path of smoke and so forth," he says;
"what is it? It is the "great accomplishment" (*mahāsiddhi*), which is the accomplishment of *Mahāmudrā*. Is it desired? It is supramundane.
What more is there to say? The meaning is that without the instruction on the path of smoke and so forth, this accomplishment simply does not exist.

Now, one might ask: does this instruction on the path arise for everyone whose minds are intent upon attaining perfect enlightenment from every [source], or rather only for certain pure ones who are diligent in their enthusiasm for accomplishing the welfare of the world from some [specific source]? To this, he says "The path," and so forth.
The true guru is the venerable Guru; his characteristics have been explained in detail through the service of the ultimate reality (paramārtha), as follows:

he is a meditator liberated from attachment to worldly meditation, yet one who possesses desire with a mind bound to the great desire; he is a keeper of the great vow, whose passion remains undestroyed even in the engagement with a mudrā during the union of the bliss of the two organs.

Expert in the paths of the moon and sun, having entered the fire of wisdom through the power of yoga, he is the sprinkling of the nectar of infinite bliss; that glorious Guru is the Vajra-holder, the destroyer of evil.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
His clarity of mind consists in his favoring them with instruction in reality;
from that [clarity], may there arise in him compassion for sentient beings and a constant exertion toward the welfare of others.
This jewel of the excellent path, given to another heedless being,
is carried away by the thieves of evil sense-objects as he has entered the forest of his own home.
The jewel of the excellent path is stolen by the thieves of doubt, remorse, sleep, laziness, and restlessness for one who has entered the thicket of the household.

Thus it arises for certain pure disciples; "pure" refers to those disciples whose stains of ordinary ego-clinging have been eliminated through empowerments (*sekha*) and so forth, and who are to be instructed in performing the welfare of others and other such duties.
As it is said in the *Mahāmudrātilaka*:
"Just as poison, when being purified by means of mantras and so forth, becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*)."
In the same way, through the consecrations and other rites, the impure disciple becomes pure.
Thus,
their endeavor for the welfare of others' affairs is called "noble enthusiasm."
Now, [the author] speaks of "others" and so forth, in order to show the cause for the loss of the path for those who have now attained it but are negligent.
This aforementioned Buddhahood is the "path" (mārga), because by means of it, [Buddhahood] is easily sought or pursued.

It is called a *ratna* because it extends delight (*rati*), like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*); it is a jewel because it is difficult to find and because it bestows the fruit of one's desired aims. Furthermore, it is a "jewel of the excellent path" (*sumārgaratna*). Subsequently, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*): a *sattva* is one who is heedless, acting with negligence, indifferent to welfare and happiness, and who sinks into the lower realms (*sadgati*).

For another person who is devoid of qualities such as compassion and whose mind is not intent upon the welfare and happiness of others, his own home— wherein he has entered— is itself a forest inhabited by cruel creatures, even if it be with a wife.

"By the thieves of evil objects": objects (*viṣaya*) are those things such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth that intoxicate the senses; they are external enjoyments. They are "evil" (*ku*) because they provide little relish, because they are adverse [to liberation], and because one serves unrighteousness with a mind of infatuation (*mūrchā*). These very things are "thieves" (*caura*); for even the jewel of the excellent path, once given, is stolen—that is, carried away—by them.

Not only is the jewel of the excellent path stolen from one who has entered the forest of his own home by these [faults], but for one who has entered the thicket of the household, the household—consisting of wife, children, grandchildren, and so forth—is stolen by the thieves of doubt and the like; and the thicket of the forest is [stolen] by the three [unwholesome actions]: killing, false speech, and taking what is not given, as well as adultery, harsh speech, and slander.
And by the thieves of divisive speech, covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.
By these five thieves— namely, major sins, minor sins, killing, malice, and attachment to the sense faculties— the jewel is constantly carried away.
Furthermore, even when the jewel of the Excellent Path has been ascertained through conditions, there is doubt (*saṃśaya*) or hesitation (*vicikitsā*), such as "Is this the Excellent Path or not?";
there is remorse (*kaukṛtya*) characterized by the thought, "A despicable deed was committed by me; therefore, I shall not realize the Path";
and there is sleep (*nidrā* or *svāpa*), which is to say, *styāna-middha*, characterized by the production of unfitness in body and mind.

Laziness, lack of enthusiasm, restlessness, and mental distraction— meaning the wandering of the mind toward cities and such— are these impediments to meditative concentration (samādhi) described by this noble verse for those cultivating the path.
Not only is the jewel of the excellent path carried away by these similar factors, but it is also carried away by [the ten non-virtues] such as the taking of life; thus,
at all times throughout the three periods, [one must guard it].
Taking life is the killing of a sentient being;
falsehood is speaking untruth;
and taking what is not given is the seizing of another's property.
Adultery is sexual misconduct; harsh speech is the wounding of another's vital points;
malicious speech is the utterance intended to divide others by one with an afflicted mind.
Frivolous speech is speech associated with sensual desires and so forth, such as "Alas! Oh! Come here! which generates passion;
covetousness is improper longing for the property of others;
and malice is the intent to kill.
A false view is the view of non-existence.
Likewise, there are the five major evils, namely the five beginning with violence;
the five minor evils; and the five [evils] beginning with gambling.
The five beginning with the killing of a cow, the five beginning with treachery against a friend,

and the five consisting of attachment to the sense organs such as the eyes— since these constitute its measure, they are called "the five-folds" (pañcaka); and by those very five [groups], it is like "by the five thieves."
For thus:
abandon violence, untruth, another’s wife, another’s wealth, and likewise the drinking of intoxicants; these five are the vajra-noose in saṃsāra, the destruction of one’s own merit, and evil.

One should not commit these five killings—of gambling, eating forbidden food, reciting wicked words, [killing] the lords of the spirits and daityas, and [killing] cows, children, women, and men—nor should one act with excessive eating and drinking, various enjoyments, or through those many thieves, O Teacher of Gods and Men.
Even one who possesses vigor is carried away when he has fallen into the stupor of negligence.
For an examiner himself should not show another's jewel so that he may know whether it is of great value or not; rather, he releases the jewel from that person's words.
Betrayal of friends, masters, and the Teacher of gods and men; and attachment to the senses—these, O Lord of the World, are the twenty-five vows.
Thus,
it is declared that even for those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, this evil karma— which causes obstacles— is here understood to be included.
Not only is the jewel of mindfulness carried away by these, but also by excessive eating and drinking and various enjoyments; here, "eating" refers to the consumption of meat,
"drinking" to the drinking of liquor and the like, and "enjoyments" refers to things such as garlands and sandalwood paste, which are experienced excessively through worldly dharma.

"Various and manifold" refers to even one who possesses vigor (*vīryavat*) and is enthusiastic about cultivating the path—not only for the one previously mentioned who lacks vigor, but for the vigorous one as well; this is the meaning of the word "even" (*api*).

"Negligence" (*pramāda*) consists of excessive eating and drinking, as well as association with unwholesome friends. Because of that, for one whose mind has reached a state of stupor and impairment, [the roots of merit] are indeed carried away.
It has been stated that attachment to existence, enjoyments, and so forth, acts as an obstacle even for those who perform wholesome deeds.

Now, one might object: "If these faults that create obstacles have been described with reference to one who examines the jewel of the path, what then is the situation for one who does not examine that path himself? To this he says, "Himself," and so forth.

Because he himself is not an examiner, he shows it to another, someone else who is an expert appraiser and a doer of great merit, so that [the latter] may know, "This is a highly precious great jewel.
That person says, "It is not so"; therefore, because of those words—that speech of the expert—he simply lets go of it.
In exactly the same way, one has those who are experts in fine jewels perform the examination of the great jewel for them.

Indeed, by means of their pure words, one’s own jewel should be recognized. [15] Māra creates obstacles through the forms of fully awakened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as those of fathers, mothers, daughters, sisters, sons, brothers, and wives. [16]
Therefore, disciples must diligently keep secret the jewel of the excellent path bestowed by the true guru, having abandoned the company of thieves.

[17] One of a foolish nature may abandon even the priceless jewel of the excellent path once obtained, due to the words of evil friends; thus, the fault of associating with evil friends is stated even for those seeking to examine the path.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can the jewel of the path be known by one who does not examine it himself?"—it is true. However, if one causes a great examination of the jewel to be conducted by those who are experts in fine jewels, then through their pure words and non-deceptive speech, it is clearly known and ascertained that "this is priceless. In exactly the same way, a son of noble family who has attained the path should, having examined it through the words of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), realize "this is priceless," and should follow it and not abandon it. Thus, for those cultivating the path, reliance upon a spiritual friend is superior.

Thus, even for one who has set out upon the cultivation of the path, the mind does not become stable without abandoning the activities of Māra; therefore, demonstrating this very point, he says "Māra," and so forth.

For Māra, the Evil One, manifests in the form of a Buddha or others and creates obstacles for the practitioner, such as saying, "This is not the path to enlightenment; no one has ever emerged by means of this," and so on. This should be understood from the *Mārakarmaparivarta*.

Having thus introduced the fault of the deeds of Māra and summarizing everything, he says "therefore," and so forth: Because this exists as a cause for the theft of the path, therefore, having abandoned the "thieves' family"—which is a figurative term for doubt and the like—one must diligently keep secret the jewel of the path bestowed by a true guru. The Heroic Stage (*vīrakrama*) is not the path; the Self-Consecration Stage (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) is also not [the path]; rather, the Single Most Pure Stage (*suviśuddhakrama*) alone has been shown by the Buddhas for the sake of liberation. [18]

By means of which bliss even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution are gathered; for that purpose of consecration (*seka*), the Lords of Jinas [taught] the tantra consisting of wisdom and method.
[19] The "Heroic Progression" (*vīrakrama*) is not external; it is indeed said to be the destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body.
Self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the three realms within emptiness. [20]

Regarding the phrase "by the disciples," the protection of the path has been explained. Now, one might ask: "Is there not yet another path for liberation? To this he says, "The *vīra*-sequence," and so forth. The *vīra*-sequence consists of taking as its objective support the worship of external fierce deities and the like. The *svādhiṣṭhāna*-sequence consists of taking as its objective support the bliss of yoga with peaceful deities by means of the mind. These were not taught by the Buddhas for the sake of liberation. If so, which one was taught? He says:
The stage of perfect purity is one; the yoga of the stage of completion is without a second.
If it is asked, "How is this known? he says, "By happiness," and so forth;
for by that reason, all those who have committed the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) were gathered together and brought [to liberation] by the Lords of Jinas.
The immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are the killing of one’s mother, father, or an Arhat; causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
and drawing blood from a Tathāgata with a malicious mind.
Because one remains in the Avīci hell for exactly one eon immediately after committing any one of these, they are called "immediate" (*ānantarya*).
By means of bliss, by means of the method of bliss, and by means of the fourth [empowerment] for the sake of consecration;

otherwise, for those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, there is the cessation of fierce karma through the *vīrakrama* (heroic method), and liberation is attained through *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which increases the continuity of the habitual tendencies toward the happiness of cyclic existence— for that reason.

Now, if it is asked: "If these two stages called the Hero’s Empowerment (*vīrādhiṣṭhāna*) are considered to be indeed the non-sequential (*akrama*), then for what purpose were they spoken by the Blessed One? he says: "The Hero," and so forth. For since this [empowerment] has been stated to be the exhaustion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body, therefore the stage of the Hero is not external. Now, if it is argued: "In that case, let the Empowerment (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) be clearly established externally," [the answer is] no. Why? Because the Empowerment of one's own mind is its manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), and that is the vision of the triple world within emptiness. The fruit is Buddhahood, which is without saṃsāra and without essence; it arises from the exhaustion of that [manifestation]. Therefore, for persons...
Like a ripe plantain fruit, it comes into being through the destruction of the plantain;
just as scorpions and crabs are destructive to that [plantain], so too does that mind of yoga perish through illusion. [21–22]

Non-dual, immovable, and without succession, it is held to be the supreme syllable, the great passion (mahārāga), well-known as "Me. Thus has been stated the establishment of the stage of perfect purity for those who act for the benefit of the world.

Now, one might ask: since it has been said that the vision of the three realms is self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), and because that vision does not cease, how can Buddhahood—which is characterized by the cessation of saṃsāra—possibly come to be? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "saṃsāra" and so forth:

within saṃsāra—the triple world which is characterized by falsehood and deception—Buddhahood, whose nature consists of the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience, becomes the essential fruit (*sāra*). This occurs through its exhaustion; that is, immediately upon the exhaustion of saṃsāra.

To the question "In what manner?", he says: "Like the fruit of the plantain tree. Just as when the plantain tree is devoid of essence, the ripe fruit becomes the essence through the destruction of the plantain tree, so too is Buddhahood.

Now, it might be argued: "Since it is stated that 'the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is the means for attaining Buddhahood' and 'the reality (tattva) is the means for attaining reality,' and since that [thought] arises from illusion and exists as ignorance (avidyā), which is not reality, how can it be the means for attaining Buddhahood? To this, he says "scorpion," and so forth.

Just as scorpions, thorny insects, crabs, and *karkaṭa* [crabs] are destructive to whichever mother they belong to, so too is that mind—which is the fourth consecration (*caturthābhiṣeka*) arising from recollection—destructive to that illusion which possesses the nature of ignorance and death. Through the cessation of illusion, the non-returning of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is taught for the sake of encouraging those who practice reality (*tattva-yogin*).
Now, is it not the case that "bodhicitta" here refers to the seminal essence (*śukradhātu*)?
How then is the accomplishment of non-inert Buddhahood, which is the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣarajñāna*), explained?
It is indeed correctly explained by the statement:
"One should accomplish the supreme unchanging through the nature of the immutable seminal essence (*śukrākṣara*)."
Therefore, revealing this very reality—the mind of yoga—in its form as the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*) with its sixteen and fourfold divisions, he says "non-dual" and so forth:
duality is existence and non-existence; non-duality is gnosis, the *sattva*, and Samantabhadra. [23]
The passionless and the great passion, the innate, the bearer of the drops of the glorious *bodhicitta*, the glorious *Kālacakra-vajra*, the yoga whose nature consists of wisdom and means.
Thus, this Vajrayoga has been practiced, taught, and chanted by immeasurable Sugatas, and by all the Bodhisattvas who hold the supreme thunderbolt and are knowers of mantra.

At the outset, the guru who is to be served is one who observes the commitments (*samaya*), is mounted upon the Vajrayāna, meditates on reality (*tattva*), is free from greed, devoid of defilement, possessed of patience, established on the path, the giver of the way to disciples, the remover of the fear of hell, a true celibate (*brahmacārī*), and a vajra-staff against the Māras; he is renowned on the surface of the earth as Vajrasattva.
Because he does not waver from the lotus, he is called "Immovable" (*acala*).
It is called "without lineage" (*ananvaya*) because it lacks a lineage consisting of the portions of wisdom and means;
it is desired as such because it bestows unsurpassed bliss. This is the fourth yoga, the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*), resulting from the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths.

Because there is neither staying nor going between passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*), which are white and black respectively, he is Great Passion (*mahārāga*). Because he is liberated from both form and formlessness, he is the absence of existence and non-existence. Because he perceives all that is to be known, he is Knowledge (*jñāna*). This is the third yoga.

Because he is unattached to the welfare of sentient beings preceded by bringing joy to the world, he is the Benefactor of Beings (*sattva*). Because he brings about excellence in the beginning, middle, and end, he is Samantabhadra.

Because he is free from the conceptual constructions of Māra and the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no conflict (*raṇa*)—that is, no internal or external verbal discourse, nor any battle consisting of the roar of a lion that is purified and liberated. Thus, he is "without conflict" (*araṇa*). Because his nature is the sound of the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*), he possesses a great conflict; thus, he is "of great conflict" (*mahāraṇa*). This is the second yoga. Because he has abandoned worldly conduct, it is innate (*sahaja*).
Due to the exhaustion of the obscurations of the four bodies, he is the Holder of the Bindu of the Glorious Bodhicitta;
because emptiness and compassion are non-dual, he is the Glorious Kālacakra-Vajra;
and because he is fully endowed with the accumulations of wisdom and ethical discipline, he is Yoga whose essence is Prajñā and Upāya—this is the first yoga.
Now, for the sake of propitiating the guru, he states the examination of the Vajrācārya:
"At the beginning" means that here in the Mantra system, a guru must be served by disciples who desire mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*).
And one should examine him correctly; thus it is said:
because he guards the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the practitioner of the commitments (*samayin*) is to be served and honored with sons, wives, and so forth;

he has ascended the Vajrayāna—that is, he has ascended the Mantrayāna—because he cultivates the knowledge of supreme unchanging syllables (*paramākṣara-jñāna*), he is a meditator on reality (*tattva*).

Because of being indifferent toward one's own body, including all sons, wives, and so forth, [the practitioner] is free from greed. Here, the visualization of the deity is twofold: there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) through union with reality (*tattva-yoga*), which is like the sky; and there is inference (*anumāna*) regarding that which is not directly perceived, which is a conceptualization (*kalpanā*) based on unreality, like a corpse, to be shown in paintings and such for the sake of meditation by yogins of immature intellect. (LKC IV, 232) Thus, according to the dispositions of sentient beings, the visualization of the deity for yogins is twofold: direct perception and inference.

Of those two, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), that which is direct perception is like the circle of stars in the sky through its union with reality (*tattva-yoga*); it is the manifold *saṃbhogakāya*, graspable by the eye of flesh and so forth, resembling an illusion or a dream—the three realms of existence throughout the three times. Here, first, the beginner (*ādikarmika*), through the eye of flesh, perceives the universal image (*viśvabimba*) without the superknowledges (*abhijñā*);
thereafter, he perceives through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) by virtue of the limit of the superknowledges.
Then he sees with the Buddha-eye by virtue of the limit of those free from passion;
then he sees with the wisdom-eye by virtue of the limit of the Bodhisattvas;
then he sees with the knowledge-eye by virtue of the mind of the limit of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, being thus liberated from all substrates of existence.
Thus, the five eyes of the Tathāgata, beginning with the flesh-eye, have been described in relation to the vision of emptiness;
he is unstained because of the removal of other defects such as passion and so forth.

One whose conduct is characterized by patience is "one of patient discipline" (*kṣāntiśīla*), meaning his activity is natural and independent of [worldly] results. One who abides on the path—that is, the path of the Buddha—is "path-abiding" (*adhvavartin*).
Such a teacher, having been propitiated, becomes the giver of the path to disciples and the remover of the fear of hell.
And he, in reality a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who has attained the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*),
is like a vajra-staff (*vajradaṇḍa*) to the Māras— the four Māras— because of his power to destroy them;
and that aforementioned glorious Guru (*śrī-guru*), being the embodiment empowered by Vajrasattva upon the surface of the earth, is renowned as Vajrasattva through his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Now, for the sake of attaining mundane and supramundane accomplishments, the objective support of the deity is described as "direct perception. This is because, through the yoga of reality and the yoga of meditating on the universal image (*viśvabimba*),

one first beholds the enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) of infinite, boundless Buddhas within the center of a drop (*bindu*) shaped like a lunar disc of sapphire, like the wheel of Tārā, and [perceives] the three realms...

The perception of jars, cloths, and so forth is by means of the fleshly eye; beings separated by a distance of a hundred *yojanas* are like those blind from birth regarding the object of the vision of emptiness—this is the rule for the cultivation of reality (*tattva-bhāvanā*). Furthermore, when establishing what is not reality, inference regarding that which is not directly perceived is a conceptualization based on unreality, like a dead body; this should be shown in paintings and the like. Having drawn a painting, a cast image, a molded figure, or the maṇḍala-circle of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it should be displayed in its fixed form for the sake of meditation by dull-witted beginner yogins—this is the rule for the cultivation of conceptualization (*vikalpa-bhāvanā*).

Service (*sevā*) is performed with the five nectars and so forth, with the ocean and the vajra, with mantra recitation and the like, and with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and other practices. Accomplishment (*upasiddhi*) occurs through the nectar born from the vajra-lotus. Meditation (*bhāvanā*), which has reached the state of the single flavor of the three vajras and the lotus through [the stages of] bliss and so forth, constitutes the practice (*sādhana*). Indeed, when there is union with wisdom (*prajñā*), the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) arises as the imperishable through the subtle yoga. Here, the beginner must first perform service according to the ritual procedure for accomplishment.

"Service by means of the five nectars and so forth" refers to the external practice: the five nectars are *vidā* (urine) and the rest; by the word "and so forth," cow-products (*gokvādika*) and the like are included. When these are consumed, it is service for the purpose of pleasing the deity.
Internally, the five nectars are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); by the word "and so forth," the five sense organs are the five lamps.

Their "indifference" (*nirapekṣatā*) is service consisting in the renunciation of thirst for the body and material wealth; by such service the deities become granters of boons, not by the consumption of excrement and the like. Thus, with the "ocean and vajra" [mantras], one should view the indifference toward the enjoyment of the body, the indifference toward the enjoyment of speech, and the indifference toward the enjoyment of the mind.
Mastery is the power [exercised] through the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), such as miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*) and others,
and through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which perceives forms even more subtle than those obstructed by infinite world-systems (*lokadhātu*).
With the Buddha-eye, which knows the minds of others;
with the wisdom-eye, characterized by non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena;
and with the knowledge-eye, which perceives all things in all their aspects.
Other beings, being of limited vision, perceive [the deceased] as being like a dead body— motionless and devoid of movement— because they have been composed of clay or other such materials.
Cast with brass (*pittala*) and so forth;
the five [substances] beginning with *vidā* and ending with *virasuma*,
and the five [substances] beginning with cow's urine and ending with *gokudahaṇa*.
Regarding the internal [practice], the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), the five sense organs (pañcendriya), and the five lamps (pañcapradīpa).
And it has been said:
"Service is the state of being indifferent to the pleasure of emission; it is the celibacy (brahmacarya) of body, speech, and mind—the meaning of which is restraint."
"By this [practice], the deities become bestowers of boons, not through a longing for worldly existence and enjoyments;
and by means of mantra-recitation and so forth.
Here, what is called "mantra-recitation" (mantrajāpa) is the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyama).

By the word "etcetera," the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) is meant; through constant practice of this, the deities become bestowers of boons, and not by means of uncontrolled breath or idle chatter—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), however, recitation and so forth should be performed with a rosary and other implements for the sake of ordinary accomplishments.
Now, the *upasādhana* (near-attainment) is described.

Regarding "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth: here, for those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), "food" (*āhāra*) refers to the grasping of objects such as form by means of the sense faculties, such as the eyes; the abandonment of that is called "withdrawal.

Furthermore, the grasping of other objects, such as form, by means of other [faculties]—such as the eyes and others, including the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and so on—with respect to the image of emptiness (*śūnyatābimba*), is the "near-attainment" (*upasādhana*).

Likewise, meditation, breath control, and concentration constitute the "subsidiary practice" (*upasādhana*) by means of the imperishable nectar born from the vajra-lotus; according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), this is through the internal [process], while according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it is through the external emission of the deity— thus is the accomplishment of the subsidiary practice.
That white stream which falls from the drop day and night is my liquor;
the daily radiance of the eyes and other senses is the meat of the cow and so forth;
and the service of the five nectars is performed by the deities who have entered their own family-ground within the pure body.

"Because the mind enters into emptiness, that blissful union occurs on the level of the co-emergent (*sahaja*), not in the womb. Thus, the yogas of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) are characterized by the observation of the emergence of the syllable *ĀḤ*, the entry of the syllable *OṂ*, and the abiding of the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Now the means of accomplishment is stated: for the sake of attaining common [powers], such as worldly pacification and so forth, by means of that which is uncontrolled— that is, not stabilized— the taking up of food, the bringing [of it] before oneself, serves as the antidote to the bringing of worldly forms and so forth before oneself.
"Ānanda," and so forth.

Here, the "three vajras"—the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind—attaining a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with the lotus (*abja*) constitute the meditation (*bhāvanā*), which is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). The meaning is that the stability of the drops occurs at the heart, the navel, and the secret place;
such is the means of accomplishment.
Then, when the bliss that does not fall away arises through union with wisdom, that indeed is the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). Because of its subtle yoga— that is,
because of the union of the seminal essence (*śukra*) ascending through the *suṣumnā* and other channels— it is called the "great accomplishment" according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, according to the *neyārtha* [interpretation], there is the rule that at the tip of the nose of the *prajñā-dharmodayā*, there is a mustard seed and so forth;
in this way, it becomes the *mahāsādhana*.

First indeed is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bodhi*), and then follows the gathering of the lunar drop (*candrabindu*), from which arises the production of the image (*bimba*); thereafter, by means of the excellent families of flavors, there is the very placement of the syllables (*akṣara-nyāsa*).

This is the general service; the accomplishment by means of the ocean and the vajra is the middling [accomplishment]. Here, the method is fourfold, and likewise, the soft and firm [methods] are among the branches of accomplishment.

Regarding the generation stage, "first, the realization of emptiness" refers to that interval for living beings at the end of death—following the abandonment of the aggregates and preceding the grasping of the aggregates of rebirth—which is the meaning of *pratyāhāra*.
It consists of form and so forth that transcend the nature of atoms and other [ordinary] forms, being supramundane form and so forth.
Dhyāna is characterized by unwavering bliss through the delight in wisdom, reasoning, and reflection; prāṇāyāma is characterized by the cessation of the movement of the moon and the sun;
and dhāraṇā is characterized by the restraint of the breath within the *bindu* by means of the movement and return [of the breath] through the secret place, navel, heart, throat, and forehead.
The "vajra-lotus" refers to the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus because [the bodhicitta] arises there; thus, it means by means of the "undecaying nectar" produced from that vajra-lotus, which is the bodhicitta.
"Attained to the single flavor with the lotus" means having become of one flavor within the pericarp of the heart, navel, and secret lotuses; by this, the yoga of the drop (*binduyoga*) is described.
This occurs when the *suṣumnā* channel and the *śaṅkhinī* [channel] are joined above, through the union of the semen and the movement of the bodhicitta.
By this, the subtle yoga has been explained. Now, the practice (*sevā*) and so forth are described according to the divisions of "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so on,
beginning with the words "at first," etc.

"By the relinquishing of the aggregates" means by the relinquishing of the present body; the single moment of the emptiness of rebirth is the vision of the three realms, which is indeed certainly called "empty. After that moment, there is the "collection of the lunar drop."
Here, the "grasping" (*saṃgraha*) of the drops of semen within the mother's womb by the *ālayavijñāna* refers to that [act of grasping].
From that grasping of the semen and so forth, the "arising of the image" (*bimbotpatti*) means the completion of the embryo over seven months, which is to say the completion of the body.

Thereafter, "by means of the excellent essences and families" refers to the arrangement of the letters (*akṣaranyāsa*) of the eyes and so forth, as well as the engagement with objects such as form, by means of the six aggregates (*ṣat-skandha*).
In this way, even in the accomplishment of a deity, the beginner should meditate on that which consists of conceptual construction;

this is the general service (*sāmānyasevā*). "By the oceans and vajras" refers to the middling accomplishment, which is the production of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the perfection of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis.

In this context, the means (upāya) is fourfold: it is soft in the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) and firm in the limb of near-attainment (*upasādhanāṅga*); likewise, in the limb of attainment (*sādhanāṅga*), there is a restriction until the limit of sixteen years. This is because of the grasping of the constituent parts (*aṃśika-skandha*) and because of the grasping of the future state (*bhāvibhāva*). That which is the interval between these two is characterized as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The vision of the three realms (*tribhavadarśana*) is the direct perception of the three states of existence.

The "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) of the *ālayavijñāna*—which is the substratum of all residual impressions (*vāsanā*)—is the entry of the mind into the midst of the drops of semen and blood; this gathering, which consists of the seizing of the drops of semen within the mother's womb, occurs generally over seven months, though it is said to occur in nine months according to its specific nature.

In the *devatāsādhana*, by means of the illustration of the embryo (*garbha*) starting with the words "from that" (*tena tataḥ*) and so forth, there is an indication of the three branches beginning with the *upasādhana*,
characterized by the six aggregates (*skandha*): form, sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and gnosis (*jñāna*).

This is the common service (*sāmānyasevā*), the service for worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*); likewise [there are] the near-attainment (*upāsādhana*), the attainment (*sādhana*), and the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*).
For this very reason, [it is said] "the ocean," and so forth.
By this, it is stated that there is the accomplishment of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis;
for by the phrases "the middling sādhana" and "the middling upasādhana," the sādhana is specifically characterized.

Therefore, the explanation is that "the accomplishment of the vital breaths occurs here"; "here" means within the aforementioned *sevā* and *upasādhana*, where the means (*upāya*) is fourfold—that is, fourfold as the "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so forth.
Among those four, it is twofold in this case, namely within *sevā* and *upasādhana*.
This [classification] is to be applied in two ways, to both the *sādhana* and the *mahāsādhana*;

for this very reason, it says: "the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) and the limb of near-attainment (*upasādhanāṅga*)," and by means of the "mild child" (*mṛdubāla*) mentioned immediately prior—referring to the previously mentioned *sevā* and *upasādhana* and the *sādhana* and *mahāsādhana* to be described hereafter—the "mild" is the infant (*jātabāla*), the "middling child" (*madhyabāla*) is from the eruption of teeth, the "youth" (*kumāra*) is from the falling out of teeth until the eruption of new ones, and the "adult" (*prauḍha*) is from the age of sixteen onwards, because of his capacity to produce sons and daughters.

Thus, the fourfold limb of all deities should be meditated upon by the yogin; this is the rule regarding conventional truth. Now, the production of the Buddha-image by means of ultimate truth is described:
here, first is the awakening to emptiness, wherein nothing at all should be conceptualized in the darkness.
Then, "the compendium of the lunar drop" refers to the apprehension of the signs beginning with smoke up to the point of the drop,
as well as the arising of the image; "from that" means from that drop, the vision of the universe is the arising of the image.

"By the families of excellent essences" means by the unobscured six aggregates (*ṣaṭskandha*). "The arrangement of syllables" (*akṣaranyāsa*) is the cessation of the limited aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.
Thereafter, the distinction of "soft" and so on occurs through the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*), until one becomes a master of the twelve stages.
Then, one possesses the meaning of the truths in twelve aspects and knows reality in sixteen aspects.
The connection is with the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment),
and that [connection] involves the mention of both the beginning and the end due to the requirements of the meter;
therefore, it should be understood that here the terms "child" (*bāla*) and "youth" (*kumāra*) are also included by way of abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*).
"Firm and mature at the root" means that it is thus a great limb of the sādhana;
"the youth" is soft, being the nature of the third limb.
By this, the fourfold set beginning with service is joined with the fourfold set beginning with the weak;
[here, etc.,
"weak" means one whose strength has arisen].

[The phrase] "it is soft up to the limit of birth due to the collection of drops of semen" refers to what was stated starting from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); now, by the words "the newborn and so forth," it means that once born, [the embryo] is sixteen [days old], and so on.
By means of the illustration of the body, he demonstrates the subject at hand:
"the attainment of the stages (bhūmi) through the distinctions of 'soft' and so forth" means that each of the fourfold set beginning with 'soft' is joined to three stages;
thus, by attaining the twelve stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā) and ending with the Knowledge-Possessing (jñānavatī), one becomes the Lord of the Twelve Stages.

Then, regarding the meaning of the verse beginning with "the twelve aspects" and so forth, we have explained the awakening to the twenty names in our *Amṛtakaṇikā*: "The supreme omniscient one has awakened. Likewise: "In the non-empty [center], one should meditate on the path of smoke and so forth, up to the limit of the [reflected] image (*bimba*), within the channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*) by means of the guru’s instructions. Thereafter, one makes the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds stable; subsequently, like the planet Rāhu, the yogi effects the arrest of the moon, which is the *bodhicitta*. Therefore, whatever is desired is attained here in this very life within a few days."
Thus,
this royal road,
