the instruction on the stages of meditation (*bhāvanākrama*), has been taught in the *Paramādibuddha*: "Having meditated upon smoke and the other [signs], one should make the mind immovable."
Now the path for supramundane accomplishment is described:

"In the void" means that by the power of the guru’s instructions, one should meditate on the path beginning with smoke according to the sequence to be explained. One should meditate on the "limit of the image," which is the image possessing all aspects; up to that limit is the mind.
Thus, within the wheels of the channels (*nāḍīcakra*), from that point onward, one makes both the prāṇa-wind and the apāna-wind stable.
In the navel-cakra, the yogi subsequently effects the cessation of the bodhicitta, like Rāhu seizing the moon. Here, "yogi" refers to one who possesses the mutual union of prāṇa and apāna;
he brings about the cessation—that is, the pacification—of the moment of emission of the bodhicitta, producing the immutable [state] consisting of the outflow (nisyanda) and so forth.

From that outflow, having purified the middle channel for a few moments or more, one should meditate upon the supreme immutable, which includes the matured (vipāka), the human effort (puruṣakāra), and the stainless (vaimalya), as well as whatever else is ineffable.
Having placed the vajra in the lotus, one should cause the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to enter the drop (*bindu*).
One should cause the drops to enter the wheels (*cakras*), and restrain the vibration (*spanda*) of the drops within the vajra.
With his linga perpetually erect, the yogi shall always have his semen drawn upward; empowered by the penetrations of the vajra through union with the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
O Great King, through twenty-one thousand six hundred moments of the supreme syllable, one becomes Vajrasattva himself;
otherwise, one must not form an attachment to wisdom until the ten [stages] have been aroused.

The withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) of the yogin from the discernment of external functions and their signs is the Lord of Jinas; it is tenfold. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is Akṣobhya, and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is Khaḍgin, each likewise tenfold. Furthermore, retention (*dhāraṇā*) is Ratnapāṇi, mindfulness (*anusmṛti*) in the *Ḍombī* [mudrā] is Padmadhara, and the glorious samādhi (*samādhi*) is Cakrin. Each one is further divided into five varieties according to the distinctions of the vowels and consonants.

Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the non-engagement of the ten objects and their subjects within the body; discernment (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), delight (*rati*), and immovable bliss are meditation (*dhyāna*), which is also one-pointedness of mind.

Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the halting of the two paths, as well as the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the central channel (*madhyama*); indeed, the entry of the *prāṇa* into the *bindu*, with both movements ceased, is retention (*dhāraṇā*), which is also one-pointedness of mind.

Recollection (*anusmṛti*) occurs when there is the vision of Caṇḍālī within the body and in space. Concentration (*samādhi*) is the reflection of gnosis (*jñānabimba*) by virtue of the imperishable bliss consisting of wisdom and means.

This means of accomplishment (sādhana) of the Lord of the Universe may be of three kinds according to the distinctions of "mild" and so forth; there are three mudrās and three measures (mātrās) by virtue of the three types of movement: the physical, the mental, and the divine.

Through withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the yogi, free from sense objects, is empowered by all mantras; he becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (abhijñānas), O King, purified by the yoga of meditation (dhyāna).

Purified by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and devoid of the moon and sun, he is worshipped by the Bodhisattvas; through the power of retention (dhāraṇā), he enters the One Endowed with Ten Powers (the Buddha), destroying the Māras and the afflictions (kleśas).

Through recollection (*anusmṛti*), one becomes completely purified, and the stainless halo (*bhāmaṇḍala*) arises from the reflection of gnosis (*jñānabimba*); the meaning is that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is thereby attained.
Therefore, being pure, the body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*) is perfected within a few days through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

If, through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs], that desired accomplishment does not arise for practitioners of mantra, then by the force of the practice of *nāda*, one should accomplish the jewel of the *kuliśa* within the lotus-born [vagina]. Through the restraint of the *bindu*, the primordial yoga (*ādiyoga*) occurs during the service (*sevā*).

In the sky, the tenfold [yoga] of the Wheel-Holder [Viṣṇu] occurs; and during the near-accomplishment (*upasādhana*), it occurs through the wrathful gaze of the Destroyer of Obstacles (*Vighnāntaka*) and the gaze directed toward the path of nectar.

In the accomplishment (*sādhana*), the three-syllabled [mantra] of the moon-drop emitted by Wisdom (*prajñā*) within the jewel of the *kuliśa* should be employed; here, in the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), the innate (*sahaja*) knowledge-yoga (*jñānayoga*) is the sole peace of inexhaustible bliss.
Now, the yoga with six limbs is explained, beginning with the words "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth.
Here, "withdrawal" refers to the Aggregate of Gnosis (*jñānaskandha*), which is the Lord of Jinas at the stage of the beginner;

and that Aggregate of Gnosis is of ten kinds according to the differentiation of signs, being unconstructed through the distinctions of seeing smoke, mirages, fireflies, lamps, flames, the moon, the sun, Rāhu, the digit (*kalā*), and the point (*bindu*).

Meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed Akṣobhya; it is the tenfold aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the unification of the ten [factors] consisting of the objects and their subjects within the Universal Image (*viśvabimba*).
Prāṇāyāma is also tenfold, and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the "Sword-wielder" (*khaḍgī*).

Because the ten mandalas of the left and right [channels] have become unified as one, there is again a tenfold retention (*dhāraṇā*); thus, "Ratnapāṇi" refers to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
The retention of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is tenfold according to its movement through the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown.
And through the *ḍombī*, there is recollection (*anusmṛti*); furthermore, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is tenfold, as it is said, "even by the holder of the lotus.
That recollection occurs within the *ḍombī*, that is, in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), by way of the distinctions of the ten states of passion.
Furthermore, the glorious meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the wheel-bearer (*cakrī*), which is Vairocana; this tenfold meditative absorption arises from the cessation of the ten winds.

Thus, the Blessed One is non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthitanirvāṇa*), meaning he is the source from which the winds flow. Now, the characteristics of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs] are described by the verse beginning with "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*).
Here, what is called "withdrawal" refers to the connection between the ten objects and their subjects within the body.

Now, with six verses, he explains the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), beginning with "Withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "O Lord of Jinas": Vajrasattva, by virtue of being the subject and object free from obscuration, appears in the form of the ten signs;
"Khadgin" refers to Amoghasiddhi.

"Due to the tenfold distinction of the states of desire" means that the engagement of consciousness is its engagement with objects within the image of emptiness by means of the five other types [of faculties], such as the eye;
likewise, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) in that very same image is illumination.
*Tarka* is the grasping of an entity; *vicāra* is for the purpose of its ascertainment.
Anxiety, longing, and fever, the withering of the lotus-face of the beloved, the cessation of food, trembling, madness, giddiness, mental confusion, and intense fainting arise.

Those [states] beginning with smoke belong to the Thunderbolt-Holder; they are manifest in ten ways as the conditions within the limbs of living beings in the world. These are the manifest and fixed states of Manmatha; who is the Victor, and who is the one possessed of desire?

"Each one is further divided into five types by means of the vowels beginning with *a* and so forth. Thus, by means of the thirty consonants—*ka, ca, ta, pa, ta, sa*—which have the nature of the elements of space, wind, fire, water, earth, and consciousness, and which are differentiated by the five short vowels beginning with *a*;
and likewise by those having the nature of earth and so forth, differentiated by the five long vowels beginning with *ī*, according to the sequence of emanation and reabsorption.
According to the division of the twelve transits (saṃkrānti) beginning with Mesavṛṣa and so forth, there are three hundred and sixty breaths for every ghaṭikā.

During the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana), the moon consists of a single consonant and a short vowel; during the northern transit (uttarāyana), the sun consists of a conjunct consonant and a long vowel.

At the transition, there are three conjoined consonants; the meaning is that Rāhu, moving as a *pluta* through the distinctions of the measures (*mātrā*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, undergoes differentiation.

"Beholding with other [eyes], such as the flesh-eye and so forth," refers to the delight in the universal image (*viśvabimba*); "attachment to the image" (*bimbāsakti*) means the unshakable bliss; and "unification of the mind with the image" (*bimbenāikīkaraṇaṃ cittasya*) means the merging of the mind together with the image.
Thus, meditation is tenfold here according to the distinction between the grasped and the grasper;

what is called *prāṇāyāma* is the "two paths," namely the deviation from the left and right channels and the entry into the middle channel. And that is tenfold due to the cessation of the ten mandalas; "here" refers to the drop (*bindu*).
The entry of the vital breath into the forehead is "destroyed of both movements," meaning it is devoid of going and coming;
this one-pointedness of mind upon the vital breath at the forehead is called *dhāraṇā*. 116.

The vision of the Caṇḍālī in the sky of the three realms is that tenfold recollection previously mentioned; it is known as "samādhi" because, through the union of wisdom and means, it becomes one with the object of knowledge and the knowing consciousness, and by virtue of the immutable bliss within the gnosis-image.
That [practice] is also tenfold due to the absence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth;

thus, this six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and though it is threefold according to the divisions of "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so on, it is the means of accomplishment for Kālacakra, the Sustainer of the Universe. The three seals (*mudrā*) are the three measures (*trimātrā*). Kaṇa...

The apprehension of existence (*bhāva*) is the determination of existence; its purpose is the ascertainment of that existence, which is the definitive realization of its nature as emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Attachment to the image (*bimba*) refers to the mental well-being that arises for one who, having turned away from sense objects, inwardly focuses on the self as being of the nature of the deity by means of the mind alone, and who contemplates the single flavor of unsurpassed wisdom and method while facing toward entry into reality (*tattva*); this is "joy" (*rati*), meaning "delight.
The bliss consisting of physical pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*) and so forth, the immovable bliss, is the entry into the middle path.

By means of the dissolution of the ten mandalas, beginning with space and ending with earth, there occurs the cessation of the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels and the entry, abiding, and exit [of the winds] solely through the path of the *avadhūtī*. This activity of the *prāṇa-vāyu* within the subtle channel is what is meant by "breath control" (*prāṇāyāma*).

It is called "the destruction of both movements" because, having become free from coming and going due to the absence of movement and arrival at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown, the *prāṇa-vāyu*—which serves as the vehicle for the mind—is gradually diminished and established in the *bindu*, the *bodhicitta*, as being of one flavor with emptiness; this is what is termed "retention" (*dhāraṇā*).

The tenfold [process] previously described occurs when the mind is established in *dhāraṇā*: first, there is the vision of the deities of the mandala arisen spontaneously, preceded by the appearance of the ten signs beginning with smoke; this has the form of a reflection and is non-conceptual. Following that is the radiation of manifold rays of light. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the three types of movement," here the movement of the emission (*kṣara*) of the *bodhicitta* is the soft degree, and the movement of vibration (*spanda*) is the medium degree.
The movement that is utterly motionless is the supreme;
thus, the action-seal (karmamudrā) bestows the bliss of emission,
while the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) bestows the bliss of vibration.
Mahāmudrā bestows the bliss of the motionless;
thus, the meditation on the three mudrās has been taught by the Blessed One through the yoga of the six limbs.
Therefore, the yoga of the six limbs should be meditated upon by the yogin for the sake of Buddhahood. || 117 ||
Now, the fruit of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the subsequent stages is described by the verse beginning with "by withdrawal," and so forth:

"In this system, when the yogi becomes purified through withdrawal and the *bimba* has become stable, then he is empowered by all mantras; through his speech he grants boons and so forth, and he becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), O Lord of Men, being purified by the yoga of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."

In this context, when one possesses unblinking eyes, then one possesses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); likewise, the divine ear becomes purified through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and [the body] is purified through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Here, when the yogi is devoid of the paths of the sun and moon and always flows through the central channel (*madhyamāvāha*), then, being purified by breath control, he is honored by the Bodhisattvas; the meaning is that he is praised.

He enters the "Ten-Powered One" (*daśabala*) for the destruction of Māra, the afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth; that is, he enters the image of emptiness (*śūnyatābimba*), the mind which is free from the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakacitta*).
"By the power of dhāraṇā" means that through the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) to and fro, one becomes unified as a single mass. || 118 ||

Then, preceded by the radiation of the deity-mandala throughout the three realms, there is the recollection (*anusmṛti*) characterized by the ten stages of desire, beginning with thought, due to the absence of the vital breaths and so forth. By means of being fully ignited by the flame of the *caṇḍālī*, the bodhicitta—immovable and established at the tip of the peak of the *vajramaṇi*—is [retained]. Then, gradually, the twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths are arrested within the six wheels. Thus, there is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is the nature of the Great Vajradhara, consisting of the body made of gnosis, characterized by the union (*yuganaddha*) that consists of non-conceptual yoga and great bliss.

If it is asked how one is designated as a "bodhisattva" on account of attaining the qualities of a Buddha within one's own continuum— characterized by the benefits of the six limbs and the fruit of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and so forth—
it is because of the turning of the wheel of the Dharma of the birth-enlightenment (jāti-bodhi).
However, by setting that [mind] in motion, one indeed comes to possess the designation of a "Perfectly Awakened One" (sambuddha) within the Buddha-field; such is the intention.

This refers to the ten masteries (*vaśitā*) and so forth—namely, mastery over life, karma, liberation, requisites, aspiration, supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), dharma, mind, birth, and knowledge—as well as the mind that acts as the subject and object of grasping (*grāhya-grāhaka*).
And the benefit has been stated elsewhere:
"One who is purified through recollection [attains it].

Here, "recollection" (anusmṛti) is the recognition of the image (bimba), which is the state of the mind being free from all conceptual constructions (vikalpa). When one is thus purified by that, then the stainless circle of light (prabhāmaṇḍala) arises.
Furthermore, by the word "also" (apica), it is meant that from the pores of the skin five rays flash forth and issue from the image of gnosis, which is the image of emptiness;
therefore, it is said, "pure in meditative absorption" (samādhi).
Here, the imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) that arises through the unity of the mind of the apprehended and the apprehender is called "blissful meditative absorption."

Therefore, one who is pure from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), having attained purity—that is, freedom from defilement—becomes a Bodhisattva who has attained the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*) and so forth, with a body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*). This perfection is achieved within a few days, three fortnights, or three years; such is the rule for withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs].
Now, *haṭhayoga* is described.

In this context, when the moment of the imperishable (*akṣarakṣaṇa*) does not arise despite the visualization of the *bimba* through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and other means because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is unrestrained, then—by means of the forceful practice of the *nāda*, having caused the *prāṇa* to flow into the central channel (*madhyamā*) and by arresting the drops of the bodhicitta at the jewel of the *kuliśa* situated upon the lotus of wisdom—one attains the moment of the imperishable.

Having thereby accomplished withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and having entered the meditative knowledge (*dhyānajñāna*) empowered by all mantras, one shall attain the state of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñatva*).
By means of breath control, the power for the purpose of retention is constantly observed by the Bodhisattvas; one should always enter into Vajrasattva.
Through the union of recollection, a mandala of light arises;
by the mere mastery of meditative concentration, one becomes free from obscurations.

Having pressed [the organs] together with the essence of intense joy, one should not move for a moment; then, when the arising of the flowing fluid occurs, preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should accomplish the *bodhicitta* through the experience of the fourth, innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), by means of the grace of the feet of the true guru and by way of non-emission— this is *haṭhayoga*.
The practice of *nāda* (sound) has been taught here in this very *Sādhanapatala* by the Blessed One:

"That power (*śakti*) which proceeds from the center of the navel to the supreme state, to the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] and the end of the digits (*kalā*), when restrained at the navel, resembling fire and smoke, and having arisen in the form of a staff,

moves with a soft and graceful gait from wheel to wheel along the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) until it forcibly touches the external skin like a needle, reaching as far as the aperture of the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa-raṇdhra*)."

At that time, one should forcefully impel the downward-flowing wind (āpāna) upward; having pierced the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa), it proceeds to the supreme city when the pair of winds is restrained.

Thus, from the awakening of the vajra within the mind, together with its objects, one attains the state of a sky-walker (khecara) and becomes the Mother of the Universe for yogins, possessing the nature of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā).
The meaning is that from the cessation of the *bindu*, there is the attainment of the moment of the imperishable (*akṣara-kṣaṇa*).

In this very context, the power belonging to the *Śrī Kālacakra*—namely, the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*)—proceeds to the supreme state, the supportless place, the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*). This occurs in the left nostril, extending from the element of space down to the earth mandala, from sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) down to twelve finger-breadths.

"At the end of the digits" means that, by uttering the resonance of the syllable *huṃ*, the inhaled and exhaled breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) are joined within the right nostril— extending from the earth mandala up to the ether, from twelve fingers up to sixteen fingers— and thus restrained at the navel;
that very power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*) becomes like lightning fire, resembling the fire of the dissolution of the world.
Shaken and impelled like a needle,
it goes— that is, enters— the drinking place.
Even with the desire to enter another's city—that is, another's body—entry into that other city does not occur; therefore, he says that it must be done in this way:
"In this manner," by this sequence, from the awakening of the vajra, which is the awakening of the knowledge of supreme bliss.
"In the mind" means in the consciousness that has become a single, unified mass with the apprehended object and the apprehending subject; [this refers to] the mind accompanied by [the seed-syllable].
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the image of emptiness (*śūnyatābimba*), the gaze is described, beginning with "service" (*sevā*) and so forth.
Here, "service" (*sevā*) refers to the cultivation of signs such as smoke;
within that service, "initial yoga" (*ādiyoga*) is the grasping of signs such as smoke by the mind.
That [yoga] is of ten kinds, as it occurs together with the signs beginning with smoke; therefore, it is tenfold.
And that [sign] belongs to the Wheel-bearer; by means of the gaze of the Uṣṇīṣa— that is, the wrathful gaze directed upwards with unblinking eyes—
it becomes fourfold through connection with the night and sixfold through connection with the day.
Then, the image itself,
up to the limit of the image, becomes the limb of service through withdrawal and meditation; thus it is said,
"by the vision of Vighnāntaka."
Vighnāntaka is Amṛtakuṇḍalin;
his gaze is fixed on the station of immortality, located at the forehead.
By that gaze of Vighnāntaka, which has entered the path of immortality, the six-limbed yoga is applied to the one to be accomplished.

By the word "and" (*cakārāt*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and meditative retention (*dhāraṇā*) are to be performed. When the reflection (*bimba*) has been seen, there is the "near-attainment" (*upasādhana*) of the "created moon-drop" (*srṣṭendubindu*).

Here, that which is created by the passion of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the "created moon-drop"; of that drop of bodhicitta stabilized by wisdom, when it has entered the *vajra*-jewel, there occurs the "union of the three syllables" (*tryakṣarayoga*) in the secret place, the navel, and the heart. This constitutes the third limb of the practice, namely the "accomplishment" (*sādhana*).

Thus, the member of the means should be performed as "the sole peace of inexhaustible bliss. Here, that single moment of the *bodhicitta* which is inexhaustible through bliss is called "peace" (*śānta*).
In this Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana), the "Yoga of Gnosis" (*jñānayoga*) is the innate (*sahaja*) state;
it is the oneness of the mind with immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).

This is the fourth limb of the Great Accomplishment. That [power] which has become unified with the objects of the senses is *śakti*; she attains the state of moving through space (*khecaratva*) and sovereignty as far as the Akanistha realm.
It is not only thus; so he says "five," and so forth.

Mahāmudrā is also Viśvamātā, whose nature consists of the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*)—having the nature of supernatural power, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of former abodes—and she exists through the non-conceptual flame of the Caṇḍālī ignited by the passion of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The "yoga of the three syllables" means that the mind-bindu, having entered the secret place, is restrained; and the speech-bindu, having reached the navel, is restrained.
The *kāyabindu* residing in the heart is restrained;
by means of that bliss which does not waver, the *jñānabindu* is restrained as the collection of drops (*bindusandoha*) does not fall from the opening of the *vajra*.
By the phrase ending with "the pair of winds is restrained," the accomplishment of *bhūcarī* (the earth-walker) is indicated; this is the yoga of gnosis (*jñānayoga*).

The Khecarī-mudrā, which conforms to Māyā, appearing as a form both in the mind and in space, illuminates the three worlds like a mirror; flashing forth with many rays resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, it is undivided within external bodies, yet situated in the sky of mere appearance devoid of objects; consisting of consciousness itself, it embraces the mind of the manifold world as that one reality.

The mere appearance of the mind, produced within one’s own consciousness and resembling a reflection in a mirror, is indeed to be cultivated by the lords of yogins and served by all the sons of the Victors; and that which has been served by the Buddhas, when its flame of gnosis has increased, burns away the entire grove of Māra together with its objects, and bestows equal bliss upon the bodies of yogins through the practice of yoga.
By the end of the passage "having become [one with] the essence" (*ratvaṃ prayāti*), the accomplishment of *khecarī* is stated;
by the end of "the Mother of the Universe" (*viśvamātā*), the accomplishment of *mahāmudrā* is indicated. *Mudrā* is *mahāmudrā*, which conforms to *māyā* and is like a reflection in a clear mirror.
It exists in the mind and in space, in that which is both non-mind and mind; for this very reason, he says:
And "like a form in a mirror" means they cause [the world] to expand, expanding it as if it were a form [reflected] in a mirror.

Externally, she is undivided within the illusory bodies, having become one with the objects and the sense faculties; for that very reason, she is devoid of objects in the form of the manifestation of phenomena (*dharma*) through differentiation.
Although she is one, she embraces the mind of the world of manifold forms;
therefore, she consists of consciousness (*cetomayā*), being by nature both non-mind and mind (*acittacittasvabhāvā*).

The mere appearance (*ābhāsamātra*)—which consists of the manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittapratibhāsa*)—is the divine consort (*divyamudrā*). This mere appearance is produced and born within one’s own mind in the form of all-aspectedness and formlessness. It is the flame of gnosis (*jñānārci*), the blazing wisdom (*jñāna*) intensified by the fire of the *caṇḍālī*.
It is said that it [destroys] the lotus of Māra—the conceptual web of the mind together with its objects, including the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
And it has been stated:

Māra is one's own mind; there is no other. Wisdom (*prajñā*) and gnosis (*jñāna*) are the mind, which is tenfold, and its very appearance is the consecration (*seka*). Immersion in this [consecration] is indeed like the reflection of a stainless moon in a mirror.
Therefore, that which is the bliss of nirvāṇa, unchanging, innate, and imperishable—the fourth state—is the mouth of the Buddha. He who possesses this within his heart and face is the glorious Guru.

Wisdom (*prajñā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are, respectively, the apprehending mind (*grāhakacitta*); and that which is the tenfold appearance of the apprehended—beginning with smoke and so forth—which is like a reflected army within that apprehending mind, is itself knowledge (*jñāna*), meaning the apprehended mind (*grāhyacitta*).
Thus, just as one’s own eye is reflected in a mirror, it is the apprehended by one’s own eye; this is wisdom and knowledge. "Consecration" (*seka*) is the immersion (*majjana*) therein.

In this context, the entry of the perceiving mind (*grāhakacitta*) into the perceived mind (*grāhyacitta*), the non-engagement with external objects, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*)—these are called "immersion" within the six-limbed [yoga].

Therefore, from that immersion comes the bliss of nirvāṇa, which is immutable, innate, imperishable, and indeed the fourth bliss; it is beyond the states of the infant, the mature, and the throbbing, transcends worldly analogies, and is liberated from the conduct of the three worlds—this is the meaning.

That which is free from laughing, looking, touching, embracing, grasping with the hands, and sexual union; free from the causes of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*; characterized by the appearance of all aspects within emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—this is the mouth of the Buddha, the mouth of gnosis (*jñānavaktra*). The master in whose heart this has been cultivated as a personal experience and who exists at all times for the purpose of imparting it to his disciples through his own mouth—he is the glorious Māra.

He "gives, gives" equal bliss, the bliss of co-emergent joy (*sahajānanda*), by means of the "rain-fall yoga," which means by the falling of the wheel during the period of three years and three fortnights.
"Insight (*prajñā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) correspond respectively":

insight is the realization of the emptiness of all phenomena; that is the apprehending mind (*grāhakacitta*). The appearance of smoke and so forth within the mirror [of meditative concentration] is the apprehended mind (*grāhyacitta*); that very thing is knowledge (*jñāna*).

By this it is meant that just as one's own eye reflected in a mirror is perceived by one's own eye, so too, by means of a mind whose intrinsic nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*), the mind in all its aspects (*sarvākāra-citta*)—which has emptiness as its intrinsic nature—is seen; such is the meaning. Within this apprehended mind characterized by smoke and so forth, the immersion (*majjana*) of the apprehending mind—the mind of emptiness—is its becoming one with it in a single mass (*ekalolībhāva*); this he calls "recollection" (*anusmṛti*).

Regarding the term "purification" (*vimala*), it refers to the movements (*spanda*) of the "child" (*bāla*) and the "adult" (*prauḍha*). Thus, the bliss of flux (*kṣarasukha*) of the means (*upāya*) is twofold: that of the child and that of the adult;

whereas the bliss of movement (*spandasukha*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the "grown" (*vṛddha*). Among these, the "supreme" (*parama*) is supramundane (*lokottara*). When there is the absence of movement (*niḥspanda*) of both those—wisdom and means—the meaning is that the Guru is Vajradhara.
"No others are capable of realizing the bliss of the two organs.
Thus, with minds unattached to space, with unblinking eyes, having entered the vajra-path, from emptiness there is smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly, and a lamp;
the flame, the moon, the sun, and the vajras are seen as the supreme digit, and within that, the drop (*bindu*)—the image of the Buddha, the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* free from sense objects.
Now, the entry into the appearance of this very mind is explained by the words beginning with "space" (*ākāśa*).
Here, in both the Mantra Vehicle and the Pāramitā Vehicle, the practice of yoga is twofold:
the practice of yoga in space and the practice in an open area.

He who attains yoga in space sees the signs beginning with smoke at night in a windowless house in the darkness; with his mind attached to space and his eyes unblinking, he has entered the vajra-path.

Here, having entered the central *prāṇa* and with minds attached to space, with unblinking eyes, and having entered the vajra-path from emptiness itself, [one sees] from emptiness: smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest pure firefly, and a lamp.
Thus, by means of the yoga of night, one sees;

then one sees the cloudless sky. Then, from the sky again by means of the yoga of day, the self-arisen one born from the sky—the great fire of the wisdom of insight—is seen as a flame in the cloudless sky.
In this way, Vairocana of great brilliance, the light of wisdom, Virocana, appears like the moon.
The sun that illuminates the world, the torch of wisdom, the vajra-Rāhu,
possessed of great splendor, radiant, and the lightning of supreme beauty.
"He becomes the King of Vidyās; that is the fourth, arisen from the divine mudrā"—this means that the Holder of the Vajra is the emanated body (*nirmitakāya*).
Now, the entry of this very mind into the appearance of the mind—which is like a reflection in a mirror—is described by the words beginning with "space" (*ākāśa*).
"At night" is an indication for darkness.
With minds attached to space, with minds dissolved into space—

by those whose minds are attached to space, having become of one flavor (*samarasa*) with it, and who have entered the vajra-path via the *avadhūtī* through the vital winds (*prāṇavāta*)— [one perceives] from the sky, that is, from the cloudless sky, which is the form of the causal sign (*nimitta*).
"Appearing as form" means that there is the manifestation of non-obstructive forms, comparable to reflections in a mirror;
"appearing as sound" means the experience of the mere unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*) arising from the outpouring of great bliss produced by the effort of the throat, palate, and so forth.
By this much, through this verse, the two bodies of the Blessed One, the glorious Vajradhara, are illuminated.

"The Lord of Mantras is Binduka"— thus the tenfold sign (*nimitta*) was taught by the Blessed One in the *Samāja* and other tantras through the yoga of night, and in the *Nāmasamgīti* through the yoga of day;
thereafter, "the King of Mantras, the performer of great purpose" refers to the vision of the image (*bimba*) in all its aspects, such as the jar, cloth, and so forth.

In the center of that, within the *bindu*, is the Buddha-image, devoid of sense objects due to the absence of material substance and the absence of conceptual construction; from that arises the manifold *saṃbhogakāya*.
Then, through the yoga of the image, that very sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) is heard;
thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* appears as form.
The meaning is that the *saṃbhogakāya* is that which appears as sound.

The yogi should gaze at the sky with a fixed stare until it is free of clouds; then, when a black line (*kṛṣṇarekhā*)—pure and shimmering—is seen in the *kālanāḍī*, within that [line] the image of the Omniscient One appears, like the sun in water, unclouded, possessing all colors and all forms. One’s own mind is thus devoid of objects; it is not another mind.

In this regard, the daytime yoga (*divāyoga*) is as follows: the sky, free from clouds, should be observed by the yogin with a fixed gaze during both the forenoon and the afternoon, turning his back to the sun; otherwise, darkness arises from the sun's rays, and due to that obstruction, [the vision] cannot be practiced daily. One should observe until a black line the measure of a hair, shimmering and stainless, is seen within the *bindu*. The image of the Omniscient One, which is contained within the *avadhūtī*—the channel of time (*kālanāḍī*)—is the entire threefold world, like the sun in water, unclouded, possessing all colors and all forms. One’s own mind is devoid of objects; there is no "other-mind" (*paracitta*), for there is an absence of knowledge of another's mind.

In this context, first the appearance of one’s own mind is seen by the Tathāgata with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); then, through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth, the knowledge of others' minds is seen. Thus, the five eyes of the Blessed One were described in the *Dharmasaṃgraha*.
In this manner, through the power of cultivation, there will arise in sequence the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Buddha-eye, the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), and the gnosis-eye (*jñānacakṣus*).
Consequently, for the Omniscient One, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unseen.

"Space," [is said] with a fixed gaze, that is, with an unmoving gaze, because there is an absence of knowledge of another's mind; for there is no object of knowledge consisting of another's mind apart from one's own mind.
And it has been said:

That which is the perception here of an object of knowledge that is neither born nor ceased belongs to one's own mind and not to anything else, because of the distinction from external objects of knowledge. It has the form of earth, yet it is not solid; it has the nature of water, yet it is not liquid because it lacks fluidity; it has the form of fire, yet it is not fire; it has the body of wind, yet it is not wind because it is motionless.

The aspect of emptiness is visible as white, green, and great variegated colors, yet it is not a color; though possessing all aspects, it is invisible due to the power of the Māra of the impurities of one's own heart. Earth becomes water, and fire likewise becomes water; fire becomes wind, and wind becomes emptiness; indeed, the tenfold sign becomes the sign, and the omniform becomes the immutable, supreme bliss, the unstruck body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*). From that gnosis, O Lord of Men, supernatural powers and accomplishment arise for men even in this very life.
Therefore, it is never possible for the self to seal itself;
how could a great sword cut itself with its own blade? It would be like the pleasure found in a dream through union with the daughter of a barren woman.
By this verse, "Through the service of the disk arisen from space, likewise for oneself," the means of accomplishing the *dharmakāya* is stated.
"Earth has the form [of a circle]," and so forth; this is the characteristic of the image (*bimba*).

Here, the appearance of emptiness is seen as earth and so on, yet it is not a substantial thing and is not solid. It has a fluid form like the water of a mirage, but it is not actual water because it lacks fluidity.

Thus, the form of fire is not fire, because it does not burn; that which has a body of moving wind is not the wind-element because it lacks substantiality (*adravyatva*), and that which is motionless is not the wind-element for the same reason of lacking substantiality. The form of emptiness is also seen like a city of illusion (*māyānagara*), yet even though it is endowed with colors such as white and so forth, it is not color because it lacks substantiality.
Although possessing all forms, it is always invisible to fools;
for what reason? It is the rule that this is due to the power of the *kleśamāra* and the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the left and right channels.

Now, the depletion of the five maṇḍalas is described by means of the passage beginning with "earth" (*pṛthvī*) and so forth. Here, when the yogin becomes one whose eyes do not blink, having fixed his mind upon the void with a wrathful gaze, then—whether on the left or the right—"earth" is an indicative term.
When the yogin performs the meditation at the time of the flow of earth on the right side, this is the procedure;
however, it is not [the case] during the flow of the left channel and so forth, but rather according to the sequence of the maṇḍalas beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through whichever mandala— whether on the left or the right— it possesses as its substrate, that very [mandala] is so designated. Thus,
when the vital breath of the earth-mandala moves from the right channel into the water-mandala,
and so on, up to the consciousness-mandala.

The entry of the vital breath into the center by means of space and the other elements through the left channel; the binding of the movement of the sun and moon in the right and left [channels]; the mind reaching supreme bliss during the practice of *mudrā*; the awakening of the *vajra*;

the sound of the *vajra* in the lotus, or the splashing of water from one's own hand for the sake of bliss; the non-emission of the seed—that bliss which removes the fear of death—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru.
[LKC V, Ψ] This instruction on Mahāmudrā is also proclaimed in the *Paramādibuddha*:
"One should perform the sādhana of this very [reality] through inconceivable appearances—
through those signs beginning with smoke, which are the reflections of wisdom equal to space."
It proceeds;
thus, the tenfold sign, beginning with smoke, proceeds as emptiness, and the sign proceeds as the image in all its aspects.
The image proceeds as immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).
That very knowledge is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
From that knowledge comes supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), such as traveling through the sky and so forth;
and accomplishment (*siddhi*) becomes sovereignty over the three realms, O Lord of Men, for persons in this very life. This is the rule for entering the path.
Now, the conclusion of the yoga is stated with the words "In the center, the prāṇa," and so forth.
Here, first of all, the yogin must effect the entry of the prāṇa into the center, into the avadhūtī, by which means he perceives the sign (*nimitta*).
Thus, one [aspect] is called the body-vajra, the face of the venerable Guru Buddha.
Therefore, the rule is that the binding of the breath occurs through the conjunction of the movement of the moon with the southward course of the sun, which is the movement of the *vāmanā* channel.
Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the second *vāgvajra*.
Mind is the *bodhicitta* melted and attached to the image (*bimba*) during the engagement with the *mudrā*.
The third is the mind-vajra, which has attained supreme bliss and is the awakening of the vajra. Now,
if bliss does not arise through the door of the [consort's] body-image (*bimba*),
then one should slowly produce the sound of the vajra within the lotus.
Now, if a woman is not obtained, then one should perform tossing [of the seed] with the lotus of one's own hand for the sake of increasing bliss, but not for the sake of emission.

In this way, that abandonment of the seed becomes blissful; it removes the fear of death. This is the fourth, the Knowledge-Vajra, which is the mouth of the glorious Guru. Such is the rule for the practice of yoga.
Thus.
From the *Paramādibuddha* in twelve thousand [verses], the *Sekoddeśa* begins with the words "of this very... and so forth.

A yogi should effect the accomplishment—that is, the manifestation—of this very fire of omniscient gnosis (*sarvajñajñāna*), which burns away the fuel of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable without remainder, by means of smoke and the other signs. By what means? By those signs of the object of cognition within one's own mind, which, in all the Root Tantras and the *Laghu-tantra*, transcend existence and non-existence.
Completely devoid on all sides of any collection of atoms.

[In the *Sūtrasamuccaya* (SU): By means of the "appearances"—namely smoke, mirages, fireflies, lamps, flames, the moon, and the sun—which are well-known in the tantras and in the definitive-meaning (*nītārtha*) sūtras such as the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*, because they manifest as emptiness suddenly; by means of the "signs" (*nimitta*), because they are inconceivable due to the cessation of all conceptual construction and because they are the precursor form of the fruit of reality (*tattvaphala*); by means of the "reflections" (*bimba*)—that is, the appearances of the yogi’s direct perception which is the cognition of the emptiness of intrinsic nature devoid of subject and object—because they are like the sky, being unstained by external or internal impurities.
"It exists," and so forth.

Because it is unstained by the blemishes of conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence, because it transcends being and non-being, because it is to be personally realized by the yogi through its own cognition, because it is in every way uncontrived, wondrous, and devoid of intrinsic nature, and because it is entirely free from the mass of even the subtlest atoms; [it is the ultimate reality].
"Smoke," and so forth:
this is the appearance of emptiness in the form of smoke, which pervades all external and internal [realms].
And this arises immediately after the appearance of clouds.
As it has been said: "The first appears like a cloud; the second is similar to smoke.
A mirage has the appearance of moving water.
The two forms of the firefly and the lamp are well known.
These four signs arise because of the occurrence of darkness in a windowless room; thus, they belong to the yoga of night and the yoga of space.
As it is stated in the *Śrīsamāja* and other texts, when the mind has entered the vajra of cessation through the reverse order of the first and second [stages], the apprehension of the signs arises.
That sign is explained by Bodhivajra as being fivefold:
first, the appearance of a mirage; second, resembling smoke.
The third has the form of a firefly; the fourth is a blazing lamp; the fifth is the digit of darkness; the sixth is the great bindu; and the seventh is the radiant universal image.
That reflection which is seen like a dream in the void by eyes that are both closed and open, and which is not conceptually constructed— that reflection one should always meditate upon.
In the absence of a mental image (*bimba*), that cultivation for yogins is not true cultivation;
rather, the fifth is the constant light, resembling a cloudless sky.
[GSU, cd-] Thus it is said.
Then, preceded by the appearance of a cloudless sky, there is the appearance of emptiness in the form of fire; the appearances of flame, moon, and sun are well known.
"Darkness" (*tamaḥ*) refers to the light of Rāhu, an appearance like a black gem.
"Ka" is the appearance of a flash of lightning;
"mahābindu" is the appearance in the form of a blue lunar disc that illuminates all that is moving and stationary.
These are the signs with characteristics (*san-nimitta*); because they arise from the vision of a cloudless sky, they constitute the yoga of day and the yoga of open space.

Then, preceded by the vision of the Buddha-image consisting of the *saṃbhogakāya* situated within that [clear light], there arises in a single moment the universal image (*viśvabimba*), which is luminous, transparent like water in a vessel held in the hand, and possesses all aspects such as jars, cloths, and so forth.
"Closed," and so forth.

With eyes that are both closed and not closed—meaning with eyes half-opened, directed toward the intermediate space—that which is non-conceptualized (*an-utkalpita*) in the void, which is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, namely the yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*), one should meditate upon as the "image" (*bimba*), such as smoke and so on; one should bring it into one's own experience.
Both types of yoga have been taught in the *Śrīmad-Ādibuddha* by the passage beginning with "unattached to space" (*ākāśāsakta*).
And it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"There is a samādhi called Jewel-Light;
there is a samādhi called Jewel-Lamp."
The concentration named Moonlight;
the concentration named Sun-Lamp;
up to the concentration named Seer of All Aspects, and so forth.
Therefore, one who desires Buddhahood should cultivate the path of smoke and so forth, because it is free from doubt.
[Objection: But surely, since Mahāmudrā is unstained by the slightest taint of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), meditation (*bhāvanā*) would be a superimposition (*samāropa*).
Therefore, how can it be said that one should "meditate"?
To this, he says: "Non-existence," and so forth.

According to the instruction, when there is the absence of both the external and the internal, that very cultivation of the mental image (*bimba*) by yogins is, precisely because it is a state of being, "non-cultivation" (*abhāvanā*). But is it not the case that the non-existence of an entity is itself an absence? [No,] for the mind perceives the image as something unconstructed (*akalpita*).
Just as a young girl might see a reflection of an army in a mirror, though it is not a real thing,
so too one who is disciplined in reality sees past and future phenomena in the sky.
Its existence would not be a [real] existence, because it is seen as an object devoid of substantiality;
since there is no substance, the object exists like a magical illusion, a dream, or a conjuring trick.
For even when no substratum exists, this arising of qualities is clearly perceived,
like a wish-fulfilling gem that fulfills the infinite hopes of sentient beings.
In a *pratisenā* (divinatory mirror-image), a young girl sees thieves and so forth that have not been previously seen.

Since there is no distinction between the conceptualization of existence and the conceptualization of non-existence—both being merely conceptualizations—one might ask: "How can there be no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding what is non-existent? To this he says: "Existence," and so forth. This is because for the yogi, within the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*), neither the conceptualization of existence nor the conceptualization of non-existence exists.
Why? Because in the image of emptiness, there is the perception of smoke and so forth, which are non-conceptualized.
This is the intention:
if it were conceptualized, then it would be a [real] entity, like a jar, a cloth, and so on.
If there were non-perception, then existence would be like that of the son of a barren woman and so forth;
however, in this case, because there is perception through non-conceptual direct experience (*akalpita-pratyakṣa*), everything is well-established.
In order to establish that which is seen as non-conceptual, he states a corresponding example, beginning with "pratisenā" (the reflected image):

the *pratisenā* is the visualization of the practitioner, appearing in a mirror, a sword, the thumb, a lamp, the moon, the sun, water, or the range of vision; it is devoid of substantial reality and is not produced by external conditions such as thieves and the like.
For this non-conceptual vision, existence and non-existence do not exist, because there is only the perception of causal efficiency devoid of any real entity (*nirvastuka*).
Even in the world, an object is seen despite being devoid of a real entity, as in the case of illusions, dreams, and magical nets; for this very reason, he says:
"non-existent," with respect to the self and so forth.

Since the subject (*dharmin*) does not exist, that production of non-conceptual knowledge is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) because it accomplishes the welfare of the world in all its aspects;
thus he states the establishment of the example with the words "unseen," and so forth.

Furthermore, it was previously stated that the girl, whose eyes are empowered by mantra, sees that very *pratisenā* while remaining in her place; whereas the practitioners who are the bringers of the *pratisenā* go to that location described by the girl and see it with their local eyes—eyes that possess obstructions and have limited scope.
This is the intended meaning:
the practitioner, whose eyes are empowered by the mantra of the perfected one’s instruction, goes and sees [the object] with his own local eyes, just as the girl does, without stumbling.
If one sees that which has the nature of existence, why does one not see one's own face?
If one sees that which has the nature of non-existence, why does one not see a rabbit’s horn? Furthermore, one does not see with one's own eyes what is seen by the eyes of another.
That which is being perceived is unborn, just like the birth of a maiden.
Furthermore, that by which Buddhahood is accomplished is called the "means" (*upāya*), as indicated by the passage beginning with "yogitva.
Here, *yogitva* is twofold: mundane and supramundane.
In this context, supramundane yogic state is Buddhahood;

it is "supreme merit" because of the fulfillment of the accumulation of merit, and likewise "pure" and "destroyer of evil" because of the fulfillment of the accumulation of gnosis. The moon of the awakening mind perceives that supramundane reality in the sky, which is inaccessible to ordinary beings who have not been instructed.
And because that [reality] is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he says "if" (*yadi*).

Since it is not seen at other times by other eyes, and because it is obscured by the blindness of one's own eyes, by this example of non-perception, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogi is established as unborn due to the total absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), like the perception of a daughter’s son in a dream; such is the knowledge of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña-jñāna*).
And it has been said: "Just as a young girl in this dream," and so forth.
Now, by way of the Saṃvara Tantra and others, he explains the sequence of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) beginning with the words "Yogitvam," etc.;
and it has also been stated in the *Laghu-tantra*.
The state of a yogin is supreme merit, purifying and destructive of evil; it is accomplished through the recitation of mantras, through meditation, and with ease— that Buddhahood,
which is purifying and destructive of evil,
is accomplished through the recitation of mantras, through meditation, and with ease.
It is stated here that "the state of a yogi is accomplished by this means;
for yogis, it is accomplished"—this is the reading of the scripture (*āgama*).
This means is the yoga of six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), which is taught here in reverse order from the middle, omitting every other limb.
That very factor which has not been explicitly stated must first be understood through the power of the factors already stated;
just as when it is said, "This is the sun," the other, the moon, is apprehended by implication even though unstated,
so too a mutually dependent property, though unstated, is apprehended by means of the property that has been stated.

Therefore, in this tantra, the three subsequent limbs are taught with one intervening [limb]; the limb mentioned in the middle must be performed first here according to the guru’s instruction—this is the oral tradition of the gurus.
Otherwise, if one were to follow the sequence of recitation as stated in the tantra, what indeed would that "oral tradition of the gurus" be?
Therefore, it is [to be practiced] together with the oral tradition of the gurus.

By this [phrase] "mantra-recitation and so forth in reverse order from the middle," the meaning is that the word for meditation (*dhyāna*) should be recited prior to the mantra-recitation (*mantrajāpa*). This [refers to] the three limbs not previously mentioned: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and mindfulness (*anusmṛti*).
"This" refers to the sun.
The term "another" should be understood as referring to other appearances of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth;
by means of that, one should understand everything everywhere.
Alternatively, [this work] is to be understood through the commentary composed by a Bodhisattva, and not through those composed by those who are merely conceited with their own scholarship.
Therefore, in this context, the other three limbs are to be understood through the passage beginning with "by means of meditative absorption" (*dhyānena*).
The meaning condensed within these three limbs—according to the six limbs taught in other systems that are not dependent on this [text]—is to be understood here.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*:

Withdrawal (pratyāhāra), as well as meditation (dhyāna), breath control (prāṇāyāma), concentration (dhāraṇā), recollection (anusmṛti), and meditative absorption (samādhi)— this is considered the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅga-yoga). Therefore, withdrawal should be understood as preceded by meditation,
and breath control should be understood as preceded by the recitation of mantra.

In this context, by the term "recitation of mantra" (mantrajāpa), the recitation of the neuter [syllable] or the vajra-recitation, which is the sustenance of the vital breath (prāṇadhāraṇā), is expressed;
it should be understood that "recollection preceded by bliss" (sukhapūrvānusmṛti) is intended here.
In this regard, by the word "bliss" (sukha), meditative concentration (samādhi) is expressed.
Thus, by means of these six limbs, the state of a yogin—that is, Buddhahood—is accomplished.
In general, this mundane external yoga is to be understood through what is taught in other tantras, such as the *Śrīsamāja-tantra*, within this tantra; so said the noble Vajrapāṇipāda.
In the *Śrīsamājottara*, in the eighteenth chapter,

the recitation of the neuter (*napuṃsakajāpa*) consists of the observation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as it has entered the *avadhūtī*; this is the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*), the ultimate recitation (*paramārthajāpa*), which involves the mental construction of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) above the tip of the nose.
At the culmination of the excellence of that cultivation, there is the restraint of breath (*prāṇāyāma-nirodha*).
And it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*:

"For beginners and child-like yogins, the worldly fruit is attained through the recitation of mantras—which is designated as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)—through meditation on the conceptualization of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, and through the bliss of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the movement of the syllables; by means of this worldly truth, [they reach] up to the world-system of Akaniṣṭha."
Thus, through both stages, mundane and supramundane yogic accomplishment (*yogitva*) is achieved.
Herein, supramundane yogic accomplishment is achieved by means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*); how this is so is now explained:

"Withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) here refers to the non-engagement of the visual consciousness and other faculties with external objects such as forms, and the engagement of the visual consciousness and other faculties with internal objects by means of the divine eye and other divine faculties.

The limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is said to be the vision of all phenomena as unconstructed by means of the objective support of emptiness within oneself—like a young girl seeing her own reflection in an empty mirror. One should contemplate that the [breath] goes upward from the navel as the image of a Buddha of the three realms, according to one's wish, until the limit of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
One should contemplate the inhalation (*ucchvāsa*) in the nose, and likewise the exhalation (*niḥśvāsa*) below, according to one's wish, until non-apprehension.
The comprehension of the sound is the supreme, well-guarded tradition;

likewise, "by means of the recitation of the mantra" refers to withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). The utterance of the syllable *oṃ* and so forth—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the divine ear-cognition (*divyaśrotravijñāna*) and others, such as the divine eye-cognition (*divyacakṣurvijñāna*) and so on, [attained] by that name.
From that [arises] meditation (*dhyāna*); and when all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are seen as empty,
wisdom (*prajñā*) is the engagement of the mind with them.
Vitarka is the grasping of an object by the mind; vicāra is the application of that grasping of an object;
rati is the fixing of the mind upon all objects.
The so-called "immovable bliss" (*acalasukha*) is the attainment of bliss from all states;
thus, the limb of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*) is said to be fivefold.
Following that is what is called "breath control" (*prāṇāyāma*), which is the cessation of the paths of the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, the left and right channels.

The constant movement of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel (*avadhūtī*) occurs through the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*). By means of the syllable *Oṃ*, the yogi performs inhalation; by *Hūṃ*, retention; and by *Āḥ*, exhalation—having the nature of the Moon, Rāhu, and the Sun respectively. This is called the limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Following that is what is known as "retention" (*dhāraṇā*): the entry of the vital wind into the mandalas of Mahendra, Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, without its exiting to the exterior.
"The placement of the vital breath (prāṇa) in the bindu" is said to be the limb of concentration (dhāraṇā).

Following that is "recollection" (anusmṛti), which consists of the vision of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the form of a reflection; inhalation is characterized by entry, while cessation is its stabilization, and exhalation is its outward movement.

And this meaning, established by one's own experience, is of definitive import (*nītārtha*); it is approved by the great Bodhisattvas beginning with Vajrapāṇi, and is not an object of misconception. Others, however, for the sake of other purposes, [assert that] the vision of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) is the direct perception (*pratyakṣīkāra*) of the non-conceptual Caṇḍālī.
By means of the internal radiance of the twilight,
it is free from conceptual construction;
therefore, it is a circle of light whose form flashes with many rays.
Then, recollecting that which has many forms, a throbbing nature, and a pervasion of the triple world, is called the limb of recollection (*anusmṛty-aṅga*).

Then, through devotion to one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), there is the attainment of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*); the unification of the mind within that is the mind devoid of subject and object, which is called the limb of meditative absorption (*samādhy-aṅga*) by the Tathāgatas.
Thus, the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) has been explained here in brief.

In detail, this should be understood by the yogin through the instruction of a true guru for the sake of attaining Mahāmudrā, either in the *Lakṣābhidhāna* or in the *Paramādibuddha*. Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the path of the six limbs at its very beginning, it is taught in other tantras that here, in the *Śrīsamājottara*, there are the service (*sevā*), the near-attainment (*upasādhana*), the attainment (*sādhana*), and the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*).
Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"During the time of service (*sevā*), one should diligently visualize the form of Mahoṣṇīṣa;
during the time of near-attainment (*upasādhana*), however, the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī; and during the time of attainment (*sādhana*), one intent on yoga should visualize the form of the deity."

"That which reveals the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) to beings of superior inclination by means of the employment of contradictory speech— that was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*)," according to the definition thus stated.
Since it is stated in the Tantra that it possesses the characteristics of six points,
and likewise in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"The intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*), the non-intentional, the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), and the definitive meaning (*niyatārtha*)."

"At the time of the great accomplishment (mahāsādhana), however, one should establish the image of the all-pervading Lord Buddha—the uṣṇīṣa-image, the image of the Buddha—within the space of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) throughout the three realms without exception; having established the mind-vajra there, one should meditate upon it during the stage of service (sevā) at the first stage by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and stabilize it by means of the limb of meditation (dhyāna). Thus it is said here, according to another interpretation of the twilight terminology (sandhyābhāṣā).
In this regard, the Blessed One’s promise is:
"Abandoning all doubt, one should examine it for a single day;
if no conviction arises therein, then these words of mine are false."

In this context, "conviction" (*pratyaya*) refers to signs such as smoke and the like, and not other things such as mantras, by which conviction will arise for practitioners in a single day. Therefore, having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence and rendered them supportless, [the teaching] is proclaimed as the "Six Limits" (*satkoṭi*)—profound in the void, beyond literal expression, and not according to words. This clear exposition of reality is taught for the sake of awakening beings with dull faculties; it is manifest and not expressed in the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (twilight language).

In the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) concerning maṇḍalas and so forth, as well as in the stages of conduct (*caryā*), there is an explanation of the meaning that is explicit; this is called "speech according to the literal sound" (*yathāruta-bhāṣita*).
Words such as *koṭākhyaka* and others, which are excluded from worldly treatises, are the conventions of the Tathāgatas; that is proclaimed as "not according to the literal sound" (*naruta*).

The Victor speaks with "interpretable meaning" (*neyārtha*) when he explains the concealed reality. Furthermore, he speaks with "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*) for the purpose of revealing the truly existent reality.

"Thus, the 'Buddha-image' refers to the three realms; this means the vision of the three worlds as consisting of various *saṃbhogakāyas* appearing as a black line situated within the great bindu. 'All thought' refers to whatever conceptualization one might think."
The cognition becomes without support and without foundation;
that cognition, such as smoke and so forth, is cultivated by the yogin—this is the rule of the Tathāgata.
Likewise, by means of the instruments and the applications of the bonds, one should accomplish the three worlds.
Thus,
one should accomplish the image of the Buddha and the three worlds by means of the instruments, such as the eyes and so forth;
this very instruction is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
In that regard, through the instruction of the guru, the yogi first sees smoke in the sky and not a mirage; this is to be known from one's own experience.
After that, he sees the mirage, and subsequently that very same smoke and so forth, free from conceptual construction, like a prognostic image (*pratisenā*).
Thus, first is the sign of smoke,
second is the sign of a mirage,
and third is the sign of fireflies.
The fourth is the sign of illumination;
the fifth is the sign resembling a cloudless sky. This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Samājottara* and also in the *Dākinīvajrapañjara*.
Regarding that, the Blessed One said in the *Dākinīvajrapañjara*: "O Vāmā..."

The statement that "the second is the sign of the mirage" (*marīcikānimitta*) in another tantra means that it should be understood in reverse order as "first, the form of a mirage. This is to be known from the instruction of a true guru, from the commentaries composed by Bodhisattvas, and from one's own experience. Primarily through the non-duality of wisdom and skillful means, the five signs beginning with the mirage—which are the forms of the purification of the five elements—are taught in the *Śrīsamāja* and other tantras, since the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) is also mentioned in the tantras.
And it is said in the eighteenth chapter:

"I bow to all those vast ones, who resemble Bodhisattvas—the water, fire, wind, earth, and space. [This refers to] the dissolution of earth into water, appearing like a mirage, and the dissolution of water into fire, appearing like smoke.
Due to the dissolution of fire into wind, [the mind] takes on the form of a firefly;

because the three appearances enter into the subtle constituent (*sūkṣmadhātu*), it has the nature of a mass of light like a lamp. That is the cause of omniscience, for it brings about cessation when near to accomplishment.
Afterwards, it takes a form like an illusion, a form like a dream, moment by moment. And so forth.
Therefore, based on these words of the Blessed One, there is first the realization through the cultivation of signs such as smoke;
those who will say that this occurs at the time of accomplishment are all violators of the Blessed One’s promise.
Abandoning all thought, one should examine the sign for a single day; those who speak otherwise are detractors of the Blessed One’s word.

The mundane signs such as smoke and so forth that appear at the time of accomplishment are not like illusions or dreams, because they possess the actual capacity for actions such as burning with smoke, flames, and the like; likewise, there is also a rain of saffron, flowers, jewels, gold, and so on.
Therefore, the signs such as smoke and so forth arise from the yoga of the six limbs.
Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"Therefore, one should meditate upon the six limbs; thereafter, one should again perceive the signs equal to self-consecration through the sequence of the forward-order procedure."

Here, what is called "self-consecration" (svādhiṣṭhāna) is the vision of the relative truth; its sign, through withdrawal (pratyāhāra), is a manifestation resembling smoke, clouds, and so forth, appearing in the shape of a crescent moon.

Because it dissolves into the appearance of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and because its form is eternally luminous like a cloudless sky, it is said to be "equal to the cloudless sky. Thus, the signs are described as fivefold.
And it was previously stated:
"The earth may go into water, and water goes into fire..."

Fire follows after wind; wind enters into consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness, having become the constituent part of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), then enters the luminous state (*prabhāsvara*).
And that [luminosity] is first seen as far as the limit of a lamp, and thereafter as cloudless, stainless space.
In the *Māyājāla*, on the chapter concerning meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Blessed One has taught another six signs, beginning with "flame" and ending with "drop," as follows:
"The self-arisen one born from space; the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*); Vairocana, the great radiance; the light of wisdom, the illuminator."
"The lamp of the world, the torch of gnosis, of great splendor, and luminous"— thus,

in the *Māyājāla* through the yoga of day, the signs (*nimitta*) which are the forms of the purification of the [five] aggregates are taught by the passage beginning with "born from space" (*gaganodbhava*).

However, in the glorious *Ādibuddha*, the king of tantras, ten signs (*daśanimitta*) consisting of the purification of the objects, the sense faculties, wisdom (*prajñā*), and means (*upāya*) are primarily set forth.

"By these means" refers to the divine eye and so forth, which are obtained as limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Because they are the cause for binding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the conjunctions of the bonds, they take the form of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). The sense is that this very withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is [the goal], because it is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) free from conceptual construction and error;
and it is said in the *Samājottara*:

The withdrawal (pratyāhāra) of the ten sense objects, established in their own respective functions in every respect, is proclaimed as the withdrawal of each [object] with regard to the consumption of desires;
this is its specific definition.

The sense faculties (*indriya*) and the objects of the sense faculties (*indriyārtha*), their respective functions (*svavṛtti*)—that is, their engagement in the form of the grasped and the grasper—and abiding therein constitute "abiding in one's own function. Regarding this, "desires" (*kāma*) refers to those things such as forms and so forth that are desired or longed for as food; they are categorized as inferior, middling, and superior.
By means of these two verses, the Blessed One has explained in the *Māyājāla* the "other sign" (*aparanimitta*) through the terminology of the twilight language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).

The manifestation that arises from the previously mentioned cloudless sky is the "sky-born self-arisen one" (*gaganodbhava-svayambhū*), which refers here to the mind free from all conceptual constructions (*sarva-vikalpa-rahitacitta*).
In this context, "the fire of the wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñānānala*) refers to the manifestation of flames,
and "Vairocana of great radiance" (*vairocano mahādīptiḥ*) refers to the manifestation of the moon.
That very light of knowledge is the Radiant One;
it is the Lamp of the World; it is the manifestation as the Sun; it is the Torch of Knowledge; it is the manifestation as Rāhu.
The one of great splendor, "the radiant," appears as a flash of lightning;
the King of Knowledge, the Lord of Supreme Mantras, appears as a drop (*bindu*) in the form of a blue-colored lunar mandala.

The King of Mantras, "the accomplisher of the great purpose," is seen by the yogi through the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)—by means of the eyes and other sense organs—as the appearance of all phenomena within the three realms in every aspect, resembling an illusion, a dream, or a reflected image. Following that, [it is perceived] through the binding of the breath (*prāṇāyāma*).

By means of these instruments and the conjunctions of bondage, one should accomplish the three worlds— characterized by the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and consisting of the nature of the stable and the moving.
Thus, in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*, the Blessed One said:
"The entire threefold world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is accomplished without exception or remainder."
In all world-systems, as many as there are possessors of the vajra-body;
"That which is a repeated bringing back, again and again, toward each [object of] grasping—that is *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal)"; this is the definition of the first limb.
Thus is the Lord's rule regarding the cultivation of the sixfold yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

Likewise, in the *Śrīsamāja*, the Blessed One said: "In the absence [of an object], there is no cultivation; cultivation is not [truly] cultivation. Thus, existence is not existence, and cultivation is not perceived."

Thus, here, in the absence [of objects], the cultivation [of the mind] in a cloudless sky is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); that very thing is "cultivation in the absence," which is the non-existence of cultivation—
that is, cultivation is indeed no cultivation at all.

In this context, the cultivation of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) which occurs in the absence [of objects], like a cloudless sky—that cultivation is not truly a cultivation because it is devoid of the cultivation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That entity which is seen through withdrawal would not be an entity, because one sees entities as non-entities—past, future, and present—when they are free from conceptualization.
Therefore, the cultivation of conceptual construction is not perceived within the cultivation of withdrawal; such is the word of the Blessed One.
This cultivation was also taught by the Blessed One in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, as follows:
"That entity which is seen and made manifest through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) according to the described characteristics is neither an entity nor a conceptualized form."

Why? Because through one-pointedness of the non-conceptual mind, there is the vision of past, future, and present entities as they are not conceptually constructed; thus it is called a limb of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*).
And it is said:
"In brief, the five sense-desires [arise] from the application of the five Buddhas."
Conceptualization is called meditation; that meditation is of five kinds.

"O Noble Subhūti, where will he who attains yoga in this Perfection of Wisdom attain that yoga— [he who attains] both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), as well as joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*)? Subhūti said:
O Kauśika, he who will attain yoga in the perfection of wisdom will attain yoga in space;
O Kauśika, that is yoga in the open air, as well as one-pointedness of mind—these five are the summaries of the meditations.
The three secrets, as well as applied thought and sustained thought, are the enjoyment of that.
The third is like joy; the fourth is the gathering of bliss;
one's own mind is to be known as the fifth, which is the arising and passing away of knowledge and the object of knowledge.
"Pervaded by all Buddhas, peaceful, and established in all space"—this is the detailed explanation of the second limb for the purpose of purifying withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).

The five objects of desire, form and so forth, are the objective domains of the sense faculties; through the "union" (*yojana*)—that is, the unification with the sense faculties in brief—the five Buddhas, such as the Eye and so forth, are joined by means of the application of the five Buddhas. Therefore, the pure conceptualization that "form and the others are also the five Buddhas" is *dhyāna*. And that consists of five types, distinguished by vitarka and the others.
Regarding the passage beginning with "vitarka" and so forth, it is an explanation of the classifications:
the "three secrets" (*guhyatraya*) refers to the sense organs, their objects, and consciousnesses;
the five sense organs, the cognitions of those organs, and their respective objects are of the nature of the five Tathāgatas. The thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of this is *vitarka*.
The state of investigation within that very [state] is "investigation" (*vicāra*).
For one who investigates in this way, that which is characterized by mental well-being (*saumanasya*) through the orientation toward entering reality is "resembling joy" (*prītisaṃkāśa*).
And the bliss (*sukha*) characterized by physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) and so forth, which is attained through adherence to reality—that is the "inclusion of bliss" (*sukhasaṃgraha*).

For one who practices in this way, through reaching the ultimate limit of excellence, there arises the knowledge and the object of knowledge (*jñānajñeyodaya*). This refers to the arising of the six functioning consciousnesses, beginning with the eye-consciousness, within the range of objects from form (*rūpa*) up to the *dharmadhātu*. The "destruction" (*kṣaya*) of that [arising] is the one-pointedness of mind characterized by the thorough knowledge of the emptiness of subject and object; this is called "one's own mind.

Such a mind—consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful, mere appearance, and culminating in the single reality of universal emptiness—is born. Thus, the second limb, consisting of five divisions, is "space" (*ākāśa*) according to the night yoga.
"In an open space" means that one who, through association with the daytime, desires to attain [the goal] and thinks, "I must train in the perfection of wisdom."
The meditation on Mahāmudrā is equal to a prognostic image (pratisenā) or an illusion, as taught by the Blessed One in the cloudless sky;
thus, through withdrawal and meditative concentration, the branch of service is described.
Thereafter, by means of the designation "the form of Amṛtakundalī" or in another intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā), the wind is spoken of.
And that is of five kinds;
