thus the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*:
"The breath consists of the five jewels and is empowered by the five Buddhas."
Having emanated it in the form of a single mass, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose.

Thus, here, by the term "five jewels" (pañcaratna), the five elements beginning with earth— which possess the nature of the five mandalas of the tongue— are meant; the breath consisting of these is "consisting of the five jewels," [referring to] the right nostril.
Likewise, the five Buddhas possess the nature of the five mandalas of the *lalanā* and are the five aggregates beginning with consciousness;
the breath presided over by them in the left nostril is called the third limb of *prāṇāyāma*, by means of the designation "the form of the nectar-curling one" (*amṛtakundalī*) and so forth.
And it has been said:
The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*;
having meditated on one's own mantra in the heart, one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *bindu*.
Thus the detailed explanation is stated: it is five-colored and consists of the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
for this very reason, it is a great jewel. That by which the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—life—is extended (*āyāmyate*), lengthened, and expanded is known as *prāṇāyāma*.

Having meditated upon that very [seed-syllable] in the heart of one's own mantra— that is, in the lotus of one's own heart— as a *bindu* whose nature is entry and so forth, because it is practiced day and night, one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as having entered the *bindu*; this is the third limb.
"Having emitted it in the form of a *piṇḍa*":
here, the *piṇḍa* is the unification of the left and right mandalas within the central channel, the *avadhūtī*, of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*).
Having emitted that vital breath in the form of a *piṇḍa*, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose.
Here, by the word "nose" (nāsikā), the pericarp of the lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown are meant;

one should contemplate [the breath] at the tip of that [pericarp], meaning one should contemplate it at the tip of the nose. From the pericarp, within the center of the pericarp—and not on the petals of the right or left lotus—one thus restrains the vital breath (prāṇa) in the form of a sphere (piṇḍa) at the location of the drop (bindu).
By that very means, its retention is described;
thus, through these two limbs, the subsidiary practice (*upasādhana*) is performed by means of the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
That very subsidiary practice is called the "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*).
It should be recited with the tongue not moving from the middle [channel]; that is, it is not by means of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through the left or right channel.

When the image of the *uṣṇīṣa* is perceived, the vital breath is subsequently restrained in the form of a drop (*bindu*) at the location of the *bindu* through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Therefore, this is called its "retention" (*dhāraṇā*); such is the limb of retention (*dhāraṇā-aṅga*).
And it has been said:
"When one's own sensory jewel has ceased, one should maintain [the practice]; this is known as dhāraṇā."
The detailed explanation of this is as follows:
the objects are one's own form and so forth,
and the sense faculties are the eye and so forth.

When one's own sense organ has been restrained and dissolved, and when the jewel that serves as the support for both the objects and the senses—the jewel of the mind (*cittaratna*)—has been restrained along with *prāṇāyāma* and has set, whatever one should maintain therein is "retention" (*dhāraṇā*).

What is that? It is the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoti*). This is the fourth limb, called retention, which is to be recited with the middle *mudrā* (the *abhinnāṅga*); its explanation is: "by means of the non-circulation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the left and right channels."
And it has been said:
"One who subsists on alms should not recite [mantras], nor should he be devoted to begging; rather, the practitioner of mantra should act [thus]."

It is said that the instruction of the Guru is to be understood through the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*); thus, the preliminary practice consists of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*),
followed by the visualization of the deity’s form (*devatābimba*) in the actual practice (*sādhana*).

Here, by the power of *dhāraṇā*, the yogi perceives the *caṇḍālī* situated at the navel as blazing; she is free from all obscurations, like a *pratisenā* [magical reflection], emitting clouds of infinite Buddha-rays, and resplendent with a circle of light. That is called *anusmṛti*. It is the rule that at the end of *dhāraṇā*, one should meditate on the yoga of *caṇḍālī*;
then, by the flame of her gnosis (*jñānārcis*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, are incinerated and become unified into a single mass.
The elements beginning with consciousness and ending with earth, which reside in the left and right channels and possess the nature of the maṇḍalas, enter the lunar maṇḍala in the forehead.

Then, when the moon has been melted by the fire of gnosis from Cāndālī, that bodhicitta descends in the form of a drop to the throat, the heart, the navel, and the secret lotus, having the nature of joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), and the cessation of joy (*viramānanda*); thereafter, up to the vajra-jewel, it has the nature of innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
Alternatively, it has the nature of the distinct characteristics of the *vicitra*, *vipāka*, *vimarda*, and *vilakṣaṇa* [moments].

Thus, one should recite the mantra whose limbs are unbroken, which is filled with sixteen digits (*kalā*) and effects the enjoyment of all desires. [Regarding this: "The broken form" refers to the syllables; "eating alms" refers to the utterance; "articulation" is called "perception"; "alms" is the convention; and "mantra" is called the "reality of mantra," consisting of entry, stability, emergence, and analytical observation.

It is said that the recollection of the indivisibility of the limbs of suchness— the ultimate reality— is the indivisibility of the limbs of the Middle Way, and this is declared to be the means of accomplishment.
Furthermore, it has been stated:

When that bliss which is internal gives [joy] through the power of cultivation, it is similar to the bliss of emission; this is merely a metaphorical illustration. In its true nature, the bliss born of the two organs during emission does not equal even a ten-millionth part of the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Here, that state of unchanging bliss which consists of innate joy (*sahajānanda*) is an indescribable state, unknowable by those who practice with physical power alone.

For Bodhisattvas, this is called the "emptiness samādhi," and not, according to worldly convention, that which follows the meaning of nihilism. Thus, through the six-limbed yoga, mantra recitation, meditation, and bliss, the supreme state of Buddhahood is accomplished for yogins; it is meritorious, purifying, and the destroyer of evil.

The Blessed One has declared that in this very life, the rule of the goal and the practitioner is established. One should indeed expand that stable [reality] through the vajra-path into the elements of space.

"Having visualized that which was reached through recollection, one should emanate it in its very form. Thus, by means of the vajra-path, following the sequence of the five signs that are not to be transgressed, and through the entry into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), one should emanate the stable and pure mind throughout the expanse of space (*khadhātu*) in the very nature of the *dharmakāya*.

Having thus visualized and directly realized oneself as having entered the clear light, one should emanate—in that same sequence and in that very form—that which was previously reached at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) through recollection in the form of a mirage and so forth.

This fifth limb just mentioned, "recollection" (*anusmṛti*), refers to that state whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); by the words ending with "is called the awakening to emptiness by the Bodhisattvas," meditative absorption (*samādhi*) has been described.
And it has been said:

Having briefly withdrawn all phenomena through the meditative union of wisdom and means, one should visualize the image in the center by means of the yoga of the mass. The instantaneous perfection of gnosis is designated as "samādhi" in reality;
furthermore, here the cause is both endowed with all aspects and devoid of aspects.

The entity perceived through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), such as a jar or a cloth, appears in all its aspects like a reflected image (*pratisenā*); it is non-conceptual (*kalpanāpodha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) because it is seen by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, it is formless (*nirākāra*) and transcends the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu-dharmatātīta*) because it is devoid of conceptual construction.
Since it is perceivable by eyes that are either covered or uncovered, it is therefore neither form nor other than form;
it is not accessible to the eye, nor is it without the eye.
Thus, the cause is devoid of all forms and yet possesses no form.
"The Perfection of Wisdom is the great emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects" (IYY), and so forth;
this very same meaning was stated by the venerable Mahābodhisattva Śrīvajragarbhapāda in the *Śrīhevajraṭīkā*, as follows:
Now, the meditation on the ultimate reality of the previously mentioned wisdom and means is described by the words "the state to be meditated upon" and so forth:
here, in space, the state to be meditated upon is like a dream, transcending the nature of atoms.

Through the thorough knowledge of that [non-existence], one should meditate upon the non-existence of all existence—the stationary and the moving—by means of the union of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-samāpatti*) and through the yoga of the conventional and the ultimate. Having unified this into a single form as a mass (*piṇḍarūpa*), namely the form of Mahāmudrā, one should visualize and know the state of the Great Vajradhara, whose nature is the union (*yuganaddha*), in the midst of that which is stationary and moving. By this sequence, the instantaneous accomplishment of gnosis (*jñāna*) in a single moment is "samādhi"; this is the sixth limb. Thus, according to the *Samāja* system, is the sequence of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). [This is stated] by the words beginning with "existence" and "that which is to be meditated upon."

"Direct perception is said to be that which is free from conceptual construction, devoid of mental fabrication, and non-erroneous, consisting in the observation of appearances with a mind free from conceptualization," and so forth;
thus it was stated in the *Tantrottara* by the venerable Mañjuśrī, the Lord of the Ten Bhūmis.

Through the six [practices] beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the one endowed with the power of the Ten Strengths has taught the meditation on emptiness. Furthermore, at night there is the yoga of smoke and so forth, and during the day as well the lamp and so forth in the sky;

by means of withdrawal, the yogi perceives the forms of the three times situated in the expanse of the sky. Therein, by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he makes the mind firm, abandoning external phenomena. By means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) in the darkness, he should cause the vital wind to flow, devoid of both moon and sun; furthermore, by means of the limb of retention (*dhāraṇā*), he renders it free from inhalation and exhalation within the drop (*bindu*).

Through the recollection of space, great rays of light issue forth from one’s own reflection like those from the moon; by means of the vajra-samādhi, the semen proceeds to the head, completely filled with the bliss of stainlessness. Through the vision of space, delusion reaches its end; through the vision of emptiness, passion reaches its end. When the vital wind is restrained, existence becomes that which is to be meditated upon through wisdom, and non-existence through thorough knowledge; likewise, Heruka is to be meditated upon as both existence and non-existence through thorough knowledge. Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Hevajra Tantra* by the Great Vajradhara, who possesses the strength of the ten powers.
The cultivation of emptiness is the realization of all aspects of all forms of emptiness,
both in the darkness of night and in the light of day.

The form of the three-fold sacrifice consists of the forms of desire, form, and formlessness. Because there is no outward departure [of breath] within that *avadhūtī*, it is devoid of exhalation and inhalation; [it arises] from one's own reflection, the universal reflection. Through the gaze of space—that is, the gaze resting in the intermediate state—there is the destruction of delusion, which is its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); and she is Locanā. Through the internal gaze—that is, the gaze at the emptiness of the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth—there is the destruction of passion; and she is Pāṇḍarā.

Through the gaze of the bodiless one (*anaṅgadṛṣṭi*), by means of the gaze of innate passion (*sahajānurāga*) toward the empty image (*śūnyatābimba*) endowed with the excellence of all aspects, there occurs the destruction—the state of being without intrinsic nature and the state of being free from obscuration—of hatred, that is, of worldly hatred. Through the gaze of the bodiless one, the destruction of hatred occurs by virtue of the bliss of the purity of the seminal essence (*śukra*). Through the gaze of the nose (*ghrāṇadṛṣṭi*), there occurs the destruction of pride by virtue of the unassailable Brahma-sound. When breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is restrained, the stainless maṇḍala indeed arises from the form of the Buddha; the pair of stages occurs sequentially in the head, throat, heart, navel, and secret place.

At the crown of the head: because the Buddha and the Teacher are awakened by the semen (*śukra*) moving upward and by the *rajas* below, and because they are free from the three impurities (*trimala*), they are the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind.

Great Hatred (*mahādveṣatā*) is she, the Sovereign Lady of the Vajra Realm (*Vajradhātvīśvarī*). From that bliss which arises through the purity of the semen, there is—by means of the "nose-view," that is, the vision directed toward the intermediate space characterized by the nose—the destruction of ordinary pride and the state of being free from obscurations.
And she is Māmakī.

From the unstruck sound of the Brahma-voice (*anāhata-brahmaghoṣa*), through the arising of the resonance of unstruck great bliss (*anāhata-mahāsukha-dhvani*), when [the breath] is restrained within *prāṇāyāma* due to the absence of outward emission and the manifestation of the limb of *dhāraṇā*, there occurs—through the vivid appearance of the non-conceptual innate *caṇḍālī*—the stainless lunar disk, the mandala of pure radiance, from the Buddha-image, the universal image (*viśvabimba*). This arises from the inexhaustibility of the mundane.
And she is Tāraṇī.

When the semen (*śukra*) has ascended through the wheels (*cakra*) and the menstrual blood (*rajas*) has descended, from the unstruck sound of Brahma (*anāhata-brahmaghoṣa*), there arises the manifestation of the supreme syllable and great bliss (*paramākṣara-mahāsukha*), whereby there is the destruction of envy; she is Viśvamātā.
And thus, by means of the sequence of perceiving two stages (*bhūmi*) at each wheel, one becomes a master of the twelve stages (*dvādaśabhūmīśvara*).
For instance, by the cessation of three thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations at the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*), the two stages of *pramuditā* and *vimalā* are attained;
likewise, by such cessation at the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*), the two stages of *prabhākarī* and *arciṣmatī* are attained;
and similarly, by such [cessation] at the heart lotus (*hṛdayābja*), the two stages of *sudurjayā* and *abhimukhī* are attained.
The two stages, Dūraṅgamā and Acalā, are also in the lotus of the throat;
and in the lotus of the *ūrṇā*, the two stages, Sādhumatī and Dharmameghā.
These are the five pairs of Bodhisattva stages. Likewise, in the *uṣṇīṣa*-wheel, however, there are these two: the Buddha stage, Samantaprabhā, and the Vajradhara stage, Jñānavatī.

And thus, by the cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, one becomes the Buddha, the Blessed One—the possessor of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, free from the three stains, the lord of the twelve stages, and the teacher of non-conceptual Dharma; in this way, purity is demonstrated. Now, the individual arising of the five eyes is described: the flesh-eye belongs to dogs and the like [by virtue of their natural qualities]; the divine eye belongs to the gods; and the third, the Buddha-eye, resides in the hearts of each of the Śrāvakas and humans.

The fourth is the stainless, pure eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*) among the Bodhisattvas; the fifth is the all-seeing eye of knowledge (*jñānacakṣus*) of the Buddhas, which is free from the three stains. The immovable bliss-semen is the *vajra*, and by holding it, one is indeed Vajradhṛk. The seed of the body is semen, and the Victorious One who has conquered is the Father (*jinajig*); that bliss which exists in the navel-cakra is the target, and the Protector who perceives that target is Ārolika, the supreme bliss in the heart. That which is to be known is held in the throat, and he who experiences that immovable bliss is Ratnadhṛk.
He who holds wisdom—that which is held upon the head in the Tantra—is the bliss of the purity of semen; the unchanging supreme bliss at the *uṣṇīṣa* in the aperture of Brahmā, full of sixteen joys.

That wisdom which is devoid of intrinsic nature, the sixteenth digit of the supreme moon at the end of the full moon, is his infinite Vidyā; he whose head bears the thunderbolt is the sixth, Vajrasattva.

When the disks of the moon and sun have vanished, when the vital wind is always restrained on both paths, when the lotus and the vajra are awakened, and the molten moon has entered the great solar disk.
By the words beginning with "of them" (*nām*), [it is meant] by virtue of their natural qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and by virtue of their class-qualities (*jāti-guṇa*).

Now, he describes the nature of the six Tathāgatas residing in the pericarp of the lotuses of the six wheels, which have been rendered free from obscuration through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*), starting with the words "niḥspanda" and so forth. Vajradhṛk is Akṣobhya;
Jinajik is Vairocana.
Ārolika is Amitābha;
Ratnadhṛk is Ratnasambhava;
Prajñādhṛk is Amoghasiddhi.

By this, the purification of the six aggregates is explained. When the disks of the moon and sun have vanished and been broken within one’s own body—the *lalanā* and *rasanā*—and when the vital wind (*prāṇavāta*) is restrained in both paths, that is, in the two nostrils, due to the absence of the outward exit of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds; and when the image of emptiness has become manifest in the lotus situated in the space of the five wheels, or in the external lotus of the woman, or in the *vajra*, the *cittavajra*, or the *bola*; "when the *vajra* is awakened" means when it has been raised up according to the previously described sequence.
And at that time, when the moon has melted into semen—

that great solar disc which is the innate state where existence and non-existence are one, which pervades the three worlds, and which is the unstruck sound (anāhata)— when that has fully awakened, the yogi at that moment proceeds to the supreme state, in which there is no duality whatsoever.

When the prāṇa and apāna are restrained, the agitated moon enters the solar orb; when the lotus and the thunderbolt are awakened, that [moon] melts again by the radiance of the solar orb. Consciousness (vijñāna) and primordial wisdom (jñāna) become one with the wind when the moon and sun are restrained. In this way, in this way, and likewise in this way—thus it may be of three kinds; there is nothing else whatsoever.

The wheel is pure all around; "the three existences" is bliss. The jewel is passion for this very [bliss]; the lotus is the destruction of the afflictions; the sword is the vajra, for the body of great gnosis is indeed indivisible. The axe is the cutter of ignorance; moreover, the six families produced by these [elements] should be understood in this way: the aggregates, elements, sense-faculties, and so forth, are of equal taste, like space.
When the moon has entered the support—the circle of the vulva—and has become liquefied...

When that which is the single reality of both existence and non-existence, undivided from emptiness and compassion, pervading the three realms of existence, free from the stains of body, speech, and mind, the unstruck (*anāhata*) radiance of supreme immutable great bliss (*paramākṣara-mahāsukha*), has fully awakened—at that time, at the moment of the arising of great bliss—that yogin, who has realized the six-limbed yoga, proceeds to the supreme state, the state beyond, the foundation of innate joy and bliss.
For that yogin, there is no duality whatsoever characterized by the clinging to self and other.

When the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds have been restrained, the moon— which has been agitated and melted by the flame of the *caṇḍālī*— goes toward and embraces the solar disc. This means that when the *vajra*, which is the *bodhicitta*, and the wheels (*cakras*) within the *padma* have awakened— that is, have been raised up according to the previously mentioned sequence—
and [the moon] has melted, having become liquid.

That moon has melted away along with the radiance of the solar disc; consciousness (*vijñāna*) and gnosis (*jñāna*) become one with the vital wind (*marut*). When the moon and sun are restrained and [the central channel] is free from obscuration, that which arises is the supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*). Because it is impossible to describe, it is thus accessible only through direct experience, consisting of the essence of the letters *E* and *Vaṃ*. By means of its threefold expression, he declares its absolute reality in every respect.
The purification of the signs is expressed by the passage beginning with "the wheel" (*cakra*) and so forth.

"The triple existence" (*tribhava*) refers to that in which the form of birth (*jātirūpa*) reaches its end; that is called the Great Form (*mahārūpa*). That in which the suffering of saṃsāra reaches its end is called Great Feeling (*mahāvedanā*).

That in which the perception of saṃsāra (*saṃsārasaṃjñā*) reaches its end is the Great Vajra Perception (*mahāvajrasaṃjñā*). And that in which the notion of saṃsāra (*saṃsārabuddhi*) reaches its end is indeed Vajra Volitional Formation (*vajrasaṃskāra*).

That in which states such as sleep reach their end is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); that in which the state of ignorance reaches its end is the very wisdom (*jñāna*) of the Sage. For the sake of maturing those who are deluded, there is the clear wheel of Vairocana;
for the sake of the happiness of these three realms, there is the jewel of Ratnasaṃbhava.

By means of the dharma of unobscured perception, for those possessed of passion, there is the lotus of Amitābha as the cause of great passion; the sword of Amoghasiddhi as the destruction of the afflictions; the vajra of Akṣobhya as the indestructible body;
and the scissor of the sixth family as the cutting away of ignorance.
Through these six families, they are like space—of equal flavor and having the nature of form and so forth, free from modification.
And it is said:

"That single Vajrasattva, resembling a cloud at the time of universal dissolution, became Heruka for the sake of maturing the fierce ones; and he, the Victor of the Samaya, became Ratneśa for the sake of the happiness of the deluded. He became the Holder of the Lotus (Amitābha) for the sake of those suffering from passion, and for the sake of passion itself among the passionate, he became Amoghasiddhi with a sword in his lotus-hand for the purpose of destroying obstacles."

She who was Viśvamātā through hatred became Ḍākinī, resembling the fire of universal dissolution; through delusion she became the one named Locanā; through supreme compassion she became Māmakī; through pride she became the one named Pāṇḍarā, a treasury of all virtues; and through envy she became Tāriṇī. These two, Viśvarūpa and his consort, as well as all others—the objects and the subjects—came into being.
Thus [it is said].
Birth-form is the natural form;
the suffering of saṃsāra is the sensation of natural suffering and so forth.

Likewise, in what follows, these supreme and excellent Victors beginning with Vairocana are of six kinds and the six families; others are the divisions of the six elements: earth, fire, water, wind, space, and peace.

That Locanā in whom all delusion goes to its destruction; that Māmakī in whom all pride goes to its destruction; that Ambā herself in whom all passion goes to its destruction; that Pāṇḍarā who would be the oblation in whom all envy goes to its destruction; and that Tāriṇī who is the wind in whom all [such states] go to their destruction.

In which all hatred goes to its destruction, she is the Sovereign of the Vajra Realm; the sky is her [nature], and this is the Great Hearing of the Jina, by which one hears sound from afar as if it were manifest.
That excellent nose of the Lord, which perceives every scent that produces supreme bliss; that tongue which always tastes the nectar of its own moon and bestows happiness;
that adamantine body-faculty which always removes the vajra-touch from all sides—when one enters into equal bliss through the union of wisdom and means, that mind of his is the Dharma-faculty.

These Bodhisattvas, together with their consorts, who are divided into six types according to the distinction between subject and object, perceive the seen and the unseen, the distant and the near, within the mind, in space, and in that which is neither mind nor non-mind.
In equal bliss and immutable bliss, the phenomenon (dharma) is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
by this it is said: "Having hands, feet, and so forth everywhere; having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands pervading all.
Thus it is said.
These images—the forms and so forth—are the objects of the Supreme Victor; they exist in six modes everywhere, being transparent, unborn, and unceasing;

they produce supreme bliss, are untainted, and are accessible through gnosis. There is no other object of apprehension within the three realms, yet they are accessible through the doors of the sense faculties for the entire world.
Even for the Buddhas, she is inaccessible; yet this illusion of the Buddha’s emanation, possessing immeasurable qualities, manifests herself within the abode of the three worlds like Indra’s net.

Appearing in various diverse forms, she enters the respective minds of the Victors, gods, and men. Being of an unarisen nature, she is like the sky reflected in water; her arising here is merely the product of delusion.

The wrathful Buddhas together with their goddesses, as well as Rasakuliśa, Bhūmigarbha, and the others, indeed become directly manifest in the sky; at the time of accomplishment, during dawn or midnight on a moonlit night, the yogin’s heart becomes joyful, and his desired success occurs. Furthermore, by the conjunction of the [right] time, there is a shower of jewels or flowers upon the surface of the earth—this is the most excellent [sign].
In the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), forms and so forth are neither born nor ceased;
thus they are untroubled by the impurities of body, speech, and mind, undisturbed,
accessible through gnosis, and to be realized by the supreme immutable.
The implication is that only those things accessible through the doors of the sense faculties are to be grasped, and no others.
Because it is impossible to enumerate [them] as being "unreachable even by the Buddhas," it is said:
"Victorious is the unique King of Bliss, devoid of causes and eternally arisen for all worlds."
And at the time of whose proclamation, even the Omniscient One became impoverished of words.
The illusory manifestation of the Buddha, the Vajra-holder, is Viśvamātā; she is the Buddha’s illusory manifestation, a net of Indra, a net of magic.
Just as the appearance of the sky in water is an error, so too is arising itself here a source of delusion.

The *rasakuliśas* are the six Tathāgatas, such as Bhūmigarbha and Kṣitigarbha. At the time of accomplishment—meaning the time of accomplishing Mahāmudrā—at dawn, when the sun has just risen, the Vajra-word was revealed in this *Ādibuddha* by the Blessed One through summary, detailed exposition, and further explanation.
For the sake of its very realization, the path of signs beginning with smoke, which is the meditation on Mahāmudrā, has been revealed.
Having made the mind one-pointed upon emptiness, one should examine it for one day.
Thus, from this word of the Blessed One, the vajra-word in the *Paramādibuddha*— the path of meditation on the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) beginning with smoke and so forth— is manifest;
it has not come down through a lineage of gurus.
There is no need for empowerment by the guru’s command;

rather, there is a means of verification for this path. According to the Blessed One’s words, "One should examine it day and night for one full day," the yogin must examine [the signs] here within a single day, setting aside other means of mantra-attainment such as the signs of smoke and so forth.
The sign (*nimitta*) is also threefold:
the initial sign, the middle sign, and the final sign.

The initial sign is the path of smoke and so forth; through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), there is the perfection of the image (*bimba*) and the attainment of the moment of the immutable (*akṣarakṣaṇa*).

The intermediate sign (*madhyanimitta*) consists of the attainment of the first stage (*ādibhūmi*), the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the manifestation of the perceived object, and the acquisition of worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*) through one thousand eight hundred moments of the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣarakṣaṇa*).

The final sign (*antanimitta*) is Buddhahood, the state of Vajradhara, which is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā through twenty-one thousand six hundred moments of the supreme unchanging, resulting from the attainment of the twelve stages (*dvādaśabhūmi*).
These *vajrapada*s and so forth, preceded by the signs (*nimitta*), were taught by the Blessed One in the *Paramādibuddha*, the king of tantras. At the time of the [sun’s] setting and at midnight—
since that too is a time for accomplishment— at the new moon of the waxing fortnight, there is the attainment of the desired goal, which is the attainment of Mahāmudrā.
Through the conjunction of the *kalās*, that is, through the conjunction of three fortnights and three years.
The vajra-word, the word of reality,
the empowerment characterized by penetration—
this refers to the various tantras such as the *Śrīmadādibuddha* and others; by the word "etcetera," there is an inclusion of the *Śrīsamāja*, *Samvara*, *Hevajra*, and *Dākinīvajrapañjara*.

By the repeated request of that steadfast upholder of the Dharma, renowned as Śrī Varapālanāyaka— who possesses devotion for his guru, compassion for the wretched, service toward Mañjuśrī the Lord of Wealth, maturity in worldly songs, and an exceeding capacity for hearing the Dharma— I have composed this commentary (*ṭippaṇī*) which bears the weight of the six ancillaries.
By whatever merit I have gained from composing this commentary on the Six-Limbed Yoga, may the entire world attain the supreme, imperishable state.
The Sadanga-yoga of the various tantras, beginning with the glorious Ādibuddha, is completed. This work is by the venerable scholar Anupamarakṣita.
The *Ṣaḍaṅgayogatippaṇī* is completed;
this work is by the great scholar Mahāpaṇḍita Raviśrījñānapāda.
The Six-Limbed Yoga, Protected by the Peerless One; in the language of India:
Ṣaḍaṅgayoga; in the language of Tibet: sbyor ba yan lag drug pa. Homage to the glorious Kālacakra!
In clearing away the net of clouds that obscures all things,
When all the counts of the winds of conceptual thought have completely subsided,
Possessing excellent light that has arisen within one's own expanse of space.
May the Lord of the World be more radiant than the full moon!
He who, though free from the objects of the four classes of beings, is not distinct from them, being the all-pervading self.
Although he is empty, this Lord of the Earth has transcended abiding in the nature of mere compassion.
Although those possessing realization cause bliss to expand without exception, they have abandoned conceptualization and are without going or coming.
May some arising that is free from the mind become an ornament for the minds of beings!

[kha] Bound by grasping at even a slight conceptualization as if it were a demon, for the sake of its destruction, one must abandon it with urgency; having thus trained for a very long time on the sublime path, by what means is the reflection of space transcended from the mind?
I constantly prostrate with joy to the supreme Guru, the Teacher whose very nature is space and compassion.
Therefore, it is precisely for this reason that one proclaims one's own realization in such a manner.
Proclaiming the great majesty of the transformed Guru:
for when the fire, which has the nature of blazing form, is absent,
the upward surging of the tips of smoke cannot be perceived.
[gha] | The pride of one's own realization is not a stream of faults;
by means of its very engagement, it accomplishes the welfare of others.
When the speaker does not have a fixed expression, [the teaching proceeds].

Just as worldly beings engage for the sake of fulfilling their desires, so too do those base practitioners of mantra— who are arrogant from understanding the provisional meaning and who have abandoned the paths—
fail to recognize even the obstacles that arise through the gateway of practice due to their own inferior wisdom.
By the command of the glorious Vajradhara, the Lord Mañjuśrī pervaded the three worlds and spoke the *Laghutantra* of the Blessed Kālacakra with clearly elucidated words;
he who is the glorious Great Compassionate One, the Blessed Lokanātha, and his emanation.
He composed the *Vimalaprabhā* extensive commentary with words that are meaningful in every respect and exceedingly clear;
having obtained the Buddha-Ratnagarbha revealed by that [commentary] through the nature of merit,
one who relies upon the nectar of the definitive meaning will overcome the poisons of existence and find joy.
The foundation and support for all the collections of objects of knowledge is the one endowed with excellence, whose name accords with that of the Omniscient One;
that very sublime jewel-ocean is explained as the root of Īśvara and the other [deities],
and it is there that the conceptual trees of the entirety of the Perfection of Wisdom also converge.
The Destroyer, born from space, the Buddha whose nature is purity, the Mother who gives birth;
she who opens the eyes upon the stainless sky, moistened by the expansion of great compassion, and nourished by the support of intention.

Free from the distinctions of existence, non-existence, both, or the presence and absence of entities, the entire range of adventitious mental states, beginning with the number two, arises following upon emptiness.

[jha] Thus, one should correctly compile the precious scriptures—such as the *Śrī-mūla-tantra* and others—which clarify the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), accord with the meditation on the path of Mahāmudrā, and bestow the fruit of perfect buddhahood itself.
That which was taught as the *Ādibuddha* in the *Buddharatnakaraṇḍa-tantrarāja*: because the vowels (*ādi*) and consonants (*kādi*), the moon and the sun, are not individually the seat of the Vajrin;
nor is there any other color or form produced from the transformation of the *hūṃ* syllable and its signs;
rather, it is endowed with the supreme faculties, being unchanging, free from birth, and devoid of decay.
To this Lord of Victors, who holds the manifold illusion and possesses all aspects and all *bindus*,
belongs [this teaching]. Because it is so, the beginner yogi— who delights in accomplishing supreme unchanging bliss,
has received the instructions of a sublime guru, has completely abandoned harmful companions, and has thoroughly meditated upon the signs such as smoke— purifies the central channel.

Bound by a mind of supreme compassion toward all sentient beings as if they were an only child, relying upon the mundane and supramundane truths, and being without regard for children, wife, and so forth, or even for one's own body.
Having turned away from the utilization of the communal hall, the temple, and the master’s property,
he dwells established in the four divine abodes— loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— which rely upon the path of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Having abandoned the desire for worldly accomplishments such as pacification and so forth,
and desiring to abide in the state of omniscience,
one completely relinquishes the cultivation of conceptualizations such as the mandala circle and so on.

In the expanse of space, emptiness endowed with all aspects is seen as clearly as a reflection in a mirror; through the certainty that phenomena are unborn, one contemplates them as being like the mental projections of one's own mind, similar to optical illusions, dreams, and the like.
By analyzing phenomena as being of the nature of an aggregation of subtle particles, one distances oneself from a nihilistic emptiness.

One who is uniquely skilled in stabilizing the bodhicitta— which consists of wisdom and skillful means— by completely relinquishing attachment to internal phenomena of bliss that are to be personally experienced, and [attachment to] external phenomena of bliss that are to be experienced by the sense faculties.

"By attaining the pith instructions on the path of the wisdom of supreme immutable great bliss, one does not desire the phenomena that are conceptually imputed as the support and the supported—the signs, colors, hands, shapes, and deities of the mandala.
Likewise:
"By means of the path of manifold conceptualization and so forth..."
That which was taught by the Tathāgata as suchness is not attained by one who is devoid of the path consisting of the sixteenfold divisions of the four [noble truths].
The yoga of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) itself is devoid of the realization of the syllables *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, and so forth,
which are taught in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
There is no other means for accomplishing reality;
just as fire, though its signs reside within wood,
is not seen by means of cutting or splitting it.
Just as fire, which resides within the fire-drill and the base-wood, becomes visible through the friction produced by the hands,
so too does the conceptualization that appears from the mind [become manifest].
It is not seen by means of the methods of meditation;
rather, it is seen in that very state through the union of lalanā and rasanā as one.
The signs such as heat and so forth also descend into the central channel through prāṇāyāma,
and the vajra [is stabilized] through the observance of the vidyā.
Without emission, [the bodhicitta] flows upward;
by these paths, the bliss of the Buddhas becomes unchanging.
Through the actualization or by means of all female messengers,
the coemergent state will be attained by the yogin;
the conceptualization of form and so forth is the maṇḍala.
Through mastery in the meditation on the wheel,
one will achieve mundane accomplishments;
how could the great accomplishment of desire ever be attained?
For those pure disciples who, out of compassion for sentient beings, constantly strive for the virtuous deeds of others, the paths—
Through the grace of the sublime Guru,
even those who have entered into the dense thicket of kinsmen and friends...
The precious Good Path is plundered by:
killing, taking what is not given, the wives of others,
lying, harsh speech, and slander.
The thieves of boastful speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong views,
as well as actual sins and proximate sins.
The executioner, the enemy, and the one who is thoroughly lustful—
these five types of thieves constantly plunder the jewel.
Those thieves of various excellent foods, drinks, and manifold enjoyments cause one to be heedless,
even if one possesses diligence.
One who is already in a state of swoon is further tormented;
for how could one who is not himself a cognizer be considered of great value? This is done for the sake of knowing.
By those words of the deceitful one who says, "I do not teach others," they cast away the jewel;
whereas those who possess great and noble knowledge—
One should cause the great jewel to enter into thorough examination.
Their own jewels are to be known through their various expressions;
[they are] the Perfect Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas.
Through the forms of father, mother, daughter,
sister, son, brother, and beloved wife,
the Māras create obstacles.
Therefore, the disciples [should practice] this excellent path, a precious jewel, granted by the sublime guru.
Having completely abandoned one's kinsmen and thieves,
one should conceal [the practice] very well with devotion.
This is the stage of the Hero, the self-consecration.
Even the gradual stages are not the path for the sake of liberation.
The Buddhas have taught this single stage of the complete purity of gnosis for the sake of liberation;
even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution [may attain it].
The meaning of empowerment is that which is bliss.
The Lord of Victors will correctly uphold the tantra whose nature is method and wisdom;
the stage of the Hero is not for those on the outside.
When his life-force was exhausted within his body, he spoke this.
In the great empowerment of the self, the eye that perceives the three realms as empty sees that saṃsāra is essence-less and has come to an end.
From that, the fruit is the Buddhahood of the person.
Just as the ripened fruits of the plantain tree arise from the very destruction of the plantain tree, so too do sinful demons,
woodworms, and sentient beings [arise].
Whatever arises from them, that very thing destroys them.
In that same way, the mind of yogins will cause illusion to perish;
it is non-dual, immovable, and free from the perception of duality.
Desire, the supreme immutable, and great passion.
Entity and non-entity,
wisdom and universal intentionality,
the absence of discordant sound, and the great sound.
The coemergent, glorious one who holds the bodhicitta-tilaka.
The glorious Kālacakra is the vajra,
the yoga whose nature is wisdom and method.
Thus, this vajra-yoga is that which is relied upon by immeasurable Sugatas and is steadfast.
The Bodhisattva Vajradhara, the Holder of the Supreme Vajra, is perfectly gathered by all the vidyās of secret mantra.
First, one should properly rely upon a guru who possesses the samaya and abides preeminently in the Vajrayāna.
Meditating on suchness, free from attachment and devoid of stains, they enter the path whose nature is patience.
To his disciples he bestows the path that robs away the fear of hell; from that very source comes the one endowed with pure conduct.
That very vajra-breath of the Māras is renowned upon the foundation of the earth as Vajrasattva.
Here, whatever the object of the deity may be, it becomes twofold: direct perception and inference.
Through the application to the reality of direct perception, the manifold sambhogakāya appears like stars in the sky.
If it were not directly perceived, it would be like the body of a deceased person; since it would not be reality, what could be inferred?
That is the object of meditation for yogins whose intellect has not yet fully matured, such as those who look at paintings and the like.
Here, according to the mental dispositions of sentient beings, the visualization of the deity for yogins becomes twofold: through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
Of these two—direct perception and inference—that which is direct perception becomes, through the yoga of reality, like stars in the sky.

Regarding the phrase "the manifold sambhogakāya like a host of stars," it means that which is to be apprehended by the eyes of the flesh and so forth—the three realms of existence and the three times—is like a dream and an illusion.
"First of all, the beginner yogin, lacking supernormal knowledge, perceives the reflected image with the physical eye."
Then, by the power of the boundary of supernormal knowledge, he sees with the divine eye.
Then, by means of the boundary of freedom from passion, he beheld them with the Buddha-eye.
Then, by virtue of the bodhisattva's boundary, he beheld with the eye of wisdom.
Then, by the power of the boundary of a perfectly awakened Buddha, he beheld with the eye of primordial wisdom:
"Completely liberated from all that remains."
Thus it is said.
Thus, the five eyes of the Tathāgata, such as the flesh eye and so forth, were taught for the purpose of perceiving emptiness.
Other sentient beings are blind regarding the object of the view of emptiness; this is the certainty of meditating on suchness.
If there is no direct perception regarding a proof that is not reality, then whatever is conceptualized as non-reality is like the inference of a dead body.
That should be viewed in paintings and so forth.
This means that one should visualize the definitive forms by drawing or fashioning paintings and statues of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or by drawing the mandala circle;
this is for the purpose of meditation for inferior, childish yogins. This is the definitive instruction on the meditation of conceptualization.
The service is performed by means of the five nectars and so forth, the vajras of the ocean of waters, and the recitation of mantras.
Through the individual withdrawal and other [preliminary practices], one will achieve the near-attainment by means of the nectar born from the vajra and lotus.
Through joy and the other [feelings], one will accomplish the meditation on the three vajras and the lotus as having become of one taste.
Through the subtle yoga of the non-transmigrating union with wisdom, the great accomplishment is definitively established.
Here, the beginner first performs the service (*sevā*) according to the ritual of the *sādhana*;
externally, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are excrement and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," one includes *go-ku* and the like;
by consuming these for the purpose of pleasing the deity, one performs the preliminary service (*sevā*).
Internally, the five nectars are the five aggregates.
By the word "and so forth," the five sense faculties are the five lamps.
To be indifferent toward those things is "service," which means completely abandoning craving for the body and material possessions.
Through that service, the deities will grant supreme boons, but not by eating excrement and the like.
"By the vajras who are treasuries of water" means being without regard for the enjoyments of the body.

It means the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-saṃvara*) regarding body, speech, and mind, which consists of being without regard for the enjoyments of speech, being without regard for the enjoyments of the mind, and being without regard for the pleasure of the enjoyment of emission.
"This supreme deity will be granted [to you], but not out of attachment to the enjoyments of existence."
Regarding the phrase "by means of mantra recitation and so forth":

Here, what is called "the recitation of mantra" refers to the binding of the vital breath (*prāṇabandha*); by the word "and so forth," it includes the yogas of exhalation, inhalation, and the vase-breath (*kumbhaka*), which constitute the constant service (*sevā*).
This is the definitive meaning: that the supreme deity will grant [the boon] through this, but not by failing to restrain one's life-force.
According to the provisional meaning, one should perform recitations and so forth using a rosary and other such implements.
This is for the sake of common accomplishments (*sādhāraṇasiddhi*). Now, the near-attainment (*upasādhanā*) shall be explained.
"Respectively," and so forth.
Regarding "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*): here, for transmigrating beings, "withdrawal" refers to the grasping of objects such as forms by the sense faculties, such as the eyes.

The complete abandonment of that [grasping] is what is called withdrawal; the grasping of objects by the others, such as the eyes, with respect to the form of emptiness (*śūnyatā-rūpa*), is the proximate accomplishment (*upāyasādhana*).

Likewise, meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*)—perfected by the nectar born from the vajra and lotus—is the "near-attainment" (*upāsādhana*) according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
According to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), it is the external elaboration of the deity; such is the near-attainment.

Now, the practice (*sādhana*) is taught, beginning with the words "joy" (*prīti*) and so forth. Here, by means of joy and the others, the three vajras—the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind—are cultivated as having become of equal taste within the lotus (*utpala*); this is the meaning of the statement that the drops abide at the heart, the navel, and the secret place. Thus is the practitioner.

Then, as for "great accomplishment" (*mahāsādhana*), when wisdom is applied and one attains the bliss that is without transition, at that time it is great accomplishment; from the phrase "from the subtle yoga," according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it should be called the great accomplishment of the definitive meaning, which arises from the perfect union of the seminal essence (*śukra*) upon the *suṣumṇā* channel.

By way of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it is certain that [the object] is mustard seeds and so forth at the tip of the nose, which is the source of the phenomena of wisdom (*prajñā-dharmodaya*).
In this way, it becomes the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*).
First, one must ascertain emptiness and awakening; thereafter, one correctly maintains the lunar drop (*candrabindu*).
Then, generating the forms, this very laughter of the families of the supreme and most excellent flavors is the general service (*sevā*).

Through the vajras of the water-treasury, the middling accomplishment (*sādhanā*) also occurs here by way of four methods; likewise, it pertains to the branches of accomplishment for those who are inferior or steadfast.

Regarding the first stage of generation, "emptiness as awakening": when sentient beings die, they completely relinquish the aggregates and take up the aggregates consisting of the factors of birth; that single moment of emptiness which perceives the three realms is what is called "empty.
This is certain, meaning it is beyond doubt.
Following that moment, one correctly holds the lunar drop (*candrabindu*).
Thus, here, the appropriation by the ālayavijñāna of the drops of semen in the mother’s womb is "perfect appropriation.

Following that, the generation of forms from the appropriated semen and so forth refers to the completion of the womb during the seventh month, which means the completion of the body. Then, by the most excellent classes of tastes...
Thus, the arrangement of syllables for the eyes and so forth is by means of the six aggregates; this refers to the thorough engagement with objects such as form and the rest.
Likewise, even in the yoga of the deity, the beginner should meditate on the nature of the conceptualized self.
This is the general service (*sevā*).

"By the vajras of the water-treasury" refers to the middling accomplishment through the completion of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis; it is also the completion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Here, "it becomes fourfold by way of method" means that within the branches of *sevā* (service) and *upasādhana* (near-accomplishment), there are the inferior and the stable.
Regarding the branch of *sādhana* (accomplishment), "precisely at the limit of sixteen years" is the definitive rule.
Here, "inferior" refers to a child who has just been born;
"one with teeth" refers to a child of middling age; and "one whose teeth have fallen out" refers to a youth.
Furthermore, it is said that after sixteen years from birth, one produces offspring, which is the state of being "grown.
Likewise, the yogi should meditate upon all the deities as having four limbs; this is the certainty of the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Now, the perfection of the Buddha’s form according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) shall be described.
Here, first, regarding "emptiness as enlightenment," one should not contemplate even slightly in the darkness.
Then, regarding "perfectly holding the lunar drop," this refers to holding the signs beginning with smoke and ending with the drop (*bindu*).
Then, regarding the phrase "generating forms" and "then seeing various forms through the bindu," this refers to the arising of form.
"By means of the supreme classes of tastes" refers to the six unobscured aggregates.
"Arranging the letters" refers to the cessation of the limited aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.
Therefore, the attainment of the stages occurs through the distinctions of the "inferior" and so on, until one becomes the sovereign of the twelve stages.
Consequently, it possesses the twelve aspects of the meaning of truth.
He who knows those very [truths] in sixteen aspects,
who awakens through twenty aspects,
the omniscient one, the supreme among all Buddhas.
Thus it is said.
Likewise, one should meditate on the reflected image at the juncture during the path of smoke and so forth, which is empty, through the power of the guru’s definitive instruction;
thereafter, one stabilizes the prāṇa and apāna winds within the root cakras.
"Subsequently, the yogi should practice the consumption of the lunar cessation (candrānta-bhakṣaṇa) through the bodhicitta.
Then, whatever slight desire one has will be attained in this very life within a few days.
Thus it is said.
The *Ādibuddha*, which teaches the supreme instructions on the stages of meditation for this king of paths, states as follows: "Having meditated upon the smoke and so forth,
and having rendered the mind unwavering,
one should then purify the central channel."
One should accomplish the supreme unchanging;
having excellently arranged the vajra within the lotus,
one should cause it to enter the vital drop (srog gi thig le).
The drop within the circle is the drop;
its movement is to be obstructed by the vajra.
The yogi is eternally constant and firm.
It will always flow upward;
through union with the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā),
one is consecrated by the descent of the vajra.
Upon the completion of six hundred [breaths], the great king himself becomes Vajrasattva;

otherwise, one should not associate with a wisdom consort until ten [days] have dawned. When the yogin’s external distractions are completely severed, he becomes the Lord of Victors through the withdrawal of signs, which is of ten types; meditative concentration is immovability itself.
Prāṇāyāma is also Khadgī; furthermore, there are ten forms. Dhāraṇā is Ratnapāṇi himself;
for Anusmṛti it is Padmadhara, and Samādhi is the glorious Cakrin.

"O, O! [The breath] is divided by the five [vāyus], and furthermore, it is differentiated by the vowels (a-series) and consonants (ka-series). Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the non-engagement of the ten objects and sense-faculties within the body. Dhyāna (meditative concentration) consists of discernment, investigation, joy, unwavering bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
Prāṇāyāma (breath control) is the exhaustion of the two paths and the entry of the vital breath into the central channel."

When the vital breath has thoroughly entered the bindu and the movement of both [channels] is ceased, that is the one-pointed concentration of the mind. Whatever appearance of *caṇḍālī* definitely arises within the body and space becomes the recollection (*anusmṛti*).
Through the nature of wisdom and method, by the power of immutable bliss, one enters meditative absorption upon the form of gnosis.
Through various distinctions such as inferior and so forth, these three types of sādhanas of the Principal One become manifold.

Through the power of traversing the three mudrās and the three stages— the karmic, the conceptual, and the supreme— the yogi, free from objects through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), is consecrated by all the pedestals.
The five superknowledges will be attained; O Lord of Men, they are purified through the application of contemplation.
Worshipped by Bodhisattvas who exert their vital breath, it is pure and free from the moon and the sun.
Through the power of grasping, one enters the ten powers while the Māras, afflictions, and so forth are destroyed;
this occurs from the form of primordial wisdom, the stainless mandala of light of perfect recollection.
Then, through the purity of meditative concentration over several days and nights, the body of gnosis (jñānakāya) is accomplished.
If, through such means as individual withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the desired goal of the mantrins and others is not accomplished, [then...]
Through familiarity with the *nāda*, one accomplishes the practice by blocking the *bindu* within the lotus-abiding *vajra-maṇi* by means of its power.
For the stage of *sevā*, there is the first yoga consisting of ten aspects, performed with the wrathful gaze of the Wheel-Bearer in the sky.
Even for one who has entered the path of nectar through the view that brings an end to obstructors, there are six branches of near-attainment.
Regarding the practice: the three unchanging [states] of the moon, the drop, and the vajra abiding in the jewel of cognition are for the sake of accomplishment.
In this yoga of innate wisdom, which is singular, peaceful, and undiminished bliss, there is the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*).
Now, the six-limbed yoga shall be explained, beginning with "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*).
For the beginner, the "Lord of Kings" refers to the aggregate of primordial wisdom.
Furthermore, there are ten types of distinctions regarding signs:
smoke,
a mirage, and so forth.
The sky-like appearance, the lamp, and the blazing light.
The moon, the sun,
and Rāhu;
The aggregate of non-conceptual primordial wisdom, distinguished by the six and the vision of the bindu.
Dhyāna is indeed Akṣobhya; it is the aggregate of consciousness.
The ten aspects consist of the ten objects and subjects as a single unity within the various forms; this is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Prāṇāyāma, or else, the wielder of the sword.
This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
it has ten aspects because the ten maṇḍalas of the left and right have become merged into one.
Furthermore, there are ten aspects, with the Holder of the Jewel in his hand.
This refers to the aggregate of sensation;
it is the life-sustaining [wind] at the navel and the heart.
There are ten types, distinguished by the movement back and forth upon the lotuses of the throat, the forehead, and the crown of the head.
"For G.yung mo, mindfulness will become Padmadhara"—this refers to the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
That recollection on the central channel of the maiden also consists of ten [recollections], according to the division of the ten stages of desire.
The glorious one who possesses the wheel of meditative concentration is Vairocana.
The ten types of meditative concentration are for the purpose of arresting the ten winds.
Thus, the Blessed One is one who has attained non-abiding nirvāṇa,
in the sense that the winds do not blow within him.
Now, the characteristics of *pratyāhāra* and the others shall be explained,
beginning with the words "individually" (*prati*) and so forth.
In this context, "withdrawal" (pratyāhāra) refers to the non-engagement of consciousness through the connection between the ten objects and their corresponding subjects within the body.
The other five [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, engage with the objects of emptiness.
Regarding that very form: "insight" (*prajñā*) refers to seeing; "discernment" (*vitarka*) refers to grasping at an entity; "investigation" (*vicāra*) refers to ascertaining its meaning;
and "joy" (*prīti*) refers to attachment to form.
"Unwavering bliss" refers to making the mind one with form.
Thus,
through the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, there are ten types of meditative concentration.
Regarding what is here called "the exertion of life-breath" (*prāṇāyāma*), it refers to the cessation of the two paths—the left and right channels—and entering the central channel.
Furthermore, there are ten aspects regarding the cessation of the maṇḍala.

Regarding the phrase "the drop here": it refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) entering the forehead, wherein both paths are blocked; by holding the vital breath at the forehead, one maintains the coming and going, which is called "one-pointedness of mind."
Whatever appearance of *caṇḍālī* arises from the space of the three realms is *anuyoga* (recollection);
its ten aspects have already been explained above.
"By means of the nature of wisdom and method" refers to the very state in which the object of knowledge and the knowing subject are merged as one;
through the power of immutable bliss, there is meditative absorption upon the form of gnosis.
Furthermore, those such as vitality and so forth are tenfold by way of their non-existence.
Thus is the means of accomplishment for the six branches of yoga.
Through the various divisions such as inferior and so forth, these become the three types of sādhana of the principal Kālacakra;
they correspond to the three mudrās and the three states.
Thus it is said:
"By virtue of the threefold path."
In this context, the state of inferiority is the stage where the bodhicitta undergoes transformation.
The moving course is the intermediate stage; the non-moving course is the supreme stage.
In this way, the action mudrā is the one who bestows the bliss of transformation.
The wisdom seal (jñānamudrā) is the one who bestows the bliss of movement.
Mahāmudrā is the one who bestows unwavering bliss.

Since the Blessed One has taught that one should meditate on the three mudrās within the six-limbed yoga practiced in this manner, the yogin should practice the six-limbed yoga for the sake of attaining buddhahood itself.
Now, the fruit of individual withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs] will be explained,
beginning with the words "individually" (*prati*) and so forth.
In this regard, whenever the yogi becomes purified through the stabilization of the form during withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), at that time he will be blessed by all mantras,
which will grant him the supreme speech and other such boons.
The five superknowledges will be attained; O Lord of Men, you are purified through the application of meditative concentration.
This means that here, whenever the eyes become unblinking, at that time they become the divine eye.
In the same way, there will be the [attainment of] the divine eyes and so forth, through the purification of meditative concentration.

Regarding the phrase "purified by the vital effort (*prāṇāyāma*)," it means that here, when the yogin is separated from the paths of the sun and the moon and [the breath] flows perpetually into the central channel (*madhyamā*), at that time, being purified by the vital effort, he is honored and praised by the Bodhisattvas.
This is the meaning of that statement.

Regarding the phrase "one will enter the ten [stages] where the Māras, afflictions, and so forth are diminished and their power lost": this means that the grasping mind enters into the apprehension of the form of emptiness by the power of grasping; this occurs because, through the cessation of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they become completely merged as one.

"Perfectly pure recollection" refers to the very state of being free from all conceptual constructions by means of a mind that embraces form; when it becomes pure through that, it becomes the mandala of stainless light.
From the word "also" (kyang), five rays of light radiate; "from the form of gnosis" means from the form of emptiness.

Then, regarding the phrase "when the concentrations are pure": here, the concentration is designated as that bliss which arises from the single state of the purified minds of subject and object, becoming an unchanging bliss.

Through that meditative concentration, becoming pure and stainless, it is said that "in a few days"—that is, within three fortnights or three years—the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*) will be accomplished; thus, one becomes a bodhisattva who has attained the ten masteries and so forth.
Thus, having established the certainty regarding withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs], the yoga of power (*balayoga*) is now taught.
Here, when [one practices] withdrawal...

When the forms of the [five] elements and so forth become visible, at that time, because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has not been restrained, the immutable moment does not arise. Then, by the power of the practice of *nāda* as it will be explained, one causes the vital breath to flow into the central channel (*avadhūtī*). By means of the immobility resulting from the arrest of the drops (*bindu*) of bodhicitta within the vajra-jewel at the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*), the immutable moments are to be accomplished; this is the yoga of power (*balayoga*).
Regarding the practice of *nāda*, the Blessed One has taught it in this very work, in the chapter on the *sādhana*:
"Whichever *śakti* proceeds from the center of the navel to another location, reaching the end of the twelve and the limit of the parts."
Having correctly restrained that at the navel, from the five [fingers] having the form of a staff resembling the fire of lightning, //
From one wheel, it is moved to another wheel by means of a slow and playful movement, [thereby] being propelled into the central channel.

As long as the crown of the head remains pierced, by the power [of the practice] itself, one should touch the outer skin like a needle; at that time, by means of the supreme forceful method, one should impel it upward through the upper path.
When the winds of the two channels are blocked, one will pass through the crown of the head and go to the city beyond.
Thus, by the thorough awakening of the vajra within the mind, one becomes a sky-farer together with the objective realm.

Having become the nature of the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), this Mother of Various Forms for yogins will once again be described as the gaze for the purpose of accomplishing the form of emptiness,
beginning with the words "the service" (*sevā*) and so forth.
Regarding "approaching" (*sevā*) here, it refers to the meditation on signs such as smoke;
in that approaching, the initial yoga consists of grasping the signs of smoke and so forth with the mind.
Furthermore, that becomes tenfold through the ten ways of gaining conviction together with the smoke and so forth; thus, there are ten aspects.
Regarding the phrase "of the Wheel-possessor," it becomes a sign through the gaze of the *uṣṇīṣa* wrathful deity—that is, by looking upward with unblinking eyes.

For the night yogin, there are four aspects, and for the day yogin, there are six; therein, reaching the limit of form constitutes the branches of *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) and *dhyāna* (meditative concentration), which serve as the stage of *sevā* (service).
Regarding the phrase "by the gaze that brings an end to obstacles" (*vighnāntaka-dṛṣṭyā*): Vighnāntaka is Amṛtakuṇḍalin.
His gaze is that which has reached the abode of nectar—that is, it has reached the location of the forehead.
By means of that gaze—having entered the path of nectar of Vighnāntaka—there are the six branches of the near-attainment (*upāsādhana*).
Furthermore, according to the *Kyangyig*, one should perform *prāṇāyāma* and *dhāraṇā*;
when the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes visible, that is the "near-attainment" (*upāsādhana*).
Regarding the phrase "the drop (*bindu*) of the radiance of wisdom," here, because of passion for wisdom (*prajñā*), this is also the "radiance" (*prapañca*).
The moon is also the *bindu*;

it is the *bodhicitta-bindu* of the elaboration of wisdom that has reached the vajra-jewel. That which becomes the three immutable [states] at the secret place, the navel, and the heart is what is meant by "the limbs of accomplishment"; thus, these three become the limbs of accomplishment, and in this way, one should perform the limbs of accomplishment.

Regarding the phrase "the peace of the single, undiminished bliss," here, that which is the single moment of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) through the non-diminishment of bliss is to be called "peace.

In this yoga of innate gnosis (*sahaja-jñāna*), it is said to be "in the great accomplishment" (*mahāsādhana*), meaning it is the oneness with the bliss of the unchanging mind; this is the fourth branch, the great accomplishment.
The mudrā conforms to an illusion; it is like a reflection in a mirror upon the mind and in space.
Illuminating the three worlds and emitting many stainless rays of light resembling lightning,
it is merely the inseparability of the external and the body, free from objects and conceptualization, abiding in space.
The nature of the mind embraces the minds of the manifold classes of beings;
it is singular, a mere manifestation of the mind, born from one's own intellect, like a reflection in a mirror.
That which is practiced by all the sons of the Victorious Ones and the Buddhas should be practiced by the lords of yogins.
That fully expanded flame of primordial wisdom incinerates all demons, together with their entire domains.
Even desire and so forth within the body bestow equal bliss upon the yogi through the application of the year;
prajñājñāna as well—the mind and its very manifestation—becomes tenfold.
That which enters this, like a stainless empowerment resembling the moon, is like a reflected image.
From that, the bliss of nirvāṇa—which is non-transmigratory, coemergent, and immutable—is the fourth.
The Buddha’s face abiding in whose heart and mouth is the glorious guru.

Here, "prajñā-jñāna" refers to the tenfold [visions] such as smoke and so forth, which are the mind that apprehends according to their number and the objects to be apprehended by that mind; it is like a reflection appearing in a mirror. This very thing is "jñāna," meaning the mind that is to be apprehended.
Just as the mirror itself, the eye, and the reflected image are [respectively] the eye and the object of perception, so too are wisdom (*prajñā*) and gnosis (*jñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "whoever has entered this empowerment," entering here into the mind that is the object of perception—the mind which performs the grasping—means not entering into external objects.

Regarding the six limbs: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*) constitute the entry; bliss that is non-transmigrating and the innate (*sahaja*) itself is the fourth.

This bliss is the supreme among those who are children, the youthful, and the aged; it transcends worldly examples and is liberated from the conduct of the three worlds—this is the meaning of "manifestation" (*utthāna*).
Embracing while gazing,
and holding hands;
"Free from the two pairs" means being devoid of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā* tantras; it is the appearance of emptiness in all its aspects (*sarvākāraśūnyatā*).
"This face of the Buddha"—that is, the face of primordial wisdom (*jñānamukha*)—resides in the heart of whichever master [possesses it]; this refers to having tasted and personally experienced it.
The meaning is that he who dwells perpetually within the mouth for the sake of causing the disciples to realize [the truth] is the glorious Guru, the Vajradhara;
it is not those who merely cause others to realize the bliss of the two organs.
Thus, with a mind entirely free from attachment, one should gaze with unblinking eyes, having entered the path of the vajra.
From emptiness arise smoke, mirages, the stainless appearance of space, and a brilliant lamp-light;

One will see the intermediate space, the moon, the sun, and vajras, as well as the supreme part and the bindu; in their center, one sees the forms of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), which are free from objects and manifold *saṃbhogakāyas*.
Now, the entry into the self-manifestation of this very mind of one's own is taught:
Regarding the phrase "the sky" (*nam mkhar*) and so forth:
here, there are two ways of practicing yoga in the Mantra Vehicle and the Pāramitā Vehicle— namely,
[yoga] in the sky and...
Regarding "in the sky without a roof":

whoever practices yoga in the sky, at night in a house without openings, amidst darkness, with a mind intensely attached to the sky and without closing the eyes, enters the vajra path; here, by the vital wind (prāṇa) entering the central channel, one perceives the signs such as smoke and so forth from emptiness alone.
With a mind of total attachment, with unblinking eyes, and having entered the vajra path,
"In emptiness, smoke, mirages, the very appearance of a stainless sky,
and a lamp"— these are seen through the yoga of the night;
thereafter, one looks at a cloudless sky.

In that sky, through the yoga of day, one sees the blazing [vision] described as: "Arising from space, self-arisen; the great fire of the wisdom of insight. This occurs in the cloudless sky. Likewise: "The great light that illuminates clearly; the radiance of wisdom, shimmering. This refers to the appearance of the moon. "The lamp of the world" refers to the sun. "The lamp of wisdom" is the vajra, the great splendor of Rāhu.
Luminosity is lightning; it is the supreme portion of gnosis.
The sovereign of supreme mantra, the king of vidyās, is the *bindu*.

Thus, there are ten types of signs (*nimitta*). The Blessed One taught that these are attained through the yoga of the night in the *Guhyasamāja* and other tantras, and through the yoga of the day in the *Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti*.
Then, "the king of secret mantra who accomplishes great purpose" means that one sees reflections of all kinds, such as vases and cloths.

In its center—that is, in the center of the *bindu*—is the form of the Buddha, which is devoid of objects because it lacks substantiality and is free from conceptual construction; thus, it is the manifold *saṃbhogakāya*.

Then, through the yoga of the reflected image, one hears that very sound which is indestructible; the meaning is that the *nirmāṇakāya* arises from the appearance of form, and the *saṃbhogakāya* arises from the appearance of sound.
The yogi should gaze with a steady eye at the sky when it has become free from clouds,

until the black line, stainless and radiating rays of light, is seen upon the channel of time (kālanāḍī). Therein, the form of the Omniscient One is like the sun in water— unstained and of manifold colors.
The mind that possesses all aspects, yet is free from objects and mental forms, is not something other [than this].
Here, the daytime yoga consists of looking at a sky free from clouds with the yogi’s fixed gaze; one should face away from the sun in the morning and evening.
Otherwise, the rays of the sun will cause the eyes to become blurred, which results in injury.

One should observe daily during the daytime until, within the center of the *bindu*, a black line the thickness of a hair—radiating stainless rays of light—is seen upon the temporal channel, the *avadhūtī*.

Internally gathered, the omniscient form is like the sun in water within the three realms without exception: stainless, multicolored, endowed with all aspects, and the one's own mind free from objects.
The mind is indeed not other [than that].

It is not the mind of another, because there is no knowledge of another's mind. Here, first of all, the appearance of one's own mind is seen by the Tathāgata’s fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*); then, through the power of cultivation, the fleshly eye, the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and the gnosis eye (*jñāna-cakṣus*) will arise. Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that the Omniscient One does not see.
That [entity] is not of the nature of earth, for it is not solid; nor is it the body of water, for it is not liquid, as it lacks the quality of moisture.
It is not of the nature of fire, for it is not hot; nor is it the body of wind, for it is not moving, despite its mobility.
Although it has the aspect of emptiness, it is not a color, even though it is seen as white, green, or various other great colors.

Although it possesses all aspects, it is not an object of vision, due to the power of the māra of afflictions—the stains within one's own heart. Individually, [the elements] enter into water, and water acts as the burner for fire; fire acts upon wind, and wind acts upon emptiness. Emptiness certainly becomes the ten types of signs, and these signs are...
It becomes endowed with all aspects; it is the supreme bliss, the indestructible gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*).
From gnosis, miraculous powers and spiritual attainments (*siddhi*) arise for men, O Lord, in this very life.
By firmly establishing the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the central channel and binding the courses of the sun and moon on the right and left, [one attains this].
When one is joined with the mudrā, abiding in the mind and supreme bliss, the vajra is truly raised;

moreover, by means of the sound of the vajra in the lotus or by churning with one’s own hand—the "water-born"—this bliss, which is the cause of bliss and does not involve the emission of the seed, is the destroyer of the fear of death; this is the face of the glorious guru.

This instruction on Mahāmudrā was also perfectly taught by the Supreme Primordial Buddha as follows: "The means for accomplishing this very [reality] is the non-conceptual reflection of appearance; through those signs such as smoke and so forth, the reflection of wisdom is equal to space, transcending existence and non-existence—the meaning that inspires confidence in one's own mind."
By completely casting off all those aggregates born from subtle particles,
there appear smoke, mirages, and the sky-like radiance.
The blazing lamp, the moon and sun,
the dark one, the parts, the great bindu,
and the luminous reflection of various forms.
Whether with eyes closed or unclosed,
one will see forms like a dream— empty and not conceptually constructed.
One should constantly meditate on that form;
that meditation on a form which is non-existent is not the meditation of a yogi.
One does not [perceive] existence or non-existence by means of the mind,
because one sees form without conceptualizing it—
just as a young girl [sees] when a mirror has been polished.
