"Thus, from the appearance of form" means from the individual appearance of forms that are stainless and unobstructed, like reflections in a mirror.

Regarding the phrase "from the appearance of sound," it means from the experience of the mere sound of the irrepressible play of great bliss, which does not arise from the exertion of the throat, feet, and so forth.
By this much, through this verse, the two bodies of the Blessed One, the glorious Vajradhara, will be made manifest.
Regarding the term "space," it is by means of a steady gaze, that is, one in which the eyes do not flicker.
Because there is no knowledge of another's mind, there is nothing to be known as another's mind that is distinct from one's own mind.

It is said: Furthermore, whatever object of knowledge (jñeya) is seen here that is neither born nor ceased, that is one’s own mind and not another's. Because it distinguishes external objects of knowledge, I am therefore unable to apply any [conceptual] expansion to myself. Is it possible for a great sword to cut itself with its own edge? Just as a dream brings pleasure to a brave companion who has fallen in love with a maiden of the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra), so too is it for me through relying on a reflection arisen from space. Thus it is said.
By this verse, the means for accomplishing the dharmakāya will be explained.

Regarding the phrase "the aspect of earth" and so forth, this refers to the characteristic of form; here, one perceives earth and so forth as the non-substantial individual manifestation of emptiness, and not as solidity.
That which has the appearance of water in a mirage is not water, because it lacks moisture.
Likewise, fire does not have my form, because there is no burning of grass [by it].
Because the body, which moves by means of wind, is itself devoid of substantiality, that which does not move is not wind.
Because it is devoid of substantiality, it has the aspect of emptiness; even so, it is to be viewed as such.
Like a city of illusions, although it possesses colors such as white and so forth, it is not color because it lacks substantial reality.
Although it possesses all aspects, it is not an object of vision for the immature at all times.
Why is that? It is because of the power of the demon of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*), arising from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flowing through the left and right channels; this is the certainty.
Now, the exhaustion of the five maṇḍalas is taught by the words beginning with "earth" (*pṛthivī*).

In this regard, when the yogin has become unblinking and has fixed his mind on emptiness with a wrathful gaze, at that time—indicated by the word "earth" (*sa*) on either the left or the right—when the yogin practices meditation at the moment the earth descends on the right, then [the earth] has transcended [conceptualization], because it is signless due to the turbidity of the left's conceptualization. This is for the purpose of bringing conviction to one's own mind, since it is to be personally realized by the yogin.
Because it is not produced in any way whatsoever, is marvelous, and has the nature of being without intrinsic essence, it completely abandons all collections arising from atoms.

Regarding the phrase "smoke" and so forth: it is the aspect of emptiness having the form of smoke that pervades both the exterior and the interior; this also arises without being interrupted by an appearance like a cloud.
As it has been said: "The first appears like a cloud;
the second is like smoke."
The appearance of moving water is a mirage.
The aspects of the "space-appearance" (*kha-snang*) and the "lamp" (*sgron-ma*) are well known.
These four signs, because they arise from darkness within a windowless house, are the yoga of night and the yoga of space.
As it is stated in the *Śrīguhyasamāja* and other [tantras], having reversed the first and second [stages]:
"From the mind that traverses the vajra of cessation,
the grasping of signs arises."
That sign was taught by Vajrabodhi in five aspects;
first, it has the appearance of a mirage.
The second is like smoke;
the third is the appearance of space;
the fourth is the blazing lamp.
The fifth, perpetual appearance,
is like a cloudless sky;
thus it is known.
Then, the appearance of emptiness characterized by the prior appearance of a cloudless sky is "blazing."
The appearances of the moon and the sun are well known.
The "muni" is the appearance of Rāhu; it appears like a black line.
The "great bindu" (thig le che) is that which clarifies both the moving and the non-moving; it appears in the center of a blue lunar mandala.
Since these six signs arise from looking at the cloudless sky, they constitute the daytime yoga and the yoga under the open sky.

Then, having entered into its center, one perceives the form of the Buddha, whose nature is the signless sambhogakāya, preceded by previous visions; in a single instant, it is as utterly transparent as water resting in the palm of the hand.
The perception of all aspects, such as vases, cloths, and so forth, is the luminous *citrabimba* (the manifold reflection).
Regarding the phrase "with eyes closed" and so forth:

with eyes that are half-closed— meaning both closed and not closed— the yogi perceives this very emptiness, which is free from the grasped and the grasper, in the space between [the eyes] as a non-conceptual direct perception (*yogipratyakṣa*).
That form should be meditated upon as smoke and so forth, and experienced within oneself.
Both types of yoga are also taught in the *Śrīparamādibuddhatantra*, beginning with the passage:
"From all-pervading space... and so forth.
It is also stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"the samādhi called Jewel Radiance (*ratnāloka*) and the samādhi called Jewel Lamp (*ratnapradīpa*)."
The meditative concentration called "Moonlight," the meditative concentration called "Sun-Lamp," and so forth, up to the meditative concentration called "Seeing All Aspects."
Therefore, those who seek buddhahood without doubt should cultivate the path of smoke and so forth.

If it is asked: "Since Mahāmudrā is not characterized by any of the turbidities of conceptual construction, and even meditation upon it is a mere mental imputation, how can it be called 'that which is to be meditated upon'?
It is said in response:
"Non-existent," and so forth.

According to the oral instructions, whatever meditation yogins perform upon a reflection—which is strictly devoid of both external and internal entities—is not [true] meditation because it is itself devoid of entity.

If one asks, "Since there is no difference between the conceptualization of an entity and the conceptualization of a non-entity, how is it that the meditation on a non-entity is not [mere] conceptualization?
it is said: "An entity..."
For this reason, the yogi has no conceptualizations of existence or non-existence regarding the form of emptiness.
Why is that?
Because in the form of emptiness, unexamined phenomena such as smoke and so forth are perceived directly.
The intended meaning is this:
if it were to become a cause, then at that time it would become a functional entity (*bhāva*), like a jar, a cloth, or the like.
If it were not perceived, then at that time it would be a non-entity,
like the son of a barren woman and so forth.
In this regard, because everything is seen directly without conceptual analysis, all is well-established.
In order to establish that seeing occurs without conceptual analysis, he provides a concordant illustration,
beginning with the words "as if [an image] were projected" (pra-phab).
"Phab pa" refers to what is visualized by the practitioner: a mirror, a sword, a thumb, a lamp,
the moon, and the sun.
Water,
fire, and that which has the eye as its object are not produced as substantial entities; they are not produced as phenomena belonging to a collection such as a thief or the like.
In this seeing that is non-conceptual, neither entities nor non-entities exist.
Because one perceives merely the activity and the fruit of that which lacks intrinsic reality.
Even for worldly people alone, the meaning of the non-existence of things is seen in illusions, dreams, optical illusions, and so forth.
For this very reason, it was said:
"Regarding the phrase 'of that which does not exist,' and so forth."
Furthermore, that arising of non-conceptual gnosis is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, because it acts through the perfect fulfillment of the welfare of beings in all its aspects.
Regarding the statement that the example is not established, it says: "not having seen."
In this place, the young woman saw with her eyes empowered by mantra a thief and others whom she had never seen before; thus, she was struck with wonder.

The practitioners engaged in the ritual of causing [the deity] to descend saw her, as she resided here and there, with their limited vision—that is, with eyes possessed of obscurations—as the young maiden spoke.

The intention is as follows: the yogi, whose eye of intelligence is blessed by the mantra of the instructions of the accomplished ones, beholds the supramundane reality within the sky of suchness—unmanifested like a maiden, not an object of realization for ordinary beings, and possessing the undiminished moon of bodhicitta.
Furthermore, it is said that "all conceptual elaborations have been abandoned," because what is seen by one person's eye at one time is not seen by another's eye,
and because one's own eyes are themselves covered by darkness and cloth.

By this example of blowing away [the dust], since the yogi’s direct perception is in every respect devoid of intrinsic nature, the omniscient gnosis is established, just as a young woman perceives a son in a dream that has not been born.
As it was said:
"Just as in a dream, so here that youth saw his son's birth and death."
Just as one who is born experiences aging and profound mental distress,
so too should all phenomena be understood through this analogy.
Thus it is said.
Now, the sequence of the six-limbed yoga according to the stages of the *Cakrasaṃvara* Tantra and others is taught,
beginning with the words "The state of being a yogin," and so forth.
As it is taught in the *Laghusamvara*:
"For the yogin himself, [this practice] is the supreme merit;
it is purifying and destroys negativity."
"Through mantra recitation, meditative concentration, and even bliss, one will achieve accomplishment.
Thus it is said.

Because it is said that "this [practice], such as the recitation of mantras and so forth, is not the middle way nor the sequential order," one should read the words concerning meditative concentration (dhyāna) prior to the recitation of mantras.
This is the meaning of that statement.
The three branches not explicitly mentioned are withdrawal, breath control, and recollection.
"This" refers to the sun;
"other" refers to the moon.
"'Dir' refers to the *Laghu-tantra* (the Short Tantra)."
It is taught in other tantras;
thus, it should be understood through what is taught in the *Śrī-guhyasamāja-tantra*, as stated by the venerable Ārya-Vajrapāṇi.
The glorious *Guhyasamāja* [is explained] in the eighteenth chapter of the later [tantra].
What is spoken by humans is the individual investigation of the vital breath within the reality of the *avadhūti*.
Vajra recitation is ultimate recitation.
The upward movement [of the breath] at the tip of the nose is the constancy of the vital effort (*prāṇāyāma*); when meditation reaches its ultimate perfection, the vital effort is ceased.
One should clearly visualize it as going upward from the navel as desired, until it reaches the limit of non-perception of the outward emission.
One should contemplate that there is no breath emerging from the nostrils.
In that very way, there is the protection of non-apprehension regarding others; it is understood through whatever words one desires.
The other is the hidden instruction.
"Likewise" means that.
Regarding the phrase "by reciting the mantra," *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) refers to that which is designated by the name of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ* and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the visual consciousness of the gods and so forth," the auditory consciousness of the gods and so forth are included.
The inhalation of breath is characterized by its thorough engagement.
Cessation is that which has become stable.
The emergence of the exhalation is the nature of going out; this point is established by one's own direct experience.
The definitive meaning is that which is correctly intended by great bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi; it is not an object for those with erroneous conceptions.
Otherwise, a different form [occurs] by the power of a different purpose.
Seeing one's own chosen deity means directly realizing the non-conceptual candālī.
Regarding the phrase "by means of another intentional language" (*saṃdhāyabhāṣā*): it refers to the manner of expressing contradictions toward sentient beings who desire excellence.
It is characterized by that which was explained as: "That which clearly illuminates the suchness of phenomena is what was concealed for the sake of the intended meaning."
For this reason, the *tantra* is said to have the characteristic of the six parameters; as it is stated in the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*:
"The intentional language and non-language, the provisional meaning and the definitive meaning..."
Just as with sound and what is not sound,
these are proclaimed as the six limits.
Through the application of stating contradictions to sentient beings who desire excellence, [the refutation is established].
That which clarifies the reality of phenomena was spoken with intentional meaning;
for the sake of realization by sentient beings of dull faculties,
it was clearly elucidated as a non-intentional, authentic explanation.
The extensive explanation of the meaning, according to the various realizations of the mandala and so forth, and according to the various modes of conduct.
Now, the etymologies are explained according to their actual sounds; words such as *koṭākṣa* and others have been established in the world through the external sciences.
That which was designated by the Tathāgata is proclaimed as not being according to the literal sound;
that which was spoken by the Victor as concealed reality was taught for the sake of provisional meaning.
"The definitive meaning is also explained as that which clarifies the ultimate reality.
Thus it is said.
The form of the uṣṇīṣa is the form of the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "the three realms": within the center of the great bindu, one perceives the three worlds as the nature of the sambhogakāya, appearing individually as various forms upon a black line.
"All intentions" refers to whatever is conceptualized by means of discursive thought.
Being without support means being without an object of perception.
The mirage is the second sign.
Thus it is stated in another tantra.
"First, it is like a mirage"—
this should be understood as an understanding that reverses the conventional way of things.
...up to this point.
This should also be understood from the instructions of the sublime guru, from the extensive commentary composed by the Bodhisattva,
and from one's own personal experience, through the distinction between wisdom and method.

Primarily, the five signs, which are the nature of the purification of the five elements, are thoroughly realized in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja* and other [tantras], because the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) is also taught therein.
As it is also stated in the eighteenth chapter:
"Water, fire, wind, earth,
and space— all of these,"
"It is perceived as being similar to a bodhisattva.
Thus it is said.
From its dissolution into water, there is the appearance of a mirage.
From water dissolving into fire, there is the appearance of smoke.
From the dissolution of my wind into space, there is the appearance of the sky-like manifestation.
Because the three appearances of the subtle elements appear in the sky like lamps—due to the *dharmatā* of the aggregates which appear like lamps—the aspect is that of a lamp.
The five signs are as follows: from the subsiding of natural appearances, the essence of constant luminosity, which is like a cloudless sky, is "that which is equal to a cloudless sky."
It is also said: "First, earth dissolves into water;
water dissolves into fire;
and fire dissolves into wind."
"Consciousness causes the wind to enter; consciousness itself is the limb that grasps. Then one enters the clear light. Thus it is said.
In the *Māyājāla*, it is stated that through the daytime yoga, the six signs—the essence of the purification of the six aggregates—are brought forth from space, and so forth.
In the supreme king of tantras, the *Śrīparamādibuddha*, ten signs—the essential nature of the purity of objects, sense faculties, wisdom, and method—are primarily realized.
"By these [practices]" means by those who have attained the branch of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), such as the divine eye and so forth.
By means of the application of binding, it is through the essential natures of prāṇāyāma, because they are the very continuum that binds the vital breath.
The intended meaning is that this very state is pratyāhāra (withdrawal), because it is direct perception itself—free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.
It is also said: "The gathering back, again and again, of the ten sense faculties from all their respective points of engagement is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal).
Regarding this, the detailed explanation refers both to the sense faculties and the objects of the sense faculties.
Their own engagement (*svapravṛtti*) is an engagement by way of the nature of the apprehended and the apprehender, just as they themselves are; to abide therein is "abiding in one's own engagement.
"From all" refers to the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior.
"Desires" (*kāma*) are those things which are to be desired and intensely craved, namely, forms and so forth, which are gathered again and again.
The gathering of those [objects] by the sense faculties into a single point is "retention" (*dhāraṇā*);
"again and again" means repeatedly;
this is "individual withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*). This concludes the detailed explanation of the first limb.

That which is clearly manifested as the object of vision, characterized by the expression of individual withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), is neither a functional entity (*bhāva*) nor a non-entity (*abhāva*), and it is not an imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Why is this?
Because, within the one-pointedness of the conceptual mind, one perceives past, future, and present entities without conceptualizing them.

Regarding the statement, "The branches of meditative concentration (dhyāna) are taught," it is said: By gathering the gods of the desire realm, Through union with the five Buddhas, That which is called "conceptualizing meditative concentration" Becomes fivefold: Conceptualization (vitarka), discernment (vicāra), Joy (prīti), likewise bliss (sukha), And one-pointedness of mind—these five Are the summary of meditative concentration.
The three secrets are conceptualization; Enjoying them therein is discernment.
The third is like joy;
the fourth is the gathering of bliss. When consciousness arises toward the object of knowledge, one should know one's own mind as the fifth;
it is the peaceful nature of all Buddhas.
"I abide individually in every way"— thus,
for the sake of purifying individual withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the second limb is explained in detail.
The five desires are those things that have become the objects of the sense faculties, such as form and so forth.
By "condensed" is meant being unified with the sense faculties;
the five meditative absorptions (dhyānas) refer to the eyes and so forth,
and their application is the stimulation [of those faculties] through the excellent application of the five Buddhas.
Therefore, when one conceptualizes in this manner that even form and the other [sensory objects] are the five Buddhas, that is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Furthermore, through the distinctions of investigation (*vitarka*) and so forth, it becomes fivefold;
thus, the classification by way of investigation and the rest has been explained.
Regarding the phrase "the three secrets" and so forth: the sense faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are the three secrets.

The thorough knowledge that the five sense faculties, the sense-consciousnesses, and their respective objects are all of the nature of the five Tathāgatas is what constitutes conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
That which investigates that very [reality] and is oriented toward entering into suchness (*tattva*) is like joy (*prīti*), characterized by mental gladness.
That bliss (*sukha*) which is attained through entering into suchness, characterized by extreme pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the body and so forth, is the "gathering of bliss.
Because one proceeds to the ultimate limit through such cultivation, it is "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Regarding the objects of knowledge of the six active consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth—ranging from visible forms up to the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu)—consciousness arises from the object of knowledge;
the exhaustion of that [object] is the mind’s grasped and grasper. One-pointedness of mind, characterized by the thorough knowledge of emptiness, is called "one's own mind."
Such a mind is the fourth nature of all Buddhas;
it arises as the ultimate state in which all mere appearances are one with emptiness. These are the five aspects of the second branch.
"In the sky" refers to the yoga of the night, and "in the open air" refers to the yoga of the day.
Regarding the statement, "The third limb, prāṇāyāma, shall be explained by means of the name 'the reflection of the swirling nectar' (*amṛtakuṇḍalī*) and so forth," it is said:
"The great jewel of five colors is explained as the life-force (*prāṇa*). Having visualized one's own mantra at the heart, one should place the life-force within the drop (*bindu*).
The detailed exposition of this shall now be related.
The five colors are the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
for that very reason, they are the "great jewel.
Life is vitality.
That which is performed with effort and extended for a long duration is explained as *prāṇāyāma*;
it is so intended because it must be practiced day and night through its nature of entering [the central channel] and so forth.
Having meditated on one’s own mantra upon the white lotus at the heart—that is, having placed it within the drop (*bindu*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—this is the third limb.
Thus, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is arrested at the location of the *bindu* in the form of a sphere, that is said to be "grasping" (*grāha*); this refers to the branch of grasping.
As it is said: "When the jewel of self-mastery is arrested, that which is to be grasped is called 'grasping'."
Its detailed explanation is as follows: "one's own" refers to the objects such as form and so forth;
"the senses" refers to the eyes and so forth.

When one's own [objects] and the senses have ceased and dissolved, that [state] abides therein. The "jewel," which serves as the support for the objects and the senses, is the jewel of the mind. When the vital winds (*prāṇāyāma*) have ceased and vanished together with it, whatever is to be grasped is what is apprehended.
"What is that?
It is called 'grasping only the limit of reality' (bhūtakoṭi);
this is the fourth limb."

Regarding the statement, "One should perform the recitation as a limb inseparable from the Middle Way," its explanation is: "because the vital breath does not flow through the left and right channels.

As it is said: "One should not subsist on alms while reciting; Even when alms are received, one should remain joyful. One should perform the recitation with the limbs of mantra inseparable, Enjoying all desires.
The syllables that possess distinct forms are described as "subsisting on alms."
It is called "the focal point of withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*).
That which arises from convention is called "the reality of mantra" (*mantra-tattva*).

It consists of the nature of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) regarding that which possesses the entry and abiding of mantra; the indivisible limb is the very limb of the indivisibility of suchness, the ultimate, and the Middle Way.
It is said that one should speak of the accomplishment of the recollections (anusmṛti):
"By means of the firm vajra-path, one emanates into the expanse of space; having meditated through recollection, one should emanate in that very form."

By means of the vajra path—that which is not to be traversed—one enters the clear light through the sequence of the five signs; thus, the stable and utterly pure mind should be projected into the realm of space, that is, into the world-realms, by way of the nature of the dharmakāya.

Having thus meditated upon and actualized oneself as having become luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), one should correctly emanate [the deity] through that very same sequence—the aspect of the attainment of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) which was previously reached through recollection in the form of a mirage and so forth.
Immediately following this is what is called "the five-limbed recollection."

The meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is taught with the conclusion: "That state, which consists of the essence of innate joy (*sahajānanda*), is to be described as the emptiness that is enlightenment for the bodhisattvas."

As it is said: "By the union of wisdom and method, Having gathered all things together, One should meditate on the reflection In the center through the application of the 'ball' (piṇḍa). The instantaneous perfection of primordial wisdom Is what is known by the name 'samādhi'. "All things" refers to the stable and the moving.
"By the union of wisdom and method" means abiding in the union of the conventional and the ultimate.

By means of the form of the *gong bu* (the seminal point), having unified them through the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), one should meditate upon and recognize the Great Vajradhara himself, whose nature is the union, in the midst of that which is stable and mobile. By this sequence, the instantaneous perfection of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) at that very moment is the samādhi; thus, according to the condensed sequence, this is the stage of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

Regarding the phrase "the entity is to be meditated upon," and so forth, it is stated in the *Śrī Hevajra Tantra*: "The wise one who meditates on the entity, through the thorough knowledge of non-entity—thus should Heruka be meditated upon; not by means of the thorough knowledge of an entity. This refers to the meditation on emptiness by the Great Vajradhara, who possesses the power of the ten powers, which is the realization of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects (*sarvākāra-śūnyatā*).
At night it is in darkness, and during the day it is in light.
The three times are the nature of the desire, form, and formless realms.
"In darkness" refers to the region of Avadhūtī.
Because there is no external emergence, the inhalation and exhalation are subtle;
"from whatever form" means from various reflected images;
"by looking at space" means with eyes fixed upon the intermediate sky.
The bringing of delusion to an end is the very absence of intrinsic nature;
that too is the mother,
through the internal view— that is, by viewing [reality] as the aggregates, sense bases, and so forth— is the bringing of attachment to an end.
Furthermore, the "white-clad one" (Pāṇḍaravāsinī) is the vision of the form of emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects; through this vision of passion for the co-emergent (*sahaja*),
there is hatred— that is, the very state of bringing worldly hatred to its end, which is the absence of intrinsic nature and the absence of obscuration, namely, great hatred itself.
Furthermore, she is Vajradhātvīśvarī.
That which is bliss, filled with the stainless semen itself, arises from that [bliss] through the gaze of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

By gazing toward the direction of the intermediate space, indicated by the vicinity of the nose, one attains the pride—the very state of bringing the ordinary pride to its end—which is the state of being unobscured.
Furthermore, it arises from the indestructible Brahma-voice of Māmakī, from the perfect play of the sound of indestructible great bliss.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and effort (*āyāma*) have ceased, because there is no outward movement, the limb of grasping becomes clear; and because the non-conceptual coemergent *caṇḍālī* becomes manifest, one arises from the form of the Buddha—that is, from various forms—as the stainless mandala, the mandala of stainless light.
Because jealousy toward the three worlds has been exhausted, she is Tārā.
In the six wheels, because the seminal essence (*śukra*) ascends above and the *rāja* descends below,
there arises the unassailable Brahma-voice; and because it intensely sports in supreme, immutable great bliss, it is the very end-maker of stinginess—
that is, the Mother of Diversity (*Viśvamātā*).
Thus, by means of the sequence of attaining two stages for each respective wheel, one becomes the sovereign of the twelve stages (*bhūmi*).

Specifically, when three thousand six hundred [breaths] have ceased in the secret wheel through the process of emission and entry, the two stages of *pramuditā* (the Joyous) and *vimalā* (the Stainless) are attained.
Likewise, when that same number has ceased in the navel wheel, the two stages of *prabhākārī* (the Luminous) and *arciṣmatī* (the Radiant) are attained.
In that same way, in the lotus at the heart are the two stages, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*) and the Manifest (*abhimukhī*);
in the lotus at the throat are the two stages, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgamā*) and the Immovable (*acalā*);
and in the lotus between the eyebrows are the two stages, the Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*) and the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*).
These are the five bodhisattva stages alone;
likewise, in the *uṣṇīṣa-cakra*, there are two: the stage of the Buddha’s Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā*) and the stage of the Knowledge-Endowed Vajradhara.

Thus, by counting twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, one becomes the Buddha, the Blessed One—the teacher of the Dharma without conceptualization, the lord of the twelve stages, and the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind, completely free from the three stains.
By means of this sequence, the purification of the six elements, such as earth and the rest, is shown through the realization of the six-limbed yoga.

The five eyes should be described individually as existing: "of dogs and so forth," and so on. This is due to the power of their natural qualities—that is, due to the power of the qualities of their respective lineages.

Now, that which abides at the filaments of the six lotuses of the wheels, having been rendered free from obscuration through the six-limbed yoga, is taught as the field whose nature is the six Tathāgatas, beginning with the words "without emission" (*niṣyanda*) and so forth.
Vajradhṛk is Akṣobhya;
Jinajik is Vairocana;
Ārolik is Amitābha.
*Ratnadhṛk* is Ratnasambhava; *prajñādhṛk* is Amoghasiddhi.
By these, the purification of the six aggregates is taught.

The forms of the moon and sun—the intrinsic natures of *lalanā* and *rasanā*—having dissolved and perished, the vital wind (*prāṇa*) is obstructed in both paths, namely the two nostrils; because the upward-moving (*prāṇa*) and downward-voiding (*apāna*) winds no longer go outside, one abides in the form of the five wheels.
Within the lotus, the form of emptiness becomes clearly manifest; externally, in the lotus of the woman, it is the vajra of bliss, that is, the vajra of mind or the male organ (*bola*).
"Upon awakening" means when one has been aroused by the sequence previously explained; it refers to the meaning of "the vajra having arisen.
At that time, "whatever is the melting of the moon" refers to the seminal essence (*śukra*).
Then, "the great form of the sun" enters into the support of the form of the coemergent *caṇḍālī*, and this occurs when the moon has melted.
When existence and non-existence become one—that is, when emptiness and compassion are inseparable;

when the fears of the three realms have departed—that is, when one is free from the stains of body, speech, and mind; and when it is invincible—that is, when one sports in and perfectly realizes the supreme, immutable great bliss—at that time, during the moment of the arising of great bliss.
That yogin is one who realizes the supreme state of the six-limbed yoga; he proceeds to abide firmly in the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*).
For that yogin, there is not even the slightest thing characterized by the attachment to self and other.
When the winds of *prāṇa* and *apāna* have been obstructed, the inner heat (*caṇḍālī*) blazes forth.
The moon, which is being moved and melted, proceeds toward the form of the sun and embraces it.
"Vajra" refers to the bodhicitta,
and "lotuses" refers to the wheels (cakras).
"When they have fully awakened" means when they have arisen according to the sequence previously described; it means "when that has occurred."
"Melting" means having become melted; "existing" means being here, together with the flames of the sun's form that holds the hare (the moon).
Consciousness and primordial wisdom become one when the moon and sun, together with the winds, cease and become unobscured.

That which has arisen as the supreme unchanging bliss cannot be expressed in words; therefore, because it is realized through such direct experience, its nature as the syllables *e* and *vaṃ* is taught in every respect as the very truth by means of the three [syllables] that possess expression.
The purity of the signs shall now be explained,
beginning with the words "the wheel" and so forth.
Regarding the "three realms," for the sake of maturing those who are completely deluded, there is the extremely pure wheel of Vairocana.
The jewel of Ratnasambhava is for the sake of the happiness of these very three realms of existence.
The lotus of Amitābha is the transformation of the great passion of those who possess passion through the dharma of perception free from obscuration.
"The exhaustion of afflictions" refers to the sword of Amoghasiddhi.
The "body of indivisible primordial wisdom" refers to Akṣobhyavajra.
"Severing ignorance" refers to the curved knife of the sixth family.
These six classes [of beings] possess the nature of form and so forth, which are equal in taste like space and unchanging.
It is also said: "This single Vajrasattva has arisen as this Heruka, who resembles a cloud of terrors, for the sake of maturing the malevolent ones."
Furthermore, for the sake of the bliss of those who are deluded regarding the Samaya-vijaya, [it is taught].
Ratnendriya is for those who possess suffering.
Furthermore, for those who possess attachment and cling to the lotus, it becomes a cause for their attachment.
For the purpose of destroying obstacles, Amoghasiddhi appeared with a sword in his lotus hand;
and from hatred, Vajrāṅkuśī, who is like the *Vajraśekhara* at the time of destruction, appeared as Viśvamātā.
From delusion comes Locanā; from the cause of pride comes Māmakī through supreme compassion.
From attachment comes the one called "Clad in White"; furthermore, that Lamp of the Treasury of All Virtues [arises] from envy.
"These two, which possess various forms, have arisen as all other objects and subjects.
Thus it is said.
The form of the lineage is the ordinary form.
It is the feeling of the suffering of saṃsāra and so forth.
The same applies to the future as well.
"Seen" and "unseen" refer to being obstructed and unobstructed, respectively.
"In the mental space" refers to the mind that is devoid of [ordinary] thought.
Regarding "equal bliss," it refers to unchanging bliss.
Phenomena [are established] in the expanse of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
He spoke as follows: "With hands and feet everywhere,
with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
and with ears on every side throughout the world."
"It abides pervading all," it is said.
Regarding "form," it refers to the reflected image; as for "unchanging bliss," it means that form and the other [sensory objects] are neither produced nor ceased.
"Untroubled" means that body and mind are not agitated by harshness.
That which is to be realized through primordial wisdom is the supreme unchanging awareness.
The remainder [of the verse] states that there is no other object to be apprehended that is to be realized through the doors of the sense faculties.
That which is not to be realized by the Buddhas is such because it cannot be individually realized through this very [means].
The Buddha’s consort, the illusory mother who is a diverse emanation of the Vajra-holder, is the illusory emanation of the Buddha;
Indra’s net is a magical optical illusion.
Just like the delusion of seeing space in water, it is precisely upon arising that this delusion is bestowed here.
The vajras of the [six] families are the six Tathāgatas.
The "essence of the ground" and so forth are the "essence of the earth" and so forth.
"At the time of accomplishment" means at the time when Mahāmudrā is accomplished.
"At dawn" means at the time when the first light of day appears.
It is also at midnight, because that too is indeed the time of accomplishment.
The day of the moon-possessor (the Moon) is the day of the new moon.
The siddhi of desire is the siddhi of mahāmudrā.
From the application of time, it arises from the application of three directions and three years.
The vajra-abode is the abode of suchness; it is characterized by the arising of the supreme dwelling.
Regarding the phrase "of the various tantras such as the *Śrī-ādyabuddha*," the word "etcetera" includes the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*, the *Cakrasaṃvara*, the *Hevajra*, and the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*.
Those who possess devotion toward their guru, compassion, and the noble Mañjuśrī;
who rely upon the "tube" (the central channel), whose nature is pure speech, who listen to the Dharma, and who are intensely attached [to it].
At the repeated request of that renowned one known as Śrīdhara, the supreme leader, who abides in the Dharma,
I have composed this *Ṣaḍaṅgāvaraṇa* manual.
This is the manual for the six branches of yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).
By whatever merit I have attained through these deeds, may the entire world, without exception,
attain the supreme state that is unchanging.
The *Yogāṅga-ṣaṭka-mañjarī*, a memorandum on the six branches of yoga composed by the great scholar, the Elder Sūryaśrījñāna, is hereby complete.
Translated by the great Paṇḍita from Eastern India, Śrī Vibhūticandra, at the temple of Śrī Rgya-btags in the region of Ru-lag-snying-po-'bring-mtshams.
The extent of the text of this [work] is six hundred and fifty [verses].

Furthermore, at the request of the great minister Chos grags dpal bzang po—who has faith in the system of the glorious Kālacakra and whose mental illumination has greatly expanded—the indolent witness-monk Dpal ldan blo gros brtan pa, who bears only the name of a translator, translated and finalized this through a thorough revision.
In the self-arisen [vision] of the Great Pandita, the Moon-Yogin, |||
Because it was translated only partially for the sake of the *’ol* (phonetic transcription),...
Blo gros brtan pa translated the words and meaning literally.
By this merit, may all beings swiftly attain omniscience.
May this bring benefit to a vast multitude of wandering beings!

Although there appear to be many points where doubt arises regarding the meaning and numerous inaccuracies in the terminology of the words, I have composed this out of a love for the view of reality itself, as it is a source of great confidence.
Thus, the second assembly of the request is completed.

All auspiciousness! In the sphere of one's own space (*svākāśadhātu*), he abides as peace, emptiness, and compassion. By means of that [abiding], wherever it may be, together with its latent predispositions (*savāsanā*), there is the universal image (*viśvabimba*) within the sphere of one's own space, which is self-illuminating. *Lokeśvara* (Lord of the World) is *śukra* (the pure/white), for the sake of reverence; "for the sake of reverence" (*sādarārtha*) is a compound where the object of reverence follows the word for reverence (*sādarārtha*). Afterwards, there is the compound of the subsequent term (*paścāt samāsa*), specifically the descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). "The great festival of the jewel of the excellent path" (*sumārgaratnamahāmahā*): *mahā* refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and she is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). He who possesses her is thus [described]. He whose great passion (*mahārāga*) consists of non-referential compassion (*anālaṃbakaruṇā*) is likewise [described]. Finally, this is a determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*).

When the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is abandoned, because there is no longer any obstruction, the light of knowledge—the direct perception of the yogi—proceeds everywhere unimpeded, like the rays of the sun in a sky free from clouds and other veils. Through the yoga of non-abiding, which is joined in pairs and grasps at nothing whatsoever, even a slight [clinging] brings about the suffering of the five desires as small as a sesame seed or a mustard grain; inevitably, the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) holds that "something exists," while the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) leads to a fall into the far-reaching abyss. There exists the universal image in all its aspects, a form of mindless-mind (*acittacitta*).

That mind which is "no-mind" is here the pure mind, whose nature is emptiness and compassion, like a reflection in a maiden’s mirror. It does not possess the characteristic of form because atoms do not exist; nor does it lack the characteristic of form because it exists within emptiness. Therefore, conventional reality has the form of emptiness, and emptiness has the form of conventional reality. Because it transcends worldly analogies, that mind which is no-mind exists—free from the characteristics of the phenomena of eternalism and nihilism, and inseparable from emptiness and compassion. This is according to ultimate truth.

Because of the difference between the two minds, the non-dual Vajrayoga—which transcends existence and non-existence and is the exhaustion of being and non-being—is suchness; this is the word of the Tathāgata. Because it is without succession (*niranvaya*), it is the Ornament (*alaṃkāra*), the Application of a Different Meaning (*arthāntaranyāsa*), the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), the negation (*niṣedha*), the injunction (*vidhi*), the poison of existence (*bhavaviṣa*), and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). It is endowed with the *Ādibuddhatantra*, the King of Tantras (*Tantrarāja*), the *Ādibuddha*, the [alphabet] beginning with *A* (*akādi*), Vajrahūṃ, Māyā, conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), configuration (*saṃsthāna*), mandalas, the rite of pacification (*śāntikarman*), the meditation on conceptualization (*vikalpabhāvanā*), the mirror-image divination (*pratisenā*), reality (*tattva*), the Tathāgata, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the Vajra-drop (*vajrabindu*), the drop (*bindu*), the Vajra, and the non-yogi Tathāgata.

Rāhu, Kālāgni, Vīrakrama, Svādhiṣṭhānakrama, the syllable, Pūrṇā, Ghūrmā, Oddā, the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, the meditation on the eon (*kalpabhāvanā*) as the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), the lalanā and rasanā channels—because it bestows unsurpassed bliss, this is the desired Fourth Yoga.

Through the cessation of twenty-one thousand breaths, one attains the supreme syllable (paramākṣara). By the departure and arrival of passion and the absence of passion, [one realizes] the Great Passion (mahārāga), which is devoid of the letters and free from the perfection of all forms, both white and black.
It is neither of the nature of existence nor non-existence; it is called "neither existence nor non-existence."
This third yoga is knowledge arising from the vision of all that is knowable;
because it is the cause for producing the bliss of the world and because it accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings,
it is "Samantabhadra" (Universally Auspicious) due to its auspiciousness in the beginning, middle, and end.
Due to the absence of the conceptualization of Māra and evil, it is external to sound, speech, and mind;
there is no recitation, vocalization, resonance, or the like, as it is devoid of sound.
Because its intrinsic nature is the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*), it is the Great Sound (*mahānāda*) together with speech.
This second yoga is the Great Sound because of the functioning of its own nature; due to that nature, there is the exhaustion of the obscurations of the four bodies (*caturkāya*).
Through the maintenance of its stable form, the gold of the noble bodhicitta [is obtained].
Because its intrinsic nature is the union of emptiness and compassion, it is the Śrī Kālacakra-vajra;
likewise [it is so] for the mantra-holders and vidyādhara-s.
To the practitioners established in the Vajrayāna,
who contemplate the meaning of reality and are free from defilement.
The mind of patience abiding in the three times;
the giver of purification to disciples; the liberator from the fear of hell; the one who practices the holy life; the Vajra-staff.
Vajrasattva, the slayer of the four Māras,
arisen from the earth.
The Guru is the Buddha, the Guru is the Dharma, and the Guru is the Sangha as well, the Holder of the Vajra.
The glorious Guru alone is the sole cause.
The support for the deity is twofold: direct perception and inference.
Through union with reality, the direct perception is like the sky and the stars, equal to the many reflections of the enjoyment body.
Inference that is devoid of direct perception is like a corpse;

being bereft of reality and constructed by mere conceptualization, it is appropriate for those whose intellects are unrefined, such as beginners in the practice of drawing mandalas and the like, but not for the lords of yogis.
The support for the deities consists of two types: direct perception and inference, which depend upon the dispositions of sentient beings.
Among these two, for yogins, this [perception] is direct perception because of its union with reality, like the stars in the sky.

At the very beginning, at the onset of vision, the yogi perceives the universal image— the three worlds of the three times— as equal to a row of stars, as equal to the many reflections of the enjoyment body (*bhogakāya*), and as like an illusion or a dream.
Then, apart from the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), by the power of the supernormal powers he has attained, he presides over the divine eye;
then, by the power of the strength of freedom from passion (*vītarāga*) he has attained, he presides over it through the Buddha-vision;
then, by the power of the bodhisattva-strength he has attained, he presides over the eye of knowledge (*jñānacakṣus*).
Then, through the vision of a Buddha, one consecrates all-encompassing reality as free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Those who are truly blind produce [this state] through another birth; such is the method of meditating on reality.
Through the non-arrival of the arrival of the scriptures of reality, consciousness is like a corpse.
Just as [a form] created by imagination and devoid of reality is shown in paintings and the like,
so too has service with the five nectars and the four vajras been demonstrated for the application of meditation by yogins of dull intellect and beginners.
Accomplishment is attained through the recitation of mantras and so forth; through withdrawal and other means, there is the practice of meditation on the nectar arising from the vajra-lotus,
which is conjoined with the lotus of the three secrets.
When it is performed with jewels and so forth, and when the entrance into the inexhaustible has been attained, then, when there is purity of wisdom,

the great accomplishment (mahāsādhana) is certain; it is perfected through subtle yoga by means of the single method of practice, while the service (sevā) is performed with the five nectars and other substances.

The five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—feces, urine, and so forth—are external; therein, "and so forth" refers to [the meat of] cows, dogs, and the like, which should be consumed for the sake of satisfaction.

The five nectars are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Ultimately, therein "and so forth" refers to the five lamps, which are the five sense faculties. In that regard, one must abandon all hope and the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) toward the body and its enjoyments.

Externally and internally, externally and internally: the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are the aggregates (*skandha*); the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*) are the sense faculties (*indriya*). Form (*rūpa*) is the body (*kāya*), blood (*rakta*) is perception (*saṃjñā*), semen (*śukra*) is feeling (*vedanā*), the tongue (*jihvā*) is the elephant (*hastin*), flesh (*māṃsa*) is the eye (*cakṣus*), the nose (*ghrāṇa*) is formation (*saṃskāra*), urine (*mūtra*) is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the ear (*śrotra*) is the general service (*sāmānyasevā*). Likewise, the "born child" (*jātabāla*) is Vajra; likewise, the "mature" (*praudha*) is the root (*mūla*); likewise, the "middle child" (*madhyabāla*) is the soft service (*mṛdu sevā*). The Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*) is the "born child"; the "born child" is the awakening to emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*), the seizing of the lunar drop (*candrabindugrahaṇa*), the arising of the image (*bimbotpatti*), and the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*). Firm is the near-attainment (*upasādhana*). The Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) is the "middle child"; the accomplishment of the vital breath (*prāṇaniṣpatti*) is the soft attainment (*mṛdu sādhana*). The Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*) is the youth (*kumāra*); firm is the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*). The Gnosis-Vajra (*jñānavajra*) is the mature (*praudha*), the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the twelve aspects, the sixteen aspects, and the twenty aspects. Vitality (*prāṇa*) and downward movement (*apāna*) are the *Paramādibuddha*. The central channel (*madhyamā*) is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Empowered is the vajra-possession (*vajrāveśa*), Vajrasattva, free from sense objects, in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*). The aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*) is the digit (*kalā*); the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the universal image (*viśvabimba*); the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*); the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

The ten states of desire, non-abiding nirvāṇa, wisdom, reasoning, existence, investigation, delight, and immovable bliss (8.3). Caṇḍālī, vital breath, bodhicitta, joy, and physical pliancy (267). The action seal (*karmamudrā*) is the bliss of emission; the knowledge seal (*jñānamudrā*) is the bliss of vibration; the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is the bliss of non-vibration (8.4). They become unified as one (8.5). Furthermore, from that arises the empty image; from that, purity; from that purity, mastery (269).

The twelve *kalās* at the end of the other [channel] are the *uṣṇīṣa*; through the upward path of the *apāna*, by the striking together of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* at the *uṣṇīṣa* and the utterance of the syllable *dhūṃ*, there is immobilization (*stambhana*) at the navel. (8.7.1) By the gaze of Vighnāntaka—Vighnāntaka being Amṛtakundalī.
His gaze is fixed on the forehead, the place of nectar.
Through this gaze, his realization (*abhisaṃbhava*) becomes sixfold; for upon realization, by means of the path of nectar, he proceeds to the gaze of Vighnāntaka.
The lunar drop (*candrabindu*) is produced from wisdom (*prajñā*).
The action seal (karmamudrā) and the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā):
here, by means of the desire for wisdom (prajñā), the lunar drop (candrabindu) is emitted—
that drop of bodhicitta which is produced from wisdom.
It enters into union with the three immutables.
8.7.3 Being non-dual and without perception, it exists through immutable bliss;
existing through immutable bliss, the single moment of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is without perception.
Through unchanging bliss, the one-pointedness of mind is attained.
That which is called Māra is the mind of sentient beings in saṃsāra, defiled by habitual tendencies; that which is called Buddhahood is the mind free from the habitual tendencies of saṃsāra. 274 10

"Space," and so forth: those whose minds have attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with the sky perceive, through the yoga of night, four signs from the void—smoke, mirage, fireflies, and a lamp—and then, through the yoga of day, six signs in the cloudless firmament: flame, moon, sun, black jewel, lightning, and the blue lunar radiance. Thus, there are ten signs. In the center of the great bindu (*mahābindu*) among them, one perceives the Buddha-image, the vision of all forms such as pots and cloths, which is empty of external objects and consists of the non-conceptual *saṃbhogakāya* appearing in manifold ways. In a single moment, there is the manifestation of all appearances like an illusion: the earth element dissolves into water, and water dissolves into fire.
Fire dissolves into the subtle element, and wind dissolves into the mind.
The mind dissolves into the mental factors, and the mental factors into ignorance;
that too goes into the luminous clarity—this is the cessation within the three realms of existence.

His cognition is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*); he does not see with other eyes, such as those produced from the forehead and so forth, nor even with his own eyes at other times, because he does not see [them] then.

Just as a maiden might see within this bed that a son has been born—being exceedingly joyful when he is born and remaining dejected when he is dead—in the same way, one should know all phenomena through this simile. (CST I, 9cd–10ab)
Through the recitation of mantras, Buddhahood is attained by means of skillful methods. The nature of the yogi is twofold: mundane and supramundane.
Of these two, the supramundane nature of the yogi is Buddhahood;
it is supreme merit because of the fulfillment of the accumulation of merit.
It is pure and destroys evil because it is fully endowed with the equipment of knowledge;
through mantra-recitation, meditation, and ease,
the nature of a yogi is accomplished by means of this skillful method.
"It is accomplished" is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
This six-limbed yoga is one in which the first two [limbs] are inverted and the limbs are separated by one.
Although stated, it is understood through its connection even with what has not been explicitly stated.
Just as when "the sun" is mentioned, the moon is also [implied] by its internal power, because dharmas are mutually dependent; for when one member of a pair is named, the other is expected.
Therefore, in this context, three things are to be understood: that which is stated in the middle, as well as the first and the last.
For this is the established conclusion transmitted through the lineage:

if there is an appearance of intentional terminology (*sandhābhāsa*) according to the sequence of recitation found in the tantras—consisting of meditation, mantra-recitation (*japa*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), bliss, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—it should be understood as such when it occurs within the tradition.
In this *Bodhisattvākṛtākhyāna*, we have relied upon direct knowledge (*jñāna*).
Through the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth, three [stages] are to be known, as well as the three that are condensed.
Because of its six-limbed nature, it is taught in another tantra; in the *Samājottara*, the Blessed One speaks of the six-limbed yoga: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and then reflection (*cintanā*).
Breath control, concentration, mindfulness, and likewise meditative absorption.
Therefore, withdrawal (pratyāhāra) precedes contemplation;
breath control (prāṇāyāma) precedes the recitation of mantras;
and through the recitation of mantras, concentration (dhāraṇā) and the binding of the vital breath (prāṇabandhana) are achieved.
First is the recollection of bliss;
concentration is likewise through bliss alone.
By means of these six factors, the yogi attains Buddhahood, which is his true nature.
The worldly nature is attained by beginner yogins, or the worldly fruit up to the Akaniṣṭha realm is attained through mantra recitation, withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
meditation, and a mind immersed in contemplation of the form of the maṇḍala.
Through the melting of bliss by means of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and the gnosis-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and in accordance with what is attained in the mundane world,
the yogi attains through both the mundane and supramundane nature of a yogi.
Therein, by following that which has been attained through the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), he attains the supramundane nature of a yogi.
Regarding the six limbs of yoga, here *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) consists of the removal of the cognition of the eyes and other senses from external objects such as form,
the directing of the cognition of the divine eyes and other senses toward their own [inner] objects, and the vision of the emptiness of all phenomena.
In emptiness, withdrawal is said to arise as the limb [of yoga] like the form of an illusory image, because of the vision of the images of the three worlds;
that which is seen through emptiness is the phenomenon (dharma), and its contemplation is known as mindfulness (smṛti).
Investigation is the perception of existence; establishment is the ascertainment of existence.
Delight of the mind toward all things arises from contemplating all objects;
the contemplation-factor regarding the state of happiness in all things is fivefold.
Now, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the cessation of the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels;
it is the continuous movement of the wind within the central path, the *avadhūtī*,
after having filled and retained the wind, and then released it through the *avadhūtī*.

Filling is performed by the syllable *oṃ* alone, retention by the syllable *hūṃ* alone, and emission by the syllable *āḥ*. Thus, breath control (*prāṇasaṃyama*) comes to possess the nature of the moon, Rāhu, and the sun. Next is retention (*dhāraṇā*), which is the internal entry of the vital breath into the spheres of Mahendra, as well as into the spheres of Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu, and into the heart, throat, and forehead.
The entry of the vital breath into the bindu and the retention [of it] as the great image of the uṣṇīṣa— the yogi should first practice this;
he should then practice the image of Amṛtakuṇḍalī when [the breath] is near.
One should practice the visualization of the deity's form when the time for meditation is near;
however, at the great time [of death], one should practice the visualization of the Blessed Buddha. Free from all conceptual constructions, one should pass the day in such a state of realization.
If they were not produced therein, my words would be false;
for even by one whose senses are overcome, the three realms are accomplished by the wise,
and even by the sense-faculties such as the eye, the three realms— the image of the Buddha— are realized.
The lunar disk consists of *ānanda*, *paramānanda*, *viramānanda*, and *sahajānanda*; [the four moments of] *vicitra*, *vipāka*, *vimarda*, and *kṣaya* (the supreme unchanging bliss);

the mantras; the practitioner (*sādhaka*); the state to be meditated upon (*bhāvya*) as non-existence (*abhāva*); the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatābhāvanā*); the human (*nara*); the limbs (*aṅga*); hatred (*dveṣa*); and the motionless bliss (*niḥspandānanda*).

Vajradhṛk, Ārolik, Prajñādhrk; in the Brahmāṇḍa is Vajrasattva, the sixth, the supreme bliss (paramānanda), full of the sixteen joys. His head is joined with the vajra; he holds the wisdom (jñāna) that is empty by nature. The sixteenth, the supreme digit of the moon, appears at the end of the day of the full moon. The Vidyā makes the vajra; having dissolved into the lotus, the lunar goddess (śaśinī) enters the center of the solar disc and pervades the three-fold delusion. Then the yogi attains the supreme state. When the prāṇa and apāna are restrained, the one who moves in the moon (the lunar essence) should enter the solar disc. When the vajra is awakened, it dissolves into the lotus; with the flames of the solar disc, the moon and sun are suppressed. Consciousness (vijñāna) and wisdom (jñāna) become one with the wind. Thus, thus, thus it exists everywhere. The pure jewel is the bliss of these; the lotus is of the nature of passion; the sword is the cutter, the destroyer of all afflictions (kleśas). The vajra is indivisible, the single wisdom that cuts through the knowledge of cutting. This sword is where the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) truly dissolve; where birth-form (jātirūpa) dissolves; where the great form (mahārūpa) and the suffering of saṃsāra dissolve; where the great sensation (mahāvedanā) and the wandering of saṃsāra dissolve; where the perception of the vajra, the formation of the vajra, and dreams dissolve; where consciousness and ignorance dissolve. Supreme wisdom is Vairocana; the six supreme Victors are the six families. Others [are distinguished] by the divisions of earth, fire, wind, space, water, and the peaceful. Locanā is earth, Māmakī is water, Pāṇḍarā is fire, Tāriṇī is wind, and Vajradhātvīśvarī is Viśvamātā. The eye sees the visible and invisible form; the mind sees the sky. The ear hears what is distant as if it were near. The nose smells all fragrances, the cause of supreme bliss. The tongue always gives pleasure through its own lunar nectar. The organ of touch always touches that which grants supreme delight; this is the faculty of the supreme joy. The Bodhisattvas together with their consorts are the subjects and objects of the senses, established in the six families. The image of the single Victors is the field of action, pure, unborn, without limit, born of supreme bliss, stainless, and the domain of wisdom. By the power of the Buddha’s intellect—which is conceptual, endowed with incomparable qualities, and like Indra’s net—it exists within the three worlds in various forms among the Victors, gods, and men. At the time of accomplishment, the wrathful Buddhas and these six Vajra goddesses, such as Bhūmigarbhā and the others, are seen by the yogi in the sky. Whether at dawn on the full moon or at midnight, whatever lotus, consciousness, array of flowers, or rain of jewels falls upon the ground at that time—through brief, detailed, and further explanations, the Lord has most clearly explained the Vajra-word in the *Ādibuddha*. Or rather, the path of the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is the path of manifestation through signs such as smoke. Holding the void one-pointedly in one place, one should examine it for one day according to the Lord’s instruction. In the *Paramādibuddha*, the Vajra-word here in the Mantra system is twofold: one is by worldly convention, and the second is from the ultimate perspective (paramārtha).

According to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), the vajra-word bestows the accomplishment of the *samaya* in rites such as slaying; according to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the fourth vajra-word likewise bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Thus, the vajra-word is "hidden" in all the kings of tantras—it does not appear explicitly—and must be understood through the lineage of the gurus. As it is said in the words of the Tathāgata:
"The Buddha, the Dharma, the Assembly, the Element, Awakening, the Qualities, and finally, the Buddha-activity."
This is, in brief, the body of the entire treatise: the seven vajra-points.
